title: Clearing eviction queue can be unnecessarily slow for large buffer pool sizes

labels.name: type: perf bug
labels.description: Issues related to a regression in the performance

body:
### Description

At the end of every checkpoint, we currently loop through the entire eviction queue and remove evicted candidates regardless of how much data was checkpointed. With large buffer pool sizes (100s of GB) this can take over a second even if we are checkpointing very little data, so we should optimize this if we can.

title: Bug: Export function Does Not Provide A Way To Set Delimiters
body:
### Kuzu version

v.0.10.1

### What operating system are you using?

macOS 15 Sequoia

### What happened?

Relates to #5550

Consider in `dataset/ldbc-sf01/Forum.csv` the lines 

```
893353212271|Group for Ferdinand_II,_Holy_Roman_Emperor in Chennai|20120420114423625
481036351856|Group for Ferdinand_II,_Holy_Roman_Emperor in Chennai|20110318075857635
```

When we export this dataset in Kuzu we get
```

481036351856,"Group for Ferdinand_II,_Holy_Roman_Emperor in Chennai",20110318075857635
```

The delimiter is not preserved. In this instance the choice of the `|` delimiter is critical. Without it, this turns into a copy exception when trying to import the database back into Kuzu. This seems to be a limitation of the export db function since I cannot find any ways to set delimiters.

I do not think it is reasonable to try to preserve the delimiter, although it maybe useful to be able to set the delimiter in the export function.

2. Use the export function to export the contents of the database
3. Attempt to use the import function to retrieve the contents of the database (from docs `The IMPORT DATABASE command can only be executed on an empty database`). This will result in a copy exception.

title: Feature: Add a concat with separator text function
body:
### API

Other (Cypher)

### Description

When creating unique string ID columns on the fly from existing columns (useful when the user doesn't already have a unique value column that could serve as the primary key beforehand), adding separators between the string values 

Currently, we can only concatenate a list of strings without any separators.
```
kuzu> return concat("university", " of", " waterloo");
┌──────────────────────────────────┐
│ CONCAT(university, of, waterloo) │
│ STRING                           │
├──────────────────────────────────┤
│ university of waterloo           │
└──────────────────────────────────┘
(1 tuple)
(1 column)
```

### DuckDB has a `concat_ws` function

We should add [this function](https://duckdb.org/docs/stable/sql/functions/text.html#concat_wsseparator-string-) that DuckDB has, so that we can do the following:

```cypher
RETURN concat_ws('_', 'University', 'of', 'Waterloo');
```
should give:
```
University_of_Waterloo
```

code_snippets.code:
kuzu> return concat("university", " of", " waterloo");
┌──────────────────────────────────┐
│ CONCAT(university, of, waterloo) │
│ STRING                           │
├──────────────────────────────────┤
│ university of waterloo           │
└──────────────────────────────────┘
(1 tuple)
(1 column)
RETURN concat_ws('_', 'University', 'of', 'Waterloo');
University_of_Waterloo

title: Bug: Multihop traversals are inefficient on large scale datasets
body:
### Kuzu version

v0.9.0

### What operating system are you using?

MacOS Sequoia 15.5

### What happened?

Running queries on large datasets with multihop traversals is not performant. Discussion discord is [here](https://discord.com/channels/1196510116388806837/1349045216623067157)
The dataset can be replicated [here](https://github.com/kuzudb/kuzu/issues/4953#issuecomment-2708380062)
I sent the database to @prrao87 as well.

## Nonperformant query
```cypher
MATCH (s:Sub{sic:6311})<-[:FILED_IN]-(n:Num{tag:'NetIncomeLoss'})-[c:COMPONENT_OF* SHORTEST 1..10 
    (r,n | where not r.is_prior_value)]->(n2:Num)
    return n.id, n2.id
```

The above query just hangs after a while. Executing on a smaller subset of the data works but is long relative to the number of records obtained.

## Comment from Discord
"Hi @Luxord, you are right, the performance overhead indeed comes from the SINGLE_SHORTEST_PATH. Let me explain here, internally we form a parallel BFS computation which requires pre-allocating a dense array with size up to number of nodes. In your case there are 300M nodes so this initialization takes about 100ms (on my M1 pro mbp). And compute 155 source nodes (as u can see in the profiler) takes about 100ms * 155 ~= 15s.
We should be able to optimize this because in your use a case a dense data structure is not needed. The connectivity seems to be pretty sparse. So we can save that initialization overhead until the frontier gets bigger.
Though this is not a one day fix. I might need a few days to get this out."



### Are there known steps to reproduce?

_No response_

code_snippets.code:
MATCH (s:Sub{sic:6311})<-[:FILED_IN]-(n:Num{tag:'NetIncomeLoss'})-[c:COMPONENT_OF* SHORTEST 1..10 
    (r,n | where not r.is_prior_value)]->(n2:Num)
    return n.id, n2.id

title: Check for duplicate fields in structs

title: Bug: implement checks for number of fields in a struct / union
body:
Currently we don't check the number of fields in a struct. While it's very unlikely anyone will need > 2^16 fields, we should still add checks, since the behaviour is buggy for structs that large

Also, at the moment, `struct_field_idx_t` and `union_field_idx_t` are defined as `uint16_t` while the return type for `getNumFields()` is a `uint64_t`. Ideally they should be the same type.

Test cases:

[test_passes.txt](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/20953264/test_passes.txt)

[test_fails.txt](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/20953265/test_fails.txt)

We should either expect both test cases to work, or for the second one to throw an error about the number of fields.

NOTE: you need https://github.com/kuzudb/kuzu/pull/5607 to run the test cases

title: Feature: Import process warnings
body:
### API

Python

### Description

Importing a data file using the COPY command with ", IGNORE_ERRORS=true" masks data issues that may be difficult to identify after the processing is complete. 

When in ", IGNORE_ERRORS=false" mode an exception thrown (presumably) terminates the import transaction leaving no data imported into the GDBMS for the entire data file. finding parsing issues in this mode may require numerous reruns to identify/fix any issues.

my suggestion would be to console log any parsing issues "found but ignored" as warnings when the import is in ", IGNORE_ERRORS=true" mode.

title: Feature: Support returning two columns with the same name
body:
### API

Python

### Description

We currently don't support returning two columns with the same name.
For example:
```
kuzu> return 1,1;
Error: Binder exception: Multiple result column with the same name 1 are not supported.
```
However, both duckdb and postgres support such grammar:

title: Refactor how UUIDs are stored internally
body:
The physical type of a UUID is a signed `int128_t`. Internally, we store it with the MSB flipped. This is so we can sort lexicographically correctly when using `ORDER BY` (i.e. UUIDs with a `1` as the MSB will appear first, since it is flipped to `0` and interpreted as positive). We flip the bit back only for the `toString` and `fromString` methods.

This took a while to notice when implementing UUID creation for the Java API.

To avoid further confusion, we shouldn't store UUIDs with the MSB flipped, rather we should just flip the bit whenever we want to sort. Alternatively, we can implement a `uint128_t` type and use that for UUIDs.

title: Feature: Support for H3 (geospatial) indexing

labels.name: type: feature
labels.description: New features or missing components of existing features

body:
### API

Other

### Description

The [H3 index](https://h3geo.org/) is a (mostly) hexagonal grid that offers indexing over existing geographical coordinate systems. Its positioning is fixed and it can therefore translate a given point (say in the WGS84 CRS) to a grid reference that is basically a very long number. For example: [Lat./Lng.: 51.50413559, -0.01645872472 is cell 8a194ad2291ffff](https://h3geo.org/#hex=8a194ad2291ffff).

One very useful application of H3 is in performing quick distance calculations. This is because, the adjacency of the hexagons at different scales is known and therefore, instead of performing relative [great circle distance calcluations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great-circle_distance), it is much faster to perform relative [distance calculations through the use of the index](https://h3geo.org/docs/api/traversal/).

If Kuzu had this ability (as an Extension), even if it was just for geographical points, then it would also be possible to take into account geospatial data in queries to order results given their relative distance from a specific point and aggregate counts of "events" over the grid itself.

title: Bug: kuzu_connection_query has a lot of segfault potential for callers
body:
### Kuzu version

v0.10.0

### What operating system are you using?

Fedora 40 X86_64

### What happened?

Royi asked me to report a issue though perhaps he meant it as a documentation or feature issue and not a bug.  We were having a discord discussion about the behavior of `kuzu_connection_query` and whether or not users are expected to call ` kuzu_query_result_get_error_message` when the return value is KuzuError.   Here are some notes I'd written on the issue from an API perspective, with specific callouts to some of the problems in `kuzu_connection_query`.

---

Many of the Kuzu APIs have signatures like this:

    `kuzu_state result = some_kuzu_call(... args ..., some_kuzu_struct* output_argument)`

Where kuzu_state is basically zero for success, one for KuzuError
and output_argument is really inout, pass a pointer to a struct that _may_
be filled in by the call.

There are some unanswered questions about the protocols that follow.

1. Will the output argument be modified if kuzu_state == KuzuError?
2. If the output argument is used across multiple calls, does it need to be
   re-initialized by each call?

Unfortunately the answer to each question seems to be yes, which put a burden on
callers because:

- Callers potentially need to examine the output parameter regardless
  of the kuzu_state return values.
- Callers aren't advised about whether they need to reinitialize the in-out
  parameter, possibly resulting stale state problems.

Let's look at kuzu_query_connection as an example.
```
    typedef struct {
        void* _query_result;
        bool _is_owned_by_cpp;
    } kuzu_query_result;

    /**
     * @brief Executes the given query and returns the result.
     * @param connection The connection instance to execute the query.
     * @param query The query to execute.
     * @param[out] out_query_result The output parameter that will hold the result of the query.
     * @return The state indicating the success or failure of the operation.
     */
    KUZU_C_API kuzu_state kuzu_connection_query(kuzu_connection* connection, const char* query,
        kuzu_query_result* out_query_result);
```

In the simplest case the caller might have:
```
    kuzu_connection conn ;
    kuzu_query_result query_result ;
    kuzu_state result = kuzu_connection_query(&conn, "CREATE ...", &result)
```

`kuzu_connection_query` looks like this:
```
    kuzu_state kuzu_connection_query(kuzu_connection* connection, const char* query,
        kuzu_query_result* out_query_result) {
        if (connection == nullptr || connection->_connection == nullptr) {
          return KuzuError;                                     // (1)
        }
        try {
            auto query_result =
                static_cast<Connection*>(connection->_connection)->query(query).release();
            if (query_result == nullptr) {
                return KuzuError;                               // (2)
            }
            out_query_result->_query_result = query_result;     // (3)
            out_query_result->_is_owned_by_cpp = false;
            if (!query_result->isSuccess()) {
                return KuzuError;                               // (4)
            }
            return KuzuSuccess;
        } catch (Exception& e) {
            return KuzuError;                                   // (5)
        }
    }
```

So there are 4 cases where the function returns KuzuError. However only one
of them in any way initializes or sets the out_query_result content
(marker 3).

If users are supposed to call kuzu_query_result_get_error_message when
KuzuError is returned and don't take extra steps to provide content of the output struct beforehand, then the content of out_query_result is unknown (initialized to potentially anything for an on-stack struct, for example).

The kuzu_query_result content would also be stale if the structure were
reused in repeated calls to kuzu_connection_query without setting them to
some known state, so if the intent is that users should call
`kuzu-query-result-get-error-message` when the return value is KuzuError,
the looks like segfault conditions to me.

It would probably be best to

- set the inout members to known state in all APIs using inout parameters.
- document the semantics of the inout parameters w.r.t. kuzu_state return
  values

Related wishlist items:
It would be really useful if the APIs could give error message
information _any_ time `kuzu_state` is `KuzuError`.  Trying to understand
why some functions return KuzuError is an enigma (even with access to the
source code), such as the values of `kuzu_system_config` on
`kuzu_database_init`, which took me a day to get working because it
silently rejected so many of my options and combinations of options.
And of course if you're providing a solution for someone who doesn't have
the kuzu github source close at hand and know how to read it, a useful error
message is a huge step up.

Second kuzu_database_init wishlist item:, it would be
good if the C API docs indicated that the `database_path` argument must name
a _directory_, and not a file, for disk-based databases.



### Are there known steps to reproduce?

_No response_

title: Bug: KuzuDB v0.10.0 (Python API, WSL2): Tables and vector indexes created and checkpointed in one process are not found by a new process opening the same database
body:
### Kuzu version

0.10.0 (Python Client and CLI)

### What operating system are you using?

WSL2 (Ubuntu 22.04 on Windows 11), Python 3.11

### What happened?

**Problem Description:**

When using KuzuDB v0.10.0 in a WSL2 (Ubuntu 22.04, Python 3.11) environment, we are encountering a cross-process schema visibility issue. 
A "writer" Python process successfully performs the following:
1. Creates a new KuzuDB database directory.
2. Copies the `vector.kuzu_extension` (for v0.10.0) to `DB_PATH/extensions/`.
3. Opens the database (`kuzu.Database(DB_PATH, read_only=False)`).
4. Gets a connection (`kuzu.Connection(db)`).
5. Executes `LOAD EXTENSION 'vector';` successfully on the connection.
6. Creates node tables (e.g., `ExtractedEntity`) and relationship tables using explicit transactions (`BEGIN TRANSACTION; ... COMMIT;`).
7. Loads data into these tables.
8. Creates an HNSW vector index (e.g., `CALL CREATE_VECTOR_INDEX('ExtractedEntity', 'idx_name', 'embedding_prop')`) in auto-transaction mode.
9. Verifies within the same writer process and connection that the tables and indexes exist using `CALL SHOW_TABLES() RETURN *;` and `CALL SHOW_INDEXES() RETURN *;`.
10. Executes `CHECKPOINT;` successfully.
11. Attempts to ensure resources are fully released using `del conn_obj`, `del db_obj`, `gc.collect()`, and `time.sleep()`.

However, after the "writer" process terminates, a new, independent "reader" Python process (or the KuzuDB CLI v0.10.0) attempting to open the *same database directory*:
1. Can successfully open the database (`kuzu.Database(DB_PATH, read_only=False)` without lock file errors after the writer process has finished and its `.lock` file might have been handled/renamed).
2. Can successfully execute `LOAD EXTENSION 'vector';` on a new connection.
3. **Crucially, when executing `CALL SHOW_TABLES() RETURN *;`, the result is an empty set, indicating that the tables created by the writer process are not visible.**
4. Consequently, any subsequent operations targeting these tables or their indexes fail, typically with a "Table does not exist" error.

**Expected Behavior:**

We expect that after the "writer" process successfully creates tables, loads data, creates indexes, executes `CHECKPOINT;`, and properly closes the database, a subsequent "reader" process (either Python API or CLI) opening the same database directory should be able to see and query these persisted schema objects and data.

**Actual Behavior:**

The "reader" process (both our Python verification scripts and the KuzuDB CLI tool) consistently fails to find the tables (e.g., `ExtractedEntity`) created by the "writer" process, even though the writer process internally confirmed their creation and executed a checkpoint. `CALL SHOW_TABLES() RETURN *;` in the reader process returns an empty result.

### Are there known steps to reproduce?

Yes, the issue can be reliably reproduced using two separate Python scripts operating on the same database directory.

**Environment Setup:**

*   KuzuDB Version: `0.10.0` (Python Client and a pre-compiled Linux x86_64 CLI)
*   Python Version: `3.11`
*   Operating System: WSL2 (Ubuntu 22.04 on Windows 11)
*   Ensure `vector.kuzu_extension` for v0.10.0 is available. The scripts below use an environment variable `KUZU_VECTOR_EXTENSION_PATH` to locate it, or default to `~/.kuzu/extension/0.10.0/linux_amd64/vector/libvector.kuzu_extension`.

**Script 1: `create_kuzu_db.py` (Simulates the writer process)**
(Run this script first to create the database, table, and index)

```python
# /home/zhz/zhz_agent/create_kuzu_db.py
import kuzu
import os
import shutil
import time
import gc
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import logging

# Configure a simple logger for this script
script_logger = logging.getLogger("KuzuCreateScript")
script_logger.setLevel(logging.INFO)
if not script_logger.hasHandlers():
    ch = logging.StreamHandler()
    formatter = logging.Formatter('%(asctime)s - %(name)s - %(levelname)s - %(message)s')
    ch.setFormatter(formatter)
    script_logger.addHandler(ch)
    script_logger.propagate = False

DB_PATH = "/tmp/kuzu_standalone_test_db" # Using a temporary path for clarity
MANUAL_EXTENSION_FILE_PATH = os.getenv(
    "KUZU_VECTOR_EXTENSION_PATH",
    os.path.expanduser("~/.kuzu/extension/0.10.0/linux_amd64/vector/libvector.kuzu_extension")
)
EMBEDDING_DIM = 1024 # Example dimension

script_logger.info(f"--- Standalone KuzuDB Creation Script ---")
script_logger.info(f"KuzuDB Python client version: {kuzu.__version__}")
script_logger.info(f"Target DB_PATH: {DB_PATH}")
script_logger.info(f"Vector extension path: {MANUAL_EXTENSION_FILE_PATH}")


if os.path.exists(DB_PATH):
    script_logger.info(f"Removing existing test DB at {DB_PATH}")
    shutil.rmtree(DB_PATH)
os.makedirs(DB_PATH, exist_ok=True)

extensions_dir_in_db = os.path.join(DB_PATH, "extensions")
os.makedirs(extensions_dir_in_db, exist_ok=True)
target_path_vector = os.path.join(extensions_dir_in_db, "vector.kuzu_extension")

if os.path.exists(MANUAL_EXTENSION_FILE_PATH):
    try:
        shutil.copy2(MANUAL_EXTENSION_FILE_PATH, target_path_vector)
        script_logger.info(f"Copied vector extension to '{target_path_vector}'")
    except Exception as e_copy:
        script_logger.error(f"ERROR copying extension: {e_copy}")
else:
    script_logger.error(f"ERROR: Manual vector extension source file not found at '{MANUAL_EXTENSION_FILE_PATH}'. Index creation might fail if KuzuDB cannot find the extension.")

db = None
conn = None
try:
    script_logger.info("Opening database for writing...")
    db = kuzu.Database(DB_PATH, read_only=False)
    conn = kuzu.Connection(db)
    script_logger.info("Database and connection opened.")

    script_logger.info("Loading VECTOR extension...")
    conn.execute("LOAD EXTENSION 'vector';") # Use quoted name
    script_logger.info("VECTOR extension loaded.")

    script_logger.info("Creating NODE TABLE ExtractedEntity (within explicit transaction)...")
    conn.execute("BEGIN TRANSACTION;")
    conn.execute(f"""
        CREATE NODE TABLE ExtractedEntity (
            id_prop STRING PRIMARY KEY,
            text STRING,
            label STRING,
            embedding FLOAT[{EMBEDDING_DIM}])
    """)
    conn.execute("COMMIT;")
    script_logger.info("ExtractedEntity table created and transaction committed.")
    
    script_logger.info("Loading sample data into ExtractedEntity (within explicit transaction)...")
    conn.execute("BEGIN TRANSACTION;")
    entities_to_load = [
        {"id_prop": "node_test_1", "text": "This is node one for test", "label": "TEST_DOC", 
         "embedding": np.random.rand(EMBEDDING_DIM).astype(np.float32).tolist()},
    ]
    for entity in entities_to_load:
        conn.execute(
            "CREATE (e:ExtractedEntity {{id_prop: $id, text: $text, label: $label, embedding: $embedding}})",
            {{"id": entity["id_prop"], "text": entity["text"], "label": entity["label"], "embedding": entity["embedding"]}}
        )
    conn.execute("COMMIT;")
    script_logger.info(f"Loaded {len(entities_to_load)} entities and transaction committed.")

    script_logger.info("Creating vector index 'entity_embedding_idx' (auto-transaction)...")
    conn.execute(f"""
        CALL CREATE_VECTOR_INDEX(
            'ExtractedEntity',
            'entity_embedding_idx',
            'embedding',
            metric := 'cosine'
        )
    """)
    script_logger.info("Vector index creation command executed (auto-committed).")

    script_logger.info("Verifying index creation in current session...")
    result_show_idx = conn.execute("CALL SHOW_INDEXES() RETURN *;") # Get all indexes
    df_show_idx = pd.DataFrame(result_show_idx.get_as_df())
    script_logger.info("Indexes visible in current session (All Tables):")
    script_logger.info(f"\n{df_show_idx.to_string()}")
    
    # Filter for the specific index
    if not df_show_idx.empty and 'table name' in df_show_idx.columns and 'index name' in df_show_idx.columns:
        condition = (df_show_idx['table name'] == 'ExtractedEntity') & (df_show_idx['index name'] == 'entity_embedding_idx')
        if not df_show_idx[condition].empty:
            script_logger.info("SUCCESS: 'entity_embedding_idx' IS VISIBLE on 'ExtractedEntity' in current session.")
        else:
            script_logger.error("FAILURE: 'entity_embedding_idx' IS NOT VISIBLE on 'ExtractedEntity' in current session.")
    else:
        script_logger.error("FAILURE: Could not verify index due to missing columns in SHOW_INDEXES output or empty result.")


    script_logger.info("Executing final CHECKPOINT...")
    conn.execute("CHECKPOINT;")
```

title: Bug: Binary File execution hits memory limit then fails, Killed response. pyinstaller, kuzu 0.10.0 import fastapi
body:
### Kuzu version


0.10.0

### What operating system are you using?

MacOS Apple M2 Max (apple silicon arm chip) Ventura 13.5

### What happened?

when Using a pyinstaller to bundle python scripts and pip packages into a binary that can be run on a smaller debian based docker image(python:3.9.20-slim-bookworm), the application runs fine until the kuzu db create, db.connection and cypher query are attempted at a fastapi end point. 

This also occurs when trying to run , kuzu-cli. 

You run the ./kuzu -h and everything is fine then run ./kuzu to create a db and it jakcs up the ram memory usage to as far as it can go and then crashes the system. 

All exports, cli flags and even deeply editing the env vars from the kuzu packages stil causes this memory overload issue. 

even reducing docker memory to 2GB it still tries to get all the meory and then crashes the unvicorn server running the fastapi app. 

Also main issue is not gracefully giving errors only real response is from the OS which will give a Killed error response without any additional context. 

why does this not happen when just running the python script? 

why does this happen only when using kuzu-cli or python binary? seems to be an issue when kuzu in any binary format with memory ignoring flags or export vars. 

Aditionally runin the kuzu pip import kuzu on a regular unvicorn and fastapi server has none of these issues and works fine, so it really is a binary execution issue with kuzu, maybe only in docker containers but not helpful if so since docker up controls many other servies required. 

I want to use kuzu and graphRAG i built with it but this it not working for production needs.

title: Bug: Kuzu Python Bindings Segmentation Fault
body:
### Kuzu version

v0.10.0

### What operating system are you using?

MacOS 15.5

### What happened?

When using the Kuzu Python bindings, segmentation faults (crashes) occur if `QueryResult` objects are garbage collected after their parent `Connection` or `Database` is closed. This is due to use-after-free in the underlying C++ code.

--
## Expected Behavior
- Python bindings should ensure that child objects (like `QueryResult`) do not outlive their parents, or at least raise a Python exception if used after parent destruction, rather than causing a hard crash.

## Workaround
- Always explicitly `del` all `QueryResult` objects before closing their parent `Connection` or `Database`.
- Immediately call `gc.collect()` after deletion to force cleanup.
- All test helpers and business logic in this project follow this pattern.

## Recommendations for Upstream Fix
- The Kuzu Python bindings should manage object lifetimes so that `QueryResult` objects cannot outlive their parent `Connection`/`Database`.
- If a `QueryResult` is used after its parent is closed, a Python exception should be raised instead of a segfault.
- Consider using weak references or parent tracking in the bindings to enforce this.

## Additional Notes
- This issue is documented in our developer and Sphinx documentation for all contributors.
- See `docs/source/kuzu_developer_guide.rst` and `docs/DEVELOPER_GUIDE.md` for more details and code examples. 

### Are there known steps to reproduce?

Minimal Reproducible Example

```python
import kuzu
import gc

db_path = "/tmp/kuzu_test_db"
db = kuzu.Database(db_path)
conn = kuzu.Connection(db)

# Create a simple schema and insert a node
conn.execute("CREATE NODE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS Variant(variant_id STRING, PRIMARY KEY (variant_id))")
conn.execute("CREATE (:Variant {{variant_id: 'v1'}})")

# Query for the node
result = conn.execute("MATCH (n:Variant) RETURN n")
for row in result:
    print(row)
# If you do not explicitly delete result and collect, the following close() may segfault
# del result
# gc.collect()

conn.close()
db.close()
# At this point, if 'result' is still alive, Python may segfault due to use-after-free
```

title: Feature: Compact how we display the results tuple/column count
body:
### API

CLI

### Description

Currently, when we display the result of a query in the CLI, we take up two lines at the bottom of the result to show how many tuples, and how many columns there are:
```
┌─────────────────────────┬──────────────┬───────────┐
│ company                 │ country_name │ commodity │
│ STRING                  │ STRING       │ STRING    │
├─────────────────────────┼──────────────┼───────────┤
│ Ramelius Resources      │ Australia    │ Gold      │
│ Northern Star Resources │ Australia    │ Gold      │
└─────────────────────────┴──────────────┴───────────┘
(2 tuples)
(3 columns)
```
It would be more. space efficient, as well as more intuitive, to just show it like this instead:
```
┌─────────────────────────┬──────────────┬───────────┐
│ company                 │ country_name │ commodity │
│ STRING                  │ STRING       │ STRING    │
├─────────────────────────┼──────────────┼───────────┤
│ Ramelius Resources      │ Australia    │ Gold      │
│ Northern Star Resources │ Australia    │ Gold      │
└─────────────────────────┴──────────────┴───────────┘
shape: (2, 3)
```
In the `shape` descriptor, the x-value would be the number of tuples and the y-value would be the number of columns. This is commonly used in other table formats too. "Tuple" isn't something people who aren't familiar with database terminology will immediately understand.

It's the same way Polars does it, see [here](https://docs.pola.rs/api/python/stable/reference/selectors.html#polars.selectors.ends_with) for an example.

```
>>> df.select(cs.ends_with("z"))
shape: (2, 1)
┌─────┐
│ baz │
│ --- │
│ f64 │
╞═════╡
│ 2.0 │
│ 5.5 │
└─────┘
```

title: Optimization: (Recursive) join order optimization
body:
### Description

This might be a potential interesting case for join optimization / recursive queries:
Joining reduces row count by factor ~ 180634, but worsens query performance by factor ~ 7.

First query part (runs quickly; low row count; optimally first join base):
```cypher
kuzu> MATCH (t1:A)-[]->(:B)-[]->(:C {name: 'Kùzu'}) RETURN count(t1);
┌──────────────┐
│ COUNT(t1._ID) │
│ INT64        │
├──────────────┤
│ 42           │
└──────────────┘
(1 tuple)
(1 column)
Time: 19.41ms (compiling), 51.99ms (executing)
```

Second query part (recursive; takes much longer; more results):            
```cypher
kuzu> MATCH (:A)-[:p_A_B|value_B_A * SHORTEST]-(t2:A) RETURN count(t2);
┌───────────────┐
│ COUNT(t2._ID) │
│ INT64         │
├───────────────┤
│ 7586664       │
└───────────────┘
(1 tuple)
(1 column)
Time: 71.17ms (compiling), 75965.74ms (executing)
```

Joining both and reducing results, query performance is ~ 7x worse than previous one:                                                                                               
```cypher                                                                                                                                                                                   
kuzu> MATCH (t1:A)-[]->(:B)-[]->(:C {name: 'Kùzu'}),
     (t1)-[:p_A_B|value_B_A* SHORTEST]-(t2:A) RETURN count(t2);
┌───────────────┐ 
│ COUNT(t2._ID) │              
│ INT64         │                     
├───────────────┤   
│ 1670          │                      
└───────────────┘   
(1 tuple)                                
(1 column)                            
Time: 11.12ms (compiling), 517672.18ms (executing)
```                                                                                                                                                                                         
                                                                                                                                                                                            
Using `WITH` clause, we currently can manually influence join order and optimization:
```cypher
kuzu> MATCH (t1:A)-[]->(:B)-[]->(:C {name: 'Kùzu'})
      WITH t1
      MATCH (t1)-[:p_A_B|value_B_A * SHORTEST]-(t2:A) RETURN count(t2);
┌───────────────┐
│ COUNT(t2._ID) │
│ INT64         │
├───────────────┤
│ 1670          │
└───────────────┘
(1 tuple)
(1 column)
Time: 25.56ms (compiling), 77257.63ms (executing)
```

- Optimally the more expensive recursive query would be only executed for those 42 rows from first query part. Judging by their similar executing time (75965.74ms vs. 77257.63ms), it currently doesn't seem to be limited.
- If non-recursive queries do receive much more optimization, perhaps it might make sense to prioritze them over recursive queries join-wise in a first step?
- Possbility for manual join sequence optimize would be awesome (e.g. via `WITH`), if query optimizer is not be able to do so automatically. Expected query time for last query would be something in the millisecond or lower seconds range.

title: Bug: MATCH clause returns nodes with unrelated properties resulting in null columns in query output
body: ### Kuzu version v0.10.0 ### What operating system are you using? MacOS Sonoma 14.1.2 ### What happened? When running a Cypher query with a `MATCH` clause that matches nodes without restricting by label (e.g., `MATCH (n)-[r:IsUser]->(m)`), the returned nodes contain properties that do not belong to the intended source or destination entities. In this case, IsUser is a rel that links a Employee and User table. Instead of retrieving only properties that belong to Employee and User tables, there appear columns belonging to other nodes tables (not linked to IsUser) in the response that appear as `null` values, cluttering the output. This seems to be happening because the query matches all nodes, regardless of their specific labels or entity types, leading to a merged result set with irrelevant properties populated as `null`. **Expected behavior:** The query should only return properties belonging to the source and destination node types specified by relationship so that the result columns correspond only to those relevant nodes and do not include unrelated columns with null values. **Workarounds:** - Post-process the results to remove properties with null columns (not ideal). - Use label-restricted patterns if possible (e.g., `MATCH (n:Employee)-[r:IsUser]->(m:User)`). It seems that removing unrelated properties can be done for all queries, not just ones with a reltype passed in. Thanks! ### Are there known steps to reproduce? This can be verified using the example dataset in Kuzu Explorer with the following query `MATCH (a)-[r]->(b) RETURN * LIMIT 5;`

title: Rework CREATE TABLE AS as binary plan

labels.name: type: feature
labels.description: New features or missing components of existing features

body:
Currently, the optimizer seems to only go down the leftmost subtrees (i.e. child at index 0) for logical operators.

For https://github.com/kuzudb/kuzu/issues/5274 we would like to ideally construct a binary logical plan so the subtree responsible for creating the table is independent from the subtree responsible for copying. This will fix the issue demonstrated below:

```
kuzu> create node table if not exists Foo as load from "test.csv" return *;
kuzu> explain logical create node table Bar as match (a:Foo) where false return a.*;
```

Currently, since we construct a linear plan, the above will result in a logical plan with an `EmptyResult` operator, but the optimizer truncates the children, which includes the `CreateTable` operator.

code_snippets.code:
kuzu> create node table if not exists Foo as load from "test.csv" return *;
kuzu> explain logical create node table Bar as match (a:Foo) where false return a.*;

title: Improve Java API's exception handling
body:
Right now we didn't explicitly `try ... catch ...` exceptions thrown from cpp side in our Java API. This can lead to unexpected crashes if users don't follow steps exactly or manually try catch as expected.

To improve the usability with exception handling, we should explicitly `try ... catch ...` exceptions thrown from cpp side and convert them into Java Exceptions.

title: Collect aggregate function scaling
body:
The collect function currently stores a FactorizedTable for each aggregate state (i.e. each group), which allocates at least one 256KB memory buffer to store its data (and an InMemOverflowBuffer, but that was changed recently to start with small blocks and scale upwards).

The FactorizedTable uses a fixed number of tuples per block, so it would slow down access time if we were to increase the size of the blocks as the number of values increase (though it should still be constant time using the same doubling strategy; albeit a more complicated calculation than just dividing by the number of tuples per block), but we could use a smaller block size and have the blocks be backed by the AggregateHashTable's shared InMemOverflowBuffer instead of being individually allocated which should make up for the performance cost of using smaller blocks.

We also don't strictly need the FactorizedTable: this table stores a single value per tuple with no factorization, and the copyToRowData and copyFromRowData functions work on arbitrary memory addresses. We could move the implementations of `getTuple`, `appendEmptyTuple` and the tracking of the number of flat tuples into the DataBlockCollection, and just use a DataBlockCollection in CollectState (and maybe rename DataBlockCollection).

title: Bug: Incorrect operator precedence parsing for unary minus with IS NOT NULL
body:
### Kuzu version

v0.9.0

### What operating system are you using?

Windows 11

### What happened?

While I was using kuzudb, I encountered the following issue:
```cypher
MATCH (t4:t4)-[e1:e1]->(t0:t0) WHERE (-1 IS NOT NULL) RETURN 1
```
The query threw a binder exception: Binder exception: Cannot match a built-in function for given function NEGATE(BOOL)
It seems that the condition ``-1 IS NOT NULL`` is parsed as ``-(1 IS NOT NULL)``, which negates a boolean value, causing the binder exception.


### Are there known steps to reproduce?

```cypher
CREATE NODE TABLE t4(c0 INT8, c1 UINT32, PRIMARY KEY (c0))
CREATE NODE TABLE t0(c0 UINT32, PRIMARY KEY (c0))
CREATE REL TABLE e1(FROM t4 TO t0)
MATCH (t4:t4)-[e1:e1]->(t0:t0) WHERE (-1 IS NOT NULL) RETURN 1
```

title: Bug: Neo4J import tool copies properties in arbitrary order
body:
### Kuzu version

master

### What operating system are you using?

Ubuntu

### What happened?

In the Neo4J import tool we use `call db.schema.nodeTypeProperties()` to get the properties for a label, and then use the queried properties in the order of the query output to determine the order of the properties to `COPY FROM`.

For example, if the output of the properties query is 
```
+--------------------------------+
| propertyName | propertyTypes   |
+--------------------------------+
| "id"         | ["Long"]        |
| "name"       | ["String"]      |
| "pets"       | ["StringArray"] |
+--------------------------------+
```

Our `COPY FROM` query will be
```
COPY FROM (LOAD WITH HEADERS(..., id int64, name string, pets string[]))
```

However, the order of the columns actually exported by Neo4J doesn't necessarily match this queried order which can cause the import to fail.

### Are there known steps to reproduce?

1. From an empty Neo4J database, run:
```sql
create (n: Node {name: 'Alice', time: datetime("2019-06-01T18:40:32.142+0100"), date: date("2019-06-01"), is
Person: true, pid: 123, eyeSight: 0.55, friends: [1, 2, 3], pets: ['dog'], score: [0.1, 0.2, 0.3]});
```
2. From kuzu run:
```sql
CALL NEO4J_MIGRATE(
    "localhost",
    "",
    "",
    ["Node"],
    []
);
```
When running that above query I get the error
`Copy exception: Error in file /tmp/Node.csv on line 2: Conversion exception: Cast failed. 2019-06-01 is not in STRING[] range. Line/record containing the error: '"0",":Node","2019-06-01"...'
`

Person: true, pid: 123, eyeSight: 0.55, friends: [1, 2, 3], pets: ['dog'], score: [0.1, 0.2, 0.3]});

CALL NEO4J_MIGRATE(
    "localhost",

title: Bug: The SHORTEST function does not take WHERE constraints into account

labels.name: type: feature
labels.description: New features or missing components of existing features

body:
### Kuzu version

_No response_

### What operating system are you using?

MacOS Sequoia 15.4.1, python kuzu==0.9.0

### What happened?

The SHORTEST function does not take WHERE constraints into account.

It seems to first find the shortest path and then apply the constraints, which often leads to no path found.

Please find below a python script to reproduce the problem.

In a graph with cities connected with routes, we first find the shortest path between Rome and Dublin. But once we had the constraint that the route should not pass by Paris, then no solution is found.


### Are there known steps to reproduce?

```python
import kuzu

db = kuzu.Database(":memory:")
conn = kuzu.Connection(db)

# Graph connecting cities with routes
conn.execute("CREATE NODE TABLE City(name STRING, PRIMARY KEY (name))")
conn.execute("CREATE REL TABLE Route(FROM City TO City)")

# Create cities
cities = ["Paris", "London", "Rome", "Milan", "Berlin", "Bern", "Amsterdam", "Dublin"]
for city in cities:
    conn.execute("CREATE (:City {name: $city});", parameters={"city": city})

# Create routes
routes = [
    ("Paris", "London"),
    ("London", "Dublin"),
    ("Rome", "Bern"),
    ("Bern", "Berlin"),
    ("Bern", "Paris"),
    ("Berlin", "Amsterdam"),
    ("Amsterdam", "London"),
]
for from_city, to_city in routes:
    conn.execute(
        "MATCH (c1:City {name: $from_city}), (c2:City {name: $to_city}) "
        "CREATE (c1)-[:Route]->(c2);",
        parameters={"from_city": from_city, "to_city": to_city},
    )

# Find the shortest path from Rome to Dublin
print("Shortest path from Rome to Dublin:")
result = conn.execute(
    "MATCH p = (:City {name: 'Rome'})-[:Route* SHORTEST]-(:City {name: 'Dublin'}) "
    "RETURN nodes(p) AS path;",
)
result = result.get_next()[0]
print(" -> ".join([node["name"] for node in result]))
# Shortest path should be Rome -> Bern -> Paris -> London -> Dublin

# Find the shortest path from Rom to Dublin without passing through Paris
print("Shortest path from Rome to Dublin without passing through Paris:")
result = conn.execute(
    "MATCH p = (:City {name: 'Rome'})-[:Route* SHORTEST]-(:City {name: 'Dublin'}) "
    "WHERE ALL(city IN nodes(p) WHERE city.name <> 'Paris')"
    "RETURN nodes(p) AS path;",
)
print("Path found?", result.has_next())
# Shortest path should now be Rome -> Bern -> Berlin -> Amsterdam -> London -> Dublin, but no path is found...

```

title: Feature: Implement an object lifecycle manager for kuzu

labels.name: type: feature
labels.description: New features or missing components of existing features

body:
### API

Python, Node.js, Java, Go

### Description

Currently the closing order of objects have to be guaranteed in kuzu (QueryResult & PreparedStatement -> Connection -> Database), otherwise it will result in corrupted memory due to missing the references. We should implement an object lifecycle manager to ensure automatically close all the allocated resources first before closing the parent, so that the users' of the client API will not need to worry about manually closing all the objects.

title: Improve test coverage for functions so that they can handle empty list/arrays

labels.name: type: usability
labels.description: Issues related to better usability experience, including bad error messages

body:
### Kuzu version

master

### What operating system are you using?

macOS

### What happened?

Taking observations from the following related issues:
- https://github.com/kuzudb/kuzu/issues/5216
- https://github.com/kuzudb/kuzu/issues/5307

These are segfaults that were totally preventable had there been an empty list included in the test suite for these functions.

In Python, we have the concept of empty lists `[]`. We really should be testing for empty lists passed over to C++ objects in every case where a list/array function is present. It's incredibly common to encounter mixed lists in Python, where you have a mix of empty lists interspersed with non-empty lists.

For example, the following function should work, but it doesn't. Kuzu should appropriately handle the empty/null array during concatenation because it's very common to encounter specific instances of null/empty arrays in the wild from a realistic dataset.
```cypher
// this fails
return list_cat(['7','3'], []);
Error: Binder exception: Cannot bind LIST_CONCAT with parameter type STRING[] and INT64[].
```

This works:
```
return list_cat(['7','3'], ['1']);
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ LIST_CONCAT(LIST_CREATION(7,3),LIST_CREATION(1)) │
│ STRING[]                                         │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ [7,3,1]                                          │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

### Rule of thumb
Any time we test a function that uses a list of lists (e.g. `[['a', 'b', 'c'], ['d']]`) in Python, we must also test for empty lists as one of the components of that list of lists (e.g. `[['a', 'b', 'c'], ['d'], []]`). This applies to pandas/polars dataframes as well (where each column of type list is basically a list of lists).

@acquamarin and @ray6080 I think the entire test suite for lists/arrays can be improved to help prevent such segfaults showing up in future bug reports. See [this test](https://github.com/kuzudb/kuzu/blob/a418cd4186c6ed779b9e375a1f67ccdc1cea0185/test/test_files/function/list.test#L462) for an example. Shouldn't we be including `[]` as one of the items in the list? If there's a better way to handle this at the Cypher layer, that's fine too, but the hope is that we prevent these kinds of cases from segfaulting.

### Are there known steps to reproduce?

_No response_

title: Uninformative error message for list function

labels.name: area: frontend
labels.description: Frontend, i.e., binder, parser, query planning-related issues

body:
### Kuzu version

v0.9.0

### What operating system are you using?

macOS

### What happened?

The following error message is unhelpful, for what seems like a common user error:
```
kuzu> return list_to_string(['travel', 'hiking']);
Error: Binder exception: Cannot match a built-in function for given function LIST_TO_STRING(STRING[]). Supported inputs are
(LIST,STRING) -> STRING
```

The issue is that the user forgot to specify the separator in the `list_to_string` function. The error message gives no indication that a parameter is *missing*, it seems to indicate that the type isn't supported.

The user could, of course, go into the docs to search the syntax and fix it, but the error message isn't helping and adds more work and effort to understand what's going wrong.

The following works, as per the example.
```
kuzu> return list_to_string(['travel', 'hiking'], '..');
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ LIST_TO_STRING(LIST_CREATION(travel,hiking),..) │
│ STRING                                          │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ travel..hiking                                  │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

Can we make the error messages for missing function parameters like this more informative? 

### Are there known steps to reproduce?

```cypher
return list_to_string(["a", "b", "c"]) CONTAINS "a"
```

title: Optimization: CSR header space optimization
body:
### Description

For CSR headers we currently always set its capacity to the node group size (128K by default). With FSM now implemented, we can now set the capacity to the maximum non-empty node offset (or the right boundary of the region containing the node offset) as we can now reclaim used pages if the header is updated out-of-place. This way we can keep the storage footprint of the CSR header small if the number of nodes in a graph is small (e.g. a few thousand). 

Note that other parts of the system (e.g. rel scanning, checkpoint) can make assumptions about the uniform capacity of CSR headers, there will need to be changed to get this optimization working. Some changes that will need to be made include:
- `CSRRegion` should be passed a `maxNumRegions` parameter that puts a upper bound on the `rightNodeOffset` of the region.
- When scanning rels, we may now try to scan from node offsets that are out of bounds for the CSR header. We should return an empty result in this case but continue scanning.

title: Migrate Maven Central deployment from OSSRH to Central Publisher Portal
body:
OSSRH will [reach end-of-life on June 30th, 2025](https://central.sonatype.org/news/20250326_ossrh_sunset/). They are forcing everyone to migrate to the new Central Publisher Portal by that date. 

I tried to work with the Central Publisher Portal last year and it was really bad. 
- There was no official support for Gradle build system.
- Third-party tools like [JReleaser](https://jreleaser.org/) did not work properly and also tried to take on the entire release workflow, not just pushing to Maven. 
- The publishing workflow was not standard for Gradle, meaning that we had to setup completely different workflow for publishing to Maven Central (for stable) and GitHub package (for nightly).

Now they claimed that they have a [staging API](https://central.sonatype.org/publish/publish-portal-ossrh-staging-api/) which behaves like the old OSSRH API, so hopefully we can use this and simply change the publishing endpoint and get it work with Gradle. Overall they are very annoying to work with, but we have to do it before **June 30th, 2025**, or we will no longer be able to publish to Maven Central.

title: Feature: Convenience methods to fetch results from Python QueryResult

labels.name: type: feature
labels.description: New features or missing components of existing features

body:
> Couple of comments. Our Python API is more or less similar to DuckDB's.
> 
> Here's an example of using the DuckDB relational API, that's similar to Kuzu's `conn.execute()`.
> ```py
> import duckdb
> 
> conn = duckdb.connect()
> 
> conn.execute("CREATE TABLE User(person STRING PRIMARY KEY, age INT)")
> 
> conn.execute("INSERT INTO User VALUES ('Adam', 25)")
> conn.execute("INSERT INTO User VALUES ('Karissa', 23)")
> 
> result = conn.execute("SELECT * FROM User")
> print(result.fetchmany(size=1))
> 
> result = conn.execute("SELECT * FROM User")
> print(result.fetchone())
> 
> result = conn.execute("SELECT * FROM User")
> print(result.fetchall())
> ```
> This outputs:
> ```
> [('Adam', 25)]
> ('Adam', 25)
> [('Adam', 25), ('Karissa', 23)]
> ```
> As a starting point, it makes sense to implement the convenience methods that DuckDB provides so that users don't need to write the `while` loops every single time they want to retrieve a subset of their result object.
> - `fetchone`
> - `fetchmany`
> - `fetchall` 

 _Originally posted by @prrao87 in [#5240](https://github.com/kuzudb/kuzu/issues/5240#issuecomment-2809544644)_

title: Feature: Iterator over query.execute() results

labels.name: type: feature
labels.description: New features or missing components of existing features

labels.name: type: usability
labels.description: Issues related to better usability experience, including bad error messages

body:
### API

Python

### Description

Upon execution of a query, the `Connection.execute()` method returns a QueryResult object (or list of such objects) through which we can explicitly iterate over one or more result sets: 
```py
result = conn.execute(query)
while result.has_next():
    row = result.get_next()
    # ...
```

Unfortunately, QueryResult does not implement the standard Python iterator protocol, which makes retrieving results a bit unusual for Python developers.

A common approach shared by many libraries (such as Alchemy) is to return an object that implements the Python iterator protocol. This would be very welcome (and easy) addition to the interface of the QueryResult class:
```py
class QueryResult:
    # ...
    def __iter__(self):
        self.reset_iterator()
        return self

    def __next__(self):
        if self.has_next():
            return self.get_next()
        raise StopIteration
```
The second improvement, could be combining the `list` and `dict` semantics in the object returned from `get_next()`. Something that BigQuery library provides with their query results. Such an object would allow retrieving individual columns from a row by either their offset (as it is today) or by column name:
```py
row = result.get_next()  # assuming `row` contains 3 columns 'id', 'name', and 'email'
email = row[2]           # as it is today
email = row['email']     # not supported, but would be nice to have 
```
This approach is more flexible as it allows to change the order of columns returned by a query without a programmer trying to discern the columns' positions through other methods.

code_snippets.code:
result = conn.execute(query)
while result.has_next():
    row = result.get_next()
    # ...

row = result.get_next()  # assuming `row` contains 3 columns 'id', 'name', and 'email'
email = row[2]           # as it is today
email = row['email']     # not supported, but would be nice to have

title: Optimization: Add a rewrite rule for queries that use WITH clauses
body:
## Use case

In Q5 and Q6 of [this benchmark](https://github.com/prrao87/kuzudb-study/tree/main/kuzudb), Kuzu is slower than it should be (in comparison to its performance on other queries in the suite).

Q5 (aggregates the returned persons):
```cypher
MATCH (p:Person)-[:HasInterest]->(i:Interest)
WHERE lower(i.interest) = lower($interest)
AND lower(p.gender) = lower($gender)
WITH p, i
MATCH (p)-[:LivesIn]->(c:City)
WHERE c.city = $city AND c.country = $country
RETURN count(p) AS numPersons
```

Q6 (aggregates the returned persons grouping on other nodes and sorts them):
```cypher
MATCH (p:Person)-[:HasInterest]->(i:Interest)
WHERE lower(i.interest) = lower($interest)
AND lower(p.gender) = lower($gender)
WITH p, i
MATCH (p)-[:LivesIn]->(c:City)
RETURN count(p.id) AS numPersons, c.city AS city, c.country AS country
ORDER BY numPersons DESC LIMIT 5
```
The usage of the `WITH` clause seems to be slowing the queries down.

In both cases, the query plan could internally be rewritten to avoid using the `WITH` clause. The plan would execute something like the following (per @andyfengHKU's advice):

```cypher
MATCH (p:Person)-[:HasInterest]->(i:Interest),
      (p)-[:LivesIn]->(c:City)
WHERE lower(i.interest) = lower($interest)
AND lower(p.gender) = lower($gender)
AND c.city = $city
AND c.country = $country
RETURN count(p) AS numPersons
```

### Benefit

A lot of users coming from Neo4j who have `WITH` clauses in their queries like this example could benefit from a performance improvement in Kuzu, without having to rewrite the query.

code_snippets.code:
MATCH (p:Person)-[:HasInterest]->(i:Interest)
WHERE lower(i.interest) = lower($interest)
AND lower(p.gender) = lower($gender)
WITH p, i
MATCH (p)-[:LivesIn]->(c:City)
WHERE c.city = $city AND c.country = $country
RETURN count(p) AS numPersons

MATCH (p:Person)-[:HasInterest]->(i:Interest)
WHERE lower(i.interest) = lower($interest)
AND lower(p.gender) = lower($gender)
WITH p, i
MATCH (p)-[:LivesIn]->(c:City)
RETURN count(p.id) AS numPersons, c.city AS city, c.country AS country
ORDER BY numPersons DESC LIMIT 5

MATCH (p:Person)-[:HasInterest]->(i:Interest),
      (p)-[:LivesIn]->(c:City)
WHERE lower(i.interest) = lower($interest)
AND lower(p.gender) = lower($gender)
AND c.city = $city
AND c.country = $country
RETURN count(p) AS numPersons

body:
### API

Python

### Description

Hi team 👋

I’d like to request support for an additional parameter in the httpfs extension for AWS access: the AWS session token.

When using the AssumeRole API to access AWS resources, AWS returns a temporary set of security credentials, which includes:

- Access Key ID
- Secret Access Key
- Session Token

Currently, httpfs allows specifying the access key and secret key, but there doesn’t appear to be a way to include the session token. (See linked issue) This makes it difficult to use KuzuDB with temporary AWS credentials acquired via AssumeRole, which is a common practice for us.

Proposed enhancement:

- Add support for a new parameter (e.g., `s3_session_token`) in the httpfs extension.
- If possible, to also support adding the `KMS_KEY_ID` (In Kuzu `s3_kms_key_id`) because it is a fairly common scenario that the S3 bucket is encrypted with a custom kms key. (This is supported by DuckDB as well. [Link](https://duckdb.org/docs/stable/extensions/httpfs/s3api.html#overview-of-s3-secret-parameters)

Example Usage:

```
INSTALL httpfs;
```

title: Feature: passing object references via "parameters" mechanism for LOAD FROM
body:
### API

Python

### Description

One can use Pandas DataFrame to scan data for `COPY <table> FROM (LOAD FROM df ...)`

The way of specifying the reference to a dataframe is by providing the name of the Python variable inside the text of the query:
```
df = pd.DataFrame({...})  # --------------vv
conn.execute("COPY Person FROM (LOAD FROM df WHERE name="Alice" and age>=18 RETURN *)")
```
IMO, this is very unusual way of passing a Python object reference to a function.

Typically, when a query text is composed in the code, we'd use either literal values, e.g. `where name='Alice' and age>=18` or
placeholders, e.g. `where name=$p1 and age>=$p2` and then we would supply the associations between placeholders and
references to Python objects: `parameters={"p1": "Alice", "p2": get_min_age()}`

Accessing a local variable by its name embedded into query text also has some minor performance penalty as the implementing code has to call `locals()` and lookup for the `df` name within a dict in order to get the object reference.

Also, it seems impossible to use a function call rather than the name of a variable. The code below will fail:
```
def build_df():
    return pd.DataFrame({...})

conn.execute("COPY Person FROM (LOAD FROM build_df() WHERE age >= 18 RETURN *)")
```

Lastly, linters will complain about "not used variable df", as from their point of view `df` is defined but never used in the code.

I suggest to consider implementing an alternative approach for passing references to Python objects (e.g. dataframes) to the
`Connection.execute()` method. Most intuitive seems to be using the existing placeholder parameters mechanism, as it will be consistent with the rest of the Python API.

code_snippets.code:
df = pd.DataFrame({...})  # --------------vv
conn.execute("COPY Person FROM (LOAD FROM df WHERE name="Alice" and age>=18 RETURN *)")

title: Bug: JSON extension returns strange errors when handling nulls

labels.name: type: usability
labels.description: Issues related to better usability experience, including bad error messages

body:
### Kuzu version

v0.9.0

### What operating system are you using?

macOS

### Summary of issue

There are 2 versions of a JSON file with `null` values, and each of them behaves differently. The error messages are impossible to understand, so there is a usability concern in this common use case for JSON.

### What happened?

Here's 3 versions of a JSON file named `customer.json`. I'm trying to `LOAD FROM` a file using the JSON extension.

### Version 1

```json
{
    "accountContacts": [
        {
        "objectType": "contact",
        "schemaVersion": "135",
        "contactIdentifier": "320864",
        "contactNamespace": "56127",
        "contactDetail": {
            "fullname": "Renee Luke",
            "email": "renee.luke@datapath.com",
            "phone": "(678) 252-4828 - Direct"
            }
        }
    ]
}
```
Runs successfully and I can get the following result from the `MATCH` query:
```
shape: (1, 5)
┌────────┬─────────────┬────────────┬─────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────┐
│ n.id   ┆ n.namespace ┆ n.fullname ┆ n.email                 ┆ n.phone                 │
│ ---    ┆ ---         ┆ ---        ┆ ---                     ┆ ---                     │
│ str    ┆ str         ┆ str        ┆ str                     ┆ str                     │
╞════════╪═════════════╪════════════╪═════════════════════════╪═════════════════════════╡
│ 320864 ┆ 56127       ┆ Renee Luke ┆ renee.luke@datapath.com ┆ (678) 252-4828 - Direct │
└────────┴─────────────┴────────────┴─────────────────────────┴─────────────────────────┘
```

### Version 2

Sometimes, the input source can provide a `null` value in the JSON (note that the source actually returns `null` and not the string `"null"`, so this is something that's hard to fix upstream). In this example, the `"schemaVersion"` key has a `null` value.

```json
{
    "accountContacts": [
        {
        "objectType": "contact",
        "schemaVersion": null,
        "contactIdentifier": "320864",
        "contactNamespace": "56127",
        "contactDetail": {
            "fullname": "Renee Luke",
            "email": "renee.luke@datapath.com",
            "phone": "(678) 252-4828 - Direct"
            }
        }
    ]
}
```
This produces the following error during `COPY` in Kuzu:
```
RuntimeError: Runtime exception: Trying to a create a vector with ANY type. This should not happen. Data type is expected to be resolved during binding.",
```

### Version 3

Let's move the null value to another key, namely the `"contactNamespace"`.

```json
{
    "accountContacts": [
        {
        "objectType": "contact",
        "schemaVersion": "135",
        "contactIdentifier": "320864",
        "contactNamespace": null,
        "contactDetail": {
            "fullname": "Renee Luke",
            "email": "renee.luke@datapath.com",
            "phone": "(678) 252-4828 - Direct"
            }
        }
    ]
}
```
A totally different error is returned:

```
RuntimeError: Binder exception: Data type of expression namespace should not be modified.
```



### Are there known steps to reproduce?

Run the following code on each JSON version:

```python
import kuzu

db = kuzu.Database()
conn = kuzu.Connection(db)

conn.execute("INSTALL json; LOAD json;")

conn.execute("CREATE NODE TABLE Contact(id STRING PRIMARY KEY, namespace STRING, fullname STRING, email STRING, phone STRING);")

res = conn.execute(
    """
    LOAD FROM 'customer.json'
    WITH accountContacts AS account_contacts
    UNWIND account_contacts AS contact
    RETURN
        contact.contactIdentifier AS id,
        contact.contactNamespace AS namespace,
        contact.contactDetail.fullname AS name,
        contact.contactDetail.email AS email,
        contact.contactDetail.phone AS phone
    """
)
print(res.get_as_pl())
```

## Desired outcome from a usability perspective

- The JSON extension should be able to handle `null` (not the string, but the actual value itself) because this is commonly output in this form from some upstream systems. Missing keys aren't the only scenario where we need to handle nulls in JSON.
- If some unexpected value is sent to the JSON that doesn't align with Kuzu's schema expectations, we should show a helpful error to help the user know what went wrong. The current errors are too hard to interpret.

title: Old dates not parsed correctly for Node.js API
body:
# Historical dates not parsed correctly

## Description of the problem

Kuzu Explorer does not seem to correctly parse historical dates, such as date objects from the Middle Ages. Such very old dates are correctly parsed and loaded into a Kuzu database from the Python client (no problem there!). But when a database with historical dates is loaded into Kuzu Explorer, the data is corrupted. And when a historical date is created in Kuzu Explorer the same problem occurs.

## Reproduce the problem

In Kuzu Explorer, a date can be created and read, as shown in the example [here](https://docs.kuzudb.com/cypher/data-types/#date).

```
RETURN date('2025-04-01') as x;
>>> 2025-04-01
```

But when we do the same for a historical date (i.e. Middle Ages), the data is incorrectly parsed.

```
RETURN date('1400-04-01') as x;
>>> 1984-10-20
```
```
RETURN date('1300-05-01') as x;
>>> 1884-11-18
```

## Conclusion

The error I encountered when loading my Kuzu database into Kuzu Explorer seems to be related to this general issue of how Kuzu Explorer creates / interprets very old date objects. Hopefully this simpler reproducibility example gets to the root issue, without the need to generate a full reproduction of creating historical date objects in a database and loading them into Kuzu Explorer.

title: Recursive query takes long time, none-recursive query returns immediately (same output row count and query structure)
body:
### Description

I am currently using a query looking similar to this one:
```cypher
MATCH (b:A)-[]->(:Attribute)-[]->(:C)<-[* SHORTEST 1..6]-(:C {name: 'Kùzu'})
      RETURN count(b);
```
Above query returns ~ 1k rows immediately.

In order to make statement a bit more concise, I changed it to:
```cypher
MATCH (b:A)-[* 2..2]->(:C)<-[* SHORTEST 1..6]-(:C {name: 'Kùzu'})
      RETURN count(b);
```
This query works hard - I skipped at "Current Pipeline Progress: 10%" after a minute or so.

Conceptually type `A` or `C` - there are more, but let's limit to these - is always followed by `Attribute`, which then is followed by `A` or `C` again, and cycle may repeat multiple times. There is a single relation type for `(A|C) --> (Attribute)` and another for `(Attribute) --> (A|C)`. `Attribute` is a reified node, hence this pairwise hopping sequence.
```
(A|C) --> (Attribute) --> (A|C) --> (Attribute) -> ...
```

In summary, given same output rows and otherwise equal query structure, there is a big performance difference between recursive and non-recursive searching. Here is the row count from splitting query parts:
```cypher
MATCH (c:C)<-[* SHORTEST 1..6]-(:C {name: 'Kùzu'}) RETURN count(c);
// 33
MATCH (b:A)-[]->(:Attribute)-[]->(:C) RETURN count(b);
// 41206
MATCH (b:A)-[* 2..2]->(:C) RETURN count(b);
// 41206
```

Is this expected behavior? 
For now I marked issue as performance optimization, not sure about a bug. Hopefully you got a hint from description, otherwise let me try to re-create a graph with dummy data.

code_snippets.code:
MATCH (b:A)-[]->(:Attribute)-[]->(:C)<-[* SHORTEST 1..6]-(:C {name: 'Kùzu'})
      RETURN count(b);

MATCH (b:A)-[* 2..2]->(:C)<-[* SHORTEST 1..6]-(:C {name: 'Kùzu'})
      RETURN count(b);
(A|C) --> (Attribute) --> (A|C) --> (Attribute) -> ...

title: WAL replaying optimization for incomplete transactions
body:
### Description

Our WAL replaying can be quite slow. This can lead to cases like in https://github.com/kuzudb/kuzu/issues/5016 where upon killing a long-lasting query and then reloading the DB it can appear like the DB is hanging (when in reality we are just replaying the query).

In the above case uncommitted records actually don't need to be replayed. Thus one possible optimization would be to deserialize records in batches and only replay the records if they are followed by a commit. In the above case this would mean that we only pay the cost of deserializing records and not the cost of replaying them.

title: Feature: Add naive hybrid search (FTS + vector search)

labels.name: type: feature
labels.description: New features or missing components of existing features

body:
### API

Python

### Description

With the upcoming vector index, we should consider adding support for hybrid search, where the user may want to combine FTS (keyword-based) and vector search results to improve the relevance of results.

A naive, simple implementation is shown in [this blog post](https://isaacflath.com/blog/blog_post?fpath=posts%2F2025-03-17-Retrieval101.ipynb) and would be a good starting point.

Here's how it would look in Python:

```py
def hybrid_search(query, top_k=5, vector_weight=0.7):
    """Perform hybrid search using both vector similarity and BM25 keyword matching."""
    # Vector search
    query_embedding = model.encode(query, normalize_embeddings=True)
    vector_results = chunk_table.search(query_embedding).metric('cosine').limit(top_k*2).to_pandas()
    vector_results['vector_score'] = 1 - vector_results['_distance']
    
    # Keyword search with BM25s
    # Create corpus from our chunks
    corpus = chunks_df['content'].tolist()
    
    # Tokenize the corpus and index it
    corpus_tokens = bm25s.tokenize(corpus)
    retriever = bm25s.BM25(corpus=corpus)
    retriever.index(corpus_tokens)
    
    # Tokenize the query and retrieve results
    query_tokens = bm25s.tokenize(query)
    docs, scores = retriever.retrieve(query_tokens, k=len(corpus))  # Get scores for all documents
    
    # Map BM25 scores to our dataframe indices
    bm25_scores = {i: scores[0, idx] for idx, i in enumerate(docs[0])}
    vector_results['bm25_score'] = vector_results.index.map(
        lambda x: bm25_scores.get(x, 0) if x in bm25_scores else 0)
    
    # Normalize BM25 scores
    if vector_results['bm25_score'].max() > 0:
        vector_results['bm25_score'] = vector_results['bm25_score'] / vector_results['bm25_score'].max()
    
    # Combine scores with weighting
    vector_results['combined_score'] = (
        vector_weight * vector_results['vector_score'] + 
        (1 - vector_weight) * vector_results['bm25_score'])
    
    return vector_results.sort_values('combined_score', ascending=False).head(top_k)
```

This maps the retrieved results from BM25 to the vector search indices, normalizes the BM25 scores to align with the vector search results, and then applies the user-specified `vector_weight`, which instructs the algorithm how much to weight the vector search results over the FTS results. 0.7 is a sensible default (because too high a weight given to FTS can result in fewer matches overall - vector search is more forgiving).

I think this would be a decent base implementation to do at the C++ level, that can then be exposed to the higher level clients with the specified arguments without too much work. Alternatively, we could only implement this in Python for an initial release, so that users at least have an option to get relevant keyword-based results alongside vector search results from their graphs.

code_snippets.code:
def hybrid_search(query, top_k=5, vector_weight=0.7):
    """Perform hybrid search using both vector similarity and BM25 keyword matching."""
    # Vector search
    query_embedding = model.encode(query, normalize_embeddings=True)
    vector_results = chunk_table.search(query_embedding).metric('cosine').limit(top_k*2).to_pandas()
    vector_results['vector_score'] = 1 - vector_results['_distance']
    
    # Keyword search with BM25s
    # Create corpus from our chunks
    corpus = chunks_df['content'].tolist()
    
    # Tokenize the corpus and index it
    corpus_tokens = bm25s.tokenize(corpus)
    retriever = bm25s.BM25(corpus=corpus)
    retriever.index(corpus_tokens)
    
    # Tokenize the query and retrieve results
    query_tokens = bm25s.tokenize(query)
    docs, scores = retriever.retrieve(query_tokens, k=len(corpus))  # Get scores for all documents
    
    # Map BM25 scores to our dataframe indices
    bm25_scores = {i: scores[0, idx] for idx, i in enumerate(docs[0])}
    vector_results['bm25_score'] = vector_results.index.map(
        lambda x: bm25_scores.get(x, 0) if x in bm25_scores else 0)
    
    # Normalize BM25 scores
    if vector_results['bm25_score'].max() > 0:
        vector_results['bm25_score'] = vector_results['bm25_score'] / vector_results['bm25_score'].max()
    
    # Combine scores with weighting
    vector_results['combined_score'] = (
        vector_weight * vector_results['vector_score'] + 
        (1 - vector_weight) * vector_results['bm25_score'])
    
    return vector_results.sort_values('combined_score', ascending=False).head(top_k)

title: Feature: Support for Atomic Backup API (Similar to SQLite Backup API)

labels.name: type: feature
labels.description: New features or missing components of existing features

body:
### API

Node.js

### Description

Kuzu currently lacks an atomic export operation to create a full database backup while allowing writes to continue. This feature would be useful for use cases such as event-sourced architectures, where backups need to be taken at a specific event index to enable point-in-time recovery.

### Use Case:

- In an event-sourced system, all writes to Kuzu are synchronized through an event log.
- During a backup, it's crucial to capture the exact event index to enable deterministic recovery.
- A feature similar to [SQLite's Backup API](https://www.sqlite.org/backup.html) would allow creating a consistent database snapshot without stopping writes.

### Proposed Solution:

- Implement a mechanism to clone or export the entire database atomically.
- Ensure that the snapshot remains consistent even if writes occur during the operation. Or automatically pause all writes on the SDK layer so the client code doesn't need to worry about locking.
- Provide an API to initiate and manage such a backup process.

title: Feature: Convenience function to return a table of database statistics

labels.name: type: feature
labels.description: New features or missing components of existing features

body:
### Feature

Return a single table containing statistics of the number of nodes and relationships (grouped by table name).

### Description

As of v0.8.2, it's quite tedious to display the summary of the number of nodes and relationships, grouped by the table name. It takes the following two queries run sequentially:

#### Query 1

```cypher
MATCH (n) 
RETURN label(n), COUNT(label(n));
```
```
┌──────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────┐
│ LABEL(n._ID,[User,City]) │ COUNT(LABEL(n._ID,[User,City])) │
│ STRING                   │ INT64                           │
├──────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────┤
│ User                     │ 4                               │
│ City                     │ 3                               │
└──────────────────────────┴─────────────────────────────────┘
```

#### Query 2
```cypher
MATCH ()-[r]->() 
RETURN label(r), COUNT(label(r));
```
```
┌──────────────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ LABEL(r._ID,[,,Follows,LivesIn]) │ COUNT(LABEL(r._ID,[,,Follows,LivesIn])) │
│ STRING                           │ INT64                                   │
├──────────────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ LivesIn                          │ 4                                       │
│ Follows                          │ 4                                       │
└──────────────────────────────────┴─────────────────────────────────────────┘
```
It takes a lot of manual typing and remembering the Cypher syntax for `label(x)` to get the results in two separate statements.

## Suggested syntax

It would be great to expose a function that does this in one single command.

```cypher
CALL get_db_stats() RETURN *;
```

Or something along those lines, to return a combined table that shows the number of nodes and relationships, grouped by the table name. Neo4j's APOC does this via [apoc.meta.stats](https://neo4j.com/labs/apoc/4.4/overview/apoc.meta/apoc.meta.stats/).

## Why is this useful?

After a large data ingestion job, it can be very useful to run a single command to check that the right number of nodes and relationships exist in the database. Many visualization tools do this by default. Examples of G.V() and Neo4j browser below.

#### G.V()

![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/cc0be4ca-0b24-4611-8148-f8246673b801)

#### Neo4j browser

![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/c038475e-57b4-41a1-8046-25f1c4058044)


## Downstream benefit

If this is implemented, we can pass the results to the Kuzu Explorer UI so that we can display the statistics when the user opens the UI, similar to how other visualization tools do it.

MATCH (n) 
RETURN label(n), COUNT(label(n));

MATCH ()-[r]->() 
RETURN label(r), COUNT(label(r));
CALL get_db_stats() RETURN *;

I don't know what the cause of this is because sometimes when I terminate the process I am able to reconnect just fine; it is not clear how to fix the database to go back to a version that I can query from and I have to reload everything from scratch which is often time consuming.
