title: Bug: Inconsistent behaviour of `to_json` function
body:
### Kùzu version

v0.8.2

### What operating system are you using?

MacOS Sequoia 15.3.1

### What happened?

First off, I'm loving kuzu -- great job everyone!

I'm attempting to write a query returning nodes for which a particular JSON property matches a user-provided query in the form of a path and expected value. In python:

```python
conn.execute(
    """\
    MATCH (n)
    WHERE json_extract(n.property, $p) = $v
    RETURN n
    """,
    parameters={
        "p": "path/into/json",
        "v": "value",
    },
)
```
This results in an exception:
```
RuntimeError: Binder exception: Data type of expression json_extract(n.property,$p) should not be modified.
```

This seems a little odd, but not the end of the world. Modifying the query slightly, wrapping the right-hand side of the comparison in `to_json` allows the query to run, but this is where I start seeing strange behaviour -- certain values yield strange results. Rather than worry about creating and populating a table to test, It's easier to illustrate with a simpler example:

```cypher
RETURN json_extract(json_object("foo", XXX), "foo") = to_json(XXX);
```
Aside from `NULL`, I'd expect the above to return `true` for any valid JSON, but it doesn't.

## Works as expected

✅ String value (`"bar"`)
```
kuzu> RETURN json_extract(json_object("foo", "bar"), "foo") = to_json("bar");
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ EQUALS(json_extract(json_object(foo,bar),foo),to_json(bar)) │
│ BOOL                                                        │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ True                                                        │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

✅ Integer value (`5`)
```
kuzu> RETURN json_extract(json_object("foo", 5), "foo") = to_json(5);
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ EQUALS(json_extract(json_object(foo,5),foo),to_json(5)) │
│ BOOL                                                    │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ True                                                    │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

✅ Boolean value (`true`)
```
kuzu> RETURN json_extract(json_object("foo", true), "foo") = to_json(true);
┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ EQUALS(json_extract(json_object(foo,True),foo),to_json(True)) │
│ BOOL                                                          │
├───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ True                                                          │
└───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

## Unexpected results

❌ String containing integer (`"5"`)
```
kuzu> RETURN json_extract(json_object("foo", "5"), "foo") = to_json("5");
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ EQUALS(json_extract(json_object(foo,5),foo),to_json(5)) │
│ BOOL                                                    │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ False                                                   │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

❌ String containing boolean (`"true"`)
```
kuzu> RETURN json_extract(json_object("foo", "true"), "foo") = to_json("true");
┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ EQUALS(json_extract(json_object(foo,true),foo),to_json(true)) │
│ BOOL                                                          │
├───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ False                                                         │
└───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

The left-hand side (`json_extract`) is always returning what I'd expect -- a JSON-encoded string. The right-hand side (`to_json`) appears to sometimes interpret its input as a literal and sometimes interpret as a JSON document. Since, in my use case, both the path and value are provided by the user, I appear to have no choice but to make use of `to_json` (else hit a binder exception) but that has gives unexpected results.

### Are there known steps to reproduce?

Prerequisite:
```
INSTALL JSON;
LOAD EXTENSION JSON;
```

Minimal examples highlighting inconsistent behaviour of `to_json`:
```
kuzu> RETURN to_json(5);
┌────────────┐
│ to_json(5) │
│ json       │
├────────────┤
│ 5          │
└────────────┘
kuzu> RETURN to_json("5");
┌────────────┐
│ to_json(5) │
│ json       │
├────────────┤
│ 5          │
└────────────┘
kuzu> RETURN to_json(true);
┌───────────────┐
│ to_json(True) │
│ json          │
├───────────────┤
│ true          │
└───────────────┘
kuzu> RETURN to_json("true");
┌───────────────┐
│ to_json(true) │
│ json          │
├───────────────┤
│ true          │
└───────────────┘

code_snippets.code:
conn.execute(
    """\
    MATCH (n)
    WHERE json_extract(n.property, $p) = $v
    RETURN n
    """,
    parameters={
        "p": "path/into/json",
        "v": "value",
    },
)
RuntimeError: Binder exception: Data type of expression json_extract(n.property,$p) should not be modified.
RETURN json_extract(json_object("foo", XXX), "foo") = to_json(XXX);

INSTALL JSON;
LOAD EXTENSION JSON;

### API

Python

### Description

I'm not deeply familiar with Kuzu's internals, so I'm not sure how feasible this would be, but I believe integrating with Apple's GPU architecture could be highly beneficial. Specifically, enabling data to reside in a central location while allowing users to select the device for executing operations could lead to significant performance gains.

I've had a great experience using Apple's [MLX library](https://ml-explore.github.io/mlx/build/html/index.html) for ML tasks that demand high memory capacity. It's early days for that library and it is not quite as mature as torch. But for what it can do I have found it more performant than torch's mps backend and I think it has potential to be a lot more performant than a purely CPU implementation especially since it can fit a lot more memory onto the GPU than NVIDIA chips can for the same hardware cost.

title: Feature: Add utility `transform` function for `RECURSIVE_REL` (named paths; recursive patterns)

labels.name: type: feature
labels.description: New features or missing components of existing features

body:
### API

Other

### Description

We get `RECURSIVE_REL`, when dealing with recursive queries or named paths, like `p` or `e`:
```cypher
MATCH p = (u:User)-[e*]->(u2:User) RETURN p, e;
```
and its output is quite verbose:
```cypher
kuzu> MATCH p = (u:User)-[*]->(u2:User) RETURN p;
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ p                                                                                                                                                                                        │
│ RECURSIVE_REL                                                                                                                                                                            │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ {_NODES: [{_ID: 0:0, _LABEL: User, name: Adam, age: 30},{_ID: 0:1, _LABEL: User, name: Karissa, age: 40},{_ID: 0:2, _LABEL: User, name: Zhang, age: 50},{_ID: 0:3, _LABEL: User, name... │
│ {_NODES: [{_ID: 0:0, _LABEL: User, name: Adam, age: 30},{_ID: 0:2, _LABEL: User, name: Zhang, age: 50},{_ID: 0:3, _LABEL: User, name: Noura, age: 25}], _RELS: [(0:0)-{_LABEL: Follow... │
│ {_NODES: [{_ID: 0:0, _LABEL: User, name: Adam, age: 30},{_ID: 0:1, _LABEL: User, name: Karissa, age: 40},{_ID: 0:2, _LABEL: User, name: Zhang, age: 50}], _RELS: [(0:0)-{_LABEL: Foll... │
│ {_NODES: [{_ID: 0:0, _LABEL: User, name: Adam, age: 30},{_ID: 0:2, _LABEL: User, name: Zhang, age: 50}], _RELS: [(0:0)-{_LABEL: Follows, _ID: 2:1, since: 2020}->(0:2)]}                 │
│ {_NODES: [{_ID: 0:0, _LABEL: User, name: Adam, age: 30},{_ID: 0:1, _LABEL: User, name: Karissa, age: 40}], _RELS: [(0:0)-{_LABEL: Follows, _ID: 2:0, since: 2020}->(0:1)]}               │
│ {_NODES: [{_ID: 0:1, _LABEL: User, name: Karissa, age: 40},{_ID: 0:2, _LABEL: User, name: Zhang, age: 50},{_ID: 0:3, _LABEL: User, name: Noura, age: 25}], _RELS: [(0:1)-{_LABEL: Fol... │
│ {_NODES: [{_ID: 0:1, _LABEL: User, name: Karissa, age: 40},{_ID: 0:2, _LABEL: User, name: Zhang, age: 50}], _RELS: [(0:1)-{_LABEL: Follows, _ID: 2:2, since: 2021}->(0:2)]}              │
│ {_NODES: [{_ID: 0:2, _LABEL: User, name: Zhang, age: 50},{_ID: 0:3, _LABEL: User, name: Noura, age: 25}], _RELS: [(0:2)-{_LABEL: Follows, _ID: 2:3, since: 2022}->(0:3)]}                │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```
There might be need for a custom and/or more concise output format like
```
[Karissa-:Follows->Zhang]
```
instead of 
```
[(0:1)-{_LABEL: Follows, _ID: 2:2, since: 2021}->(0:2)]
```
With current functions, custom `RECURSIVE_REL` is hard to implement (can it?), as nodes / `_NODES` and relations / `_RELS` are separated in `STRUCT`, `REL` instances only contain internal id of node and one might be interested in domain ID or other node descriptor like `name`.

Here is a pseudo-code implementation using fictive `list_find(["a","b","c"], "b")` function using predicates dealing with internal node ids of `_src` and `_dest` of rel. Desired rel record output here would be `SRC_NAME-:REL_LABEL->DST_NAME`, e.g. `Karissa-:Follows->Zhang`:
```cypher
MATCH p = (u:User)-[*]->(u2:User) 
RETURN list_transform(
  rels(p), 
  r -> list_find(nodes(p),n -> id(n) = r._src).name +
  "-:" + label(r) + "->" + 
  list_find(nodes(p),n -> id(n) = r._dst).name);
```


### Suggestion 
Provide `rel_transform`/`rel_map` utility function to create a custom output for `RECURSIVE_REL`.
This function receives `p` (`RECURSIVE_REL`) and a mapper lambda with parameters `src_node`, `dst_node`, `rel`.

Example 1: Format `RECURSIVE_REL` as string:
```cypher
MATCH p = (u:User)-[*]->(u2:User)
RETURN rel_transform(
  p, 
  (src_node, dst_node, rel) -> src_node.name + "-:" + label(rel) + "->" + dst_node.name)
```

Example 2: Output `RECURSIVE_REL` as mapped tuple:
```cypher
MATCH p = (u:User)-[*]->(u2:User)
RETURN rel_transform(
  p, 
  (src_node, dst_node, rel) -> [src_node.name, label(rel), dst_node.name]
```

In summary, this function can provide custom processing of `RECURSIVE_REL` data type directly within Kuzu. Currently a post-processing step is needed via client API/programming language.

### Alternative
Provide `LIST` and `ARRAY` `reduce` function in combination with `STRUCT`enhancement functions like `keys()`, `values()`, `add()`/`append()` to process `RECURSIVE_REL` (similar to Python `functools.reduce`). As described, this also would need some kind of `list_find` to map between  `_RELS` and `_NODES`.

code_snippets.code: MATCH p = (u:User)-[e*]->(u2:User) RETURN p, e;
[Karissa-:Follows->Zhang]

MATCH p = (u:User)-[*]->(u2:User) 
RETURN list_transform(
  rels(p), 
  r -> list_find(nodes(p),n -> id(n) = r._src).name +
  "-:" + label(r) + "->" + 
  list_find(nodes(p),n -> id(n) = r._dst).name);

MATCH p = (u:User)-[*]->(u2:User)
RETURN rel_transform(
  p, 
  (src_node, dst_node, rel) -> src_node.name + "-:" + label(rel) + "->" + dst_node.name)

MATCH p = (u:User)-[*]->(u2:User)
RETURN rel_transform(
  p, 
  (src_node, dst_node, rel) -> [src_node.name, label(rel), dst_node.name]

title: Feature: Possibility to use JOIN with LOAD FROM when importing data from a SQL database

labels.name: type: feature
labels.description: New features or missing components of existing features

body:
### API

Python

### Description

Hi everyone,

As previously discussed here: https://github.com/kuzudb/kuzu/discussions/4944, it would be very useful to have the capability to LOAD FROM a SQL database using JOIN operations.

My usecase is the following:

I have a complex Postgres database with a lot of tables. A part of the database corresponds to "cities" with objects "stations" connected to other stations via the object called "railroad". 

I want to leverage the power of kuzu to find paths and do analytics in this graph of cities subpart of the global database.

I would like to copy cities and the railroad connections between from my Postgres DB into kuzu using the `COPY FROM` feature.

The connections between cities can only be retrieved with JOIN operations. And in addition, some attributes of the cities are foreign keys to an attribute table.

Here is an example : 

**city table**
| id | city       | country_id |
| -- | --------- | ------- |
| 1   | Berlin  |  1   |
| 2   | Paris |  2   |
| 3   | Munich  |  1  |
| 4   | Rome  |  3  |

**country table**
| id | name       |
| -- | --------- | 
| 1   | Germany  |
| 2   | France | 
| 3   | Italy | 

**station table**
| id | name   | city_id |
| -- | ------ | ------- |
| 1   |  Gare Austerlitz  |  2  | 
| 2   |  Gare Montparnasse  |  2  | 
| 3   | Berlin Hauptbahnhof |   1  | 
| 4   | München Hauptbahnhof  |  3  | 
| 5   | Rome Termini     |  4   | 

**railroad table**
| id | name       | station_start_id | station_dest_id | travel_duration_h |
| -- | --------- | ---------- | ---------- | ------- |
| 1   |  Paris-Berlin-1  |  1  |  3  | 10  |
| 2   | Paris-Munich-SNCF  |  2  |  4  |  9  |

What I am to get into Kuzu is the following:
* Nodes of type `City` with the following attributes: `id`, `name` and `country` (field `name` from the table `country`)
* Relations of type `ConnectedTo` with the following attribute `travel_duration_h`

The connections are then:
1. `Paris - [Paris-Berlin-1 (10)] -> Berlin`
2. `Paris - [Paris-Munich-SNCF (9)] -> Munich`

It would be awesome to be able to do something like:
```
COPY City FROM pg.city
JOIN pg.country ON pg.country.id = pg.city.country_id
WHERE pg.country.name in ('Germany', 'France')
RETURN pg.city.name, pg.country.name
```

```
COPY ConnectedTo FROM pg.railroad
JOIN pg.station AS station_start ON station_start.id = pg.railroad.station_start_id
JOIN pg.city AS city_start ON city_start.id = station_start.city_id
JOIN pg.station AS station_dest ON station_dest.id = pg.railroad.station_dest_id
JOIN pg.city AS city_dest ON city_dest.id = station_dest.city_id
RETURN city_start.name, city_dest.name, pg.railroad.travel_duration_h
```

COPY City FROM pg.city
JOIN pg.country ON pg.country.id = pg.city.country_id
WHERE pg.country.name in ('Germany', 'France')
RETURN pg.city.name, pg.country.name

COPY ConnectedTo FROM pg.railroad
JOIN pg.station AS station_start ON station_start.id = pg.railroad.station_start_id
JOIN pg.city AS city_start ON city_start.id = station_start.city_id
JOIN pg.station AS station_dest ON station_dest.id = pg.railroad.station_dest_id
JOIN pg.city AS city_dest ON city_dest.id = station_dest.city_id
RETURN city_start.name, city_dest.name, pg.railroad.travel_duration_h

title: Bug: Adding Large number of edges causes database to crash without explanation
body:
### Kùzu version

v0.8.0

### What operating system are you using?

macOS Sequoia 15.3.1

### What happened?

I have an application where adding edges to the database will randomly cause kuzu to crash and the edge table needs to be deleted. The failure happens sporadically because the program will crash at different times throughout my data ingestion process and I will rerun the step where it failed and then the data ingestion process will work for that step only to fail at a later step or at a step that worked before. I have ruled out this being do to size or data types used because I have randomly generated nodes and edges of the same size and the database creation process has worked fine. I also ruled out this being due to parallelization. I added steps to reproduce below and if there is an error on schema definition or something like that, I think one improvement would be failing more gracefully than the current process which simply fails and seems to corrupt the database until the "ComponentOf" table is deleted.

### Are there known steps to reproduce?

I was not able to upload the parquet files that lead to this issue (probably because they are large) but am happy to provide them. They are quite large; about 340M records in total:
# Schema
```cypher
# Num Table
CREATE NODE TABLE Num (id SERIAL,adsh STRING,tag STRING,version STRING,ddate INT32,qtrs INT32,uom STRING,dimh STRING,iprx INT32,value DOUBLE,footnote STRING,footlen INT32,dimn INT32,coreg STRING,durp DOUBLE,datp DOUBLE,dcml INT32,partition_name STRING, PRIMARY KEY(id));
# Cal Table
CREATE NODE TABLE Cal (id SERIAL,adsh STRING,grp INT32,arc INT32,negative INT8,ptag STRING,pversion STRING,ctag STRING,cversion STRING,partition_name STRING, PRIMARY KEY(id));
# Relationship table
CREATE REL TABLE ComponentOf (FROM Num TO Num, grp INT32,arc INT32,negative INT8,MANY_MANY);
```
# Data Ingestion
```python
import kuzu
import polars as pl
import numpy as np
import tqdm
new_db = kuzu.Database("test_db") # point to wherever db is created with schema from above
conn = kuzu.Connection(new_db)
conn.execute("COPY Num from 'num/*.parquet'")
conn.execute("COPY Cal from 'cal/*.parquet'")
```
```python
all_partitions = (
    conn.execute(
        """
    MATCH (n:Num)
    return distinct n.partition_name
    """
    )
    .get_as_pl()
    .sort("n.partition_name")
)  # type: ignore
edge_partitions = conn.execute(
    """
    MATCH (n2:Num)-[c:ComponentOf]->(n1:Num)
    return distinct n1.partition_name
    """
).get_as_pl()  # type: ignore
missing_edge_partitions = all_partitions.filter(
    ~pl.col("n.partition_name").is_in([x for x in edge_partitions.to_numpy().flatten()])
).sort("n.partition_name")
for partition_name in tqdm.tqdm(missing_edge_partitions.to_numpy().flatten()):
    i += 1
    conn.execute(
        f"""
        MATCH (n1:Num{{partition_name:'{partition_name}'}}),
            (n2:Num{{partition_name:'{partition_name}'}}),
            (c:Cal{{partition_name:'{partition_name}'}})
        where n1.adsh = n2.adsh and n1.ddate = n2.ddate and n1.qtrs = n2.qtrs
        and n1.uom = n2.uom and n1.dimh = n2.dimh and n1.iprx = n2.iprx
        and n1.adsh = c.adsh
        and c.ptag = n2.tag and c.pversion = n2.version
        and c.ctag = n1.tag and c.cversion = n1.version
        MERGE (n1)-[ComponentOf{{grp: c.grp, arc: c.arc, negative: c.negative}}]->(n2)
        """
    )
```

title: An experimental integration of Kùzu-WASM
body:
Dear Kùzu Team,
We're excited to share that as soon as we heard about the release of Kùzu-WASM, we promptly integrated it into our [GraphScope portal](https://github.com/GraphScope/portal). We are pleased with the successful integration and warmly invite you to experience it. Simply follow the link below and complete two easy steps: https://gsp.vercel.app/#/explore.
 Here is a simple example to get you started.

## Step 1: Import CSVs to create graphs. 

You can upload your own files or the example CSVs under https://github.com/alibaba/GraphScope/tree/main/flex/interactive/examples. Please note that each CSV file should store vertices or edges with the same label. You don't need to specify whether each file represents vertices or edges, but you need to ensure that each CSV file includes a header.

![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/9c21f311-4ec9-47f7-a3a3-0a456fcb0034)

![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/46d0e7a8-402f-44bc-909f-f0e98dbe007f)

![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/d37dc01d-a255-4232-a0eb-3835c09152d4)


After you click the button "Load CSV Files with Kùzu-WASM", the corresponding statements of creating schemas and inserting data will be generated. And with a whoosh, the data is stored in Kuzu-WASM!

## Step 2: Query with Kùzu-WASM. 

Then, you can perform the first query with the searchbar.
![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/90dbd8b5-aa0f-4e0a-a3d8-e3a0445d6a62)


You can query papers according to their publish years and the papers will be categorized accordingly. These queries are generated and executed automatically with Kùzu-WASM.

By clicking the nodes in the graph, you can get the properties of the nodes, and the statistics about the nodes, which is also obtained by querying with Kùzu-WASM.

![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/296b4b3d-e784-4ebd-afa4-26fc390f3e39)

Of course, we also support users directly entering Cypher queries for execution.

![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/c9d88a99-01b3-4dde-886d-e8151a9550ee)

By the way, we’ve discovered that Kùzu-WASM, as an out-of-the-box graph database for browsers, helps lower development barriers and inspire innovation. This is truly beneficial for everyone. We sincerely thank the Kùzu team for their excellent work.

title: Bug: Clarify `r, n` in recursive relation filter `(r,n | WHERE ...)`
body:
### Kùzu version

nightly

### What operating system are you using?

_No response_

### What happened?

Consider following graph:
```cypher
CREATE NODE TABLE V (id int PRIMARY KEY);
CREATE REL TABLE E (FROM V TO V, val STRING);
CREATE (:V {id: 1})-[:E {val: "foo"}]->(:V {id: 2});
```
and a recursive query with predicate:
```cypher
MATCH (a)-[:E * (r,n | WHERE n.id = 1)]->(b) RETURN *;
```
I'd assume `r` is set to `:E` relation above, and `n` is NOOP/unset variable, as there is just 1 intermediate hop. Endpoint nodes are covered by `a` and `b` variables and no `n` node in-between exists with current data.

At least below queries reflect this assumption (it doesn't matter what value `x` is typed for `WHERE n.id = x`):
```cypher
kuzu> MATCH (a)-[:E * (r,n | WHERE n.id = 1)]->(b) RETURN *;
┌──────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────┐
│ a                            │ b                            │
│ NODE                         │ NODE                         │
├──────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────┤
│ {_ID: 0:0, _LABEL: V, id: 1} │ {_ID: 0:1, _LABEL: V, id: 2} │                                                                                                                                
└──────────────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────┘                                                                                                                                
                                                                                                                                                                                               
kuzu> MATCH (a)-[:E * (r,n | WHERE n.id = 100000)]->(b) RETURN *;                                                                                                                              
┌──────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────┐                                                                                                                                
│ a                            │ b                            │                                                                                                                                
│ NODE                         │ NODE                         │                                                                                                                                
├──────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────┤                                                                                                                                
│ {_ID: 0:0, _LABEL: V, id: 1} │ {_ID: 0:1, _LABEL: V, id: 2} │                                                                                                                                
└──────────────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────┘                                                                                                                                
```                                                                                                                                                                                            
                                                                                                                                                                                               
On the other side, `label(n)` is evaluated (to false in last case) and not ignored:                                                                                                            
```cypher                                                                                                                                                                                      
kuzu> MATCH (a)-[:E * (r,n | WHERE label(n) = "V")]->(b) RETURN *;                                                                                                                             
┌──────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────┐                                                                                                                                
│ a                            │ b                            │                                                                                                                                
│ NODE                         │ NODE                         │                                                                                                                                
├──────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────┤                                                                                                                                
│ {_ID: 0:0, _LABEL: V, id: 1} │ {_ID: 0:1, _LABEL: V, id: 2} │                                                                                                                                
└──────────────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────┘                                                                                                                                
                                                                                                                                                                                               
kuzu> MATCH (a)-[:E * (r,n | WHERE label(n) = "Foo")]->(b) RETURN *;                                                                                                                           
┌──────┬──────┐                                                                                                                                                                                
│ a    │ b    │                                                                                                                                                                                
│ NODE │ NODE │                                                                                                                                                                                
├──────┼──────┤                                                                                                                                                                                
└──────┴──────┘                                                                                                                                                                                
```                                                                                                                                                                                            
Hence I am not sure about current behavior of `r` and `n`: Shouldn't Kuzu raise an error, if `n` in a recursive filter predicate is used, given there are not intermediate nodes and this variable cannot be set to any node? Alternatively every expression involving `n` might be made NOOP.

_No response_

title: Optimization: Hardcoded regular expressions are being compiled many times
body:
### Description

This query from ClickBench is heavily bottlenecked by our regex performance: `MATCH (h:hits) WHERE h.Title =~ '.*Google.*' AND NOT h.URL =~ '.*\\.google\\..*' AND h.SearchPhrase <> '' RETURN h.SearchPhrase, MIN(h.URL), MIN(h.Title), COUNT(*) AS c, COUNT(DISTINCT h.UserID) ORDER BY c DESC LIMIT 10;` (not that the original query uses a regex match, but we don't have a `LIKE` operator [original sql query for reference](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickBench/blob/3255f83b92b9d1ae3cb56e1166c06026dcadb246/clickhouse/queries.sql#L23)).

See https://github.com/kuzudb/kuzu/pull/4881#issuecomment-2651119621: it takes 17s with the regex match compared to ~2.5s using `contains` instead.

Performance profiling shows that about 67% of the runtime is spent repeatedly compiling the regex (and a further 4% destroying the regex afterwards), despite it being the same each time.
Being able to compile the regex once and re-use it would speed things up significantly.
![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/a343c7e5-7a14-4e2f-929e-201a29a1c84d)

title: Feature: Support customized stopword list in full text search

labels.name: type: feature
labels.description: New features or missing components of existing features

body:
### API

Python

### Description

# Motivation
Kùzu currently uses a predefined english stopwords when building a full text search index. However, it is common for users to define their own list of stopwords in a practical use case.

For example:
The predefined english stopwords covers all english numbers: `six`, `five` ....
Users may not want to skip those keywords in their use case.

# Proposal
We are going to extend our `CREATE_FTS_INDEX` function with an additional parameter:
```
CALL CREATE_FTS_INDEX(TABLE_NAME, INDEX_NAME, PROPERTY_LIST, STOP_WORDS := STOP_WORD)
```
The `STOP_WORD` is an optional parameter and it can be:
1. A file path: contains a single column of stopwords.  (The path can be a S3/local/http path path)
2. A table name in kuzu: contains a single string column of stopwords.

For example:
```
# Create a full text search index and uses the stopwords list which stores at s3.
CALL CREATE_FTS_INDEX('doc', 'doc_idx', ['author', 'title'], STOP_WORDS := 's3://kuzu-stopwords/english.txt')

# Create a full text search index and uses a kuzu table which stores all stopwords.
CALL CREATE_FTS_INDEX('doc', 'doc_idx', ['author', 'title'], STOP_WORDS := 'doc_stopwords')
```

Rules:
1. Customized stopwords must be provided at the time when the full text search index is created. If not provided, the default english stopwords will be used.
2. Once the fts index is created, users are not allowed to modify the stopwords list of the index and the same stopwords list will be used when querying the fts index.
3.  Each full text search index can use its own stopwords list, meaning that different full text search indexes can have different sets of stopwords.

# Implementation:
When the user creates a fts index with:
1. Customized stopwords list: an internal table named `[table_id]_[index_name]_stopwords`, which stores the user given stopwords list, will be created and used for tokenizing words.
2. Default stopwords list: we will reuse the internal default englsish stopwords table for tokenizing words.
 
# Testing:
1. Test invalid s3 url stopwords.
2. Test s3 url stopwords without auth.
3. Test given stopwords path is a directory.
4. Test stopwords file with wrong format (e.g. more than one column)
5. Test given stopwords list is empty. (meaning no stopwords)
6. Test UTF8 stopwords list
7. Test INVALID-UTF8 stopwords list (we should error). 
8. Test stopwords list containing special characters (e.g. `\`, `/`)
9. Test the given stopwords file is deleted after the index is created.
10. Test the given stopwords table is dropped/altered after the index is created.

# Create a full text search index and uses a kuzu table which stores all stopwords.
CALL CREATE_FTS_INDEX('doc', 'doc_idx', ['author', 'title'], STOP_WORDS := 'doc_stopwords')

title: Optimization: remove lock from RandomEngine
body:
### Description

The lock is introduced in https://github.com/kuzudb/kuzu/pull/4827 to address race conditions, however, it creates bottleneck in the pipeline.

The correct way to handle this is to introduce `LocalState` into `ScalarFunction` and each function instance (e.g., `gen_random_uuid` in each thread) would have its own `RandomEngine` with a unique seed generated from the `randomEngine` under `ClientContext`.

This requires rework of the interface and implementation of `ScalarFunction` and `ExpressionEvaluator`.

title: [COPY FROM] Error: Binder exception: Cannot copy into <myname> table with type REL_GROUP.
body:
### Example
`user.csv`
```
id,name
ef2b4363-66ab-4a2f-af59-f7f6cd80f250,Adam
8082bb02-7c30-4a06-8600-885df4fc0eab,Karissa
```

`post.csv`
```
id,content
055f6041-8bab-4ce6-a201-b85dab43442a,content1
b510506a-1208-4c2a-a916-f83b483b0249,content2
```

`likes.csv`
```
ef2b4363-66ab-4a2f-af59-f7f6cd80f250,055f6041-8bab-4ce6-a201-b85dab43442a
ef2b4363-66ab-4a2f-af59-f7f6cd80f250,8082bb02-7c30-4a06-8600-885df4fc0eab
```

```cypher
CREATE NODE TABLE User (id UUID PRIMARY KEY, name STRING);
CREATE NODE TABLE Post (id UUID PRIMARY KEY, content STRING);
CREATE REL TABLE GROUP likes(FROM User TO User, FROM User TO Post);

COPY User FROM "user.csv" (header=true);
COPY Post FROM "post.csv" (header=true);

COPY likes FROM "likes.csv";
// Error: Binder exception: Cannot copy into likes table with type REL_GROUP.
```

### Question

Is there a solution planned to allow REL GROUP (or more in general rel unions, as REL GROUP is deprecated) + COPY FROM imports?

### Proposal

Two ideas:
- The actual rel union type can be derived by following FROM/TO id constituents, assuming node IDs are unambiguous amongst rel unions (e.g. with `UUID`).
- Allow a discriminator column for rel unions. `likes.csv` example, with discriminators for FROM/TO appended:
```
ef2b4363-66ab-4a2f-af59-f7f6cd80f250,055f6041-8bab-4ce6-a201-b85dab43442a,User,Post
ef2b4363-66ab-4a2f-af59-f7f6cd80f250,8082bb02-7c30-4a06-8600-885df4fc0eab,User,User
```

Related: https://github.com/kuzudb/kuzu/issues/3627

Kuzu 0.7.1

title: Bug: [JAVA-API] Duplicated records being returned
body:
### Kùzu version

v0.7.2-dev-37

### What operating system are you using?

MacOS & Windows

### What happened?

The Java API appears to be returning duplicated records for every query being ran.
For instance, `MATCH (s:Comment) RETURN s LIMIT 50` will return the same comment node 50 times. Each time a new query is run, that behaviour persists but with a different node.
The `FlatTuples` extracted from the `QueryResult` all point to the exact same node when using the `hasNext()`/`getNext()` pattern, so it looks like either `getNext()` is not moving the cursor on the query result or the query result itself contains duplicated information.
Variations of queries with `DISTINCT` lead to the same result, but `COUNT` queries accurately return node counts.

### Are there known steps to reproduce?

This can be reproduced on the Java API using the LDBC test sample from Kuzu Explorer. To reproduce this, you need to create a Database instance in the Java API pointing to a dataset, then run one of the queries suggested above. This appears to happen consistently for all datasets.

title: Bug: List lambda functions don't work if lists are longer than vector size
body:
### Kùzu version

master

### What operating system are you using?

Ubuntu 22

### What happened?

In `ListLambdaEvaluator`, the result vector is stored as value vector of the list's data type (instead of as the list type itself). If `evaluate()` is called on the lambda evaluator with an input vector larger than the value vector capacity, we will get an assertion error due to attempting to write a larger vector than will fit in the result vector. 

This bug can be reproduced with the following python script (the last line/query triggers the assertion failure):
```py
import kuzu
from tempfile import TemporaryDirectory

with TemporaryDirectory() as temp_dir:
    db = kuzu.Database(temp_dir)
    conn = kuzu.Connection(db)
    conn.execute("create node table tab(id int64, vals int64[], primary key (id))")
    conn.execute("create (:tab {id: 0, vals: list_creation()})")
    # for some reason using the below query only generates a list of size 2, not sure if this is also a bug
    # conn.execute(
    #     "unwind range(1, 5000) as i match (t:tab) set t.vals = list_append(t.vals, i)"
    # )
    for i in range(5000):
        conn.execute(f"match (t:tab) set t.vals = list_append(t.vals, {i})")
    print(
        conn.execute(
            "match (t:tab) return list_transform(t.vals, x -> x + 2)"
        ).get_as_df()
    )
```

A proposed solution would be the store the result vector in `ListLambdaEvaluator` as a vector of lists (which can then be resized as needed).

### Are there known steps to reproduce?

_No response_

title: Bug: Default values when adding new columns doesn't work if casting of a literal is required
body:
### Kùzu version

master

### What operating system are you using?

Ubuntu 22

### What happened?

Idea is similar to https://github.com/kuzudb/kuzu/issues/4389. Consider the queries:
```
create node table Person(id INT64, PRIMARY KEY (id))
create rel table likes (from person to person);
alter table likes add years int32 default 0
```

The query `alter table likes add years int32 default 0` will fail with the message 
```
Runtime exception: Cannot set a non-constant default value when adding columns on REL tables.
```
This is because the literal `0` needs to be casted from int64 to int32, and we don't consider the casted value a constant.

Similarly, the statement `alter table likes add years float default 5.4` will also fail.

### Are there known steps to reproduce?

_No response_

title: Feature: Better error messages when forgetting to load extension

labels.name: type: feature
labels.description: New features or missing components of existing features

body:
### API

Other

### Description

Currently, the error message displayed when I try to query the FTS index (which requires me to first load the FTS extension) isn't very informative when I actually forget to load the extension beforehand.

Here is the sequence of steps:

- I create the FTS index using a Python script
- The script runs, index finishes building, and the script exits
- I open a CLI window
- But I very commonly forget to run INSTALL FTS; LOAD EXTENSION FTS;  in the beginning to load the FTS extension
- I try to run the CALL QUERY_FTS_INDEX() command and then I get this error message:

```
Error: Catalog exception: function QUERY_FTS_INDEX does not exist.
```

Can we improve this error message a bit? Ideally, it would inform the user that this function is only accessible once the FTS extension package is loaded. At the very least, it should inform the user about something generic, like "This command requires an extension to be loaded beforehand", so that the user immediately knows what to do next.

#### Motivation for better error messages

Users coming from other systems that have these indexes inbuilt, rather than requiring an extension, may not remember or know that one needs to install and load the extension each time a new CLI or client session to the Kùzu database is opened. Having a more helpful error message that immediately tells the user what's wrong and how they can fix it is beneficial for newcomers to Kùzu, and to make it more usable.

code_snippets.code: Error: Catalog exception: function QUERY_FTS_INDEX does not exist.

title: Optimization: Enable SIP based on cardinality information without a filter
body:
### Description

When we're trying to apply SIP from the build side to the probe side, or from the probe side to the build side, we only choose to apply SIP when there is filter on the build or probe side. This is to avoid worst cases that cardinality estimation can be very wrong. However, this also limits the use of SIP in scenarios where output distinct values is small and serve as "filters": 
1. Num of distinct Dst nodes scanned from the rel table can be small. E.g., `MATCH (a)-[e]->(b) RETURN b.id`. For plan `JOIN(SCAN(b))(Scan(a)Extend(e))`, `Scan(a)Extend(e)` can be selective if `e` contains few distinct `b` nodes as dst.
2. Table function can output few distinct nodes. Vector index search can serve as an example as it usually outputs only top `k` tuples, which is usually much smaller compared to the base node table.  Note that `SIPDirection::FORCE_BUILD_TO_PROBE` is now used in vector index search to force SIP, which should be refactored away along with addressing this issue.

title: Feature: Add random sampling function to help users use Kùzu for training GNNs

labels.name: type: feature
labels.description: New features or missing components of existing features

body:
### API

Other

### Description

Kùzu is mentioned in the following paper about using a graph database as a backend while training GNNs.
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2411.11375

As described in Figure 4 of the paper, one of the key steps during training is to perform random sampling of the returned nodes from a 2-hop query as follows:

```cypher
MATCH (node_0:$NODE_TYPE)
WHERE node_0.id IN $SEED_NODES
OPTIONAL MATCH (node_0)-[rel_1:$REL_TYPE]->(node_1:$NODE_TYPE)-[rel_2:$REL_TYPE]->(node_2:$NODE_TYPE)
WITH node_0, node_1, node_2
ORDER BY rand()
LIMIT $MAX_NEIGHBOURS
RETURN
    node_0.id as src_id,
    node_1.id, node_1.features,
    node_2.id, node_2.features;
```

The `ORDER BY rand()` part is where the random sampling suffers on two counts:
- The randomness isn't truly random, as the `rand()` function doesn't offer a high enough level of randomness for the purposes of training (The author of the paper noted that they had to do some more workarounds to add more randomness)
- The above query is slow, as it's doing top-k (we could do better from a query performance perspective)

## Feature

Per the author's observations, the desired graph database feature would be to provide a function or some high-level utility in Cypher where the random sampling is pushed down to the database layer and isn't done by PyG in-memory. Could we add such a function that allows users to perform random sampling for the purposes of training GNNs using Kùzu?

title: Feature: Extend `LOAD FROM` clause with `TYPE` option

labels.name: type: feature
labels.description: New features or missing components of existing features

labels.name: area: frontend
labels.description: Frontend, i.e., binder, parser, query planning-related issues

body:
### API

C++

### Description

# Motivation:
## Current Implementation:
When kuzu scans from files, file extension is used to sniff the file format. 
For example: `LOAD FROM 'test.csv'`,
Kuzu uses the file extension `.csv` to infer the file type of `test` is in `CSV` format.

## Issue caused:
1. CSV files may end with a different extension name other than `.CSV` . (e.g. `.tsv`, '.xlsx')
`LOAD FROM 'test.tsv'`. => Exception
2. Certain file formats store data in a directory rather than a single file. Inferring those file formats is quite difficult. (e.g. delta lake, iceberg)
`LOAD FROM 'person-delta-lake'`

# Solution:
I propose that we extend our `LOAD FROM` grammar to accept an additional option: `TYPE`, which indicates the type of the file in the `LOAD FROM` clause. 

## Grammar:
1. Load from
```
LOAD FROM <file_path> (type=<file_format>)
RETURN XXXX
```

2. Copy from
```
COPY FROM <file_path> (type=<file_format>)
```

## Example:
```
LOAD FROM '/tmp/student' (type=delta)
RETURN name, age
```

```
COPY student FROM '/tmp/student' (type=delta)
```

We can make `TYPE` optional, meaning that kuzu still tries to infer the file format when the `TYPE` option is not provided. So:
```
LOAD FROM '/tmp/university.csv'
RETURN name, age
```
still works. However, kuzu should throw an exception when the type inference is impossible:
```
LOAD FROM '/tmp/student'
RETURN name, age
```

title: Optimization: `yy_json` memory allocation improvement

labels.name: type: feature
labels.description: New features or missing components of existing features

body:
### API

C++

### Description

Internally, we use the library `yy_json` to parse `json` strings. 

`yy_json` uses the system default allocator: `malloc` to allocate memory if no allocator is provided. However, fragmentation can be easily caused when the number of allocations is large. To resolve this issue, Duckdb implemented their own allocator which allocates memory from their own `memoryManager` and pass to `yy_json`.

I suggest we do something similar as duckdb to solve this issue.

title: Question: why is the rust build in the Makefile using the MSVC "Debug" Runtime?
body:
0.7.0

in Makefile

```
rust:
ifeq ($(OS),Windows_NT)
	set CFLAGS=/MDd
```

`/MDd` means using Debugging-Runtime as DLL (that means the Runtime is doing the typical more deep testing like Debug-Heap etc. )

https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/cpp/build/reference/md-mt-ld-use-run-time-library?view=msvc-170

Debug builds should(could) use `/MDd`
but Release builds should use `/MD` - without the `d`

Microsoft MSVC behavior is different to Linux here because they provide Debug and Release Versions of Runtime - which are different in speed and active testing (same like with STL - which does in Debug builds also more testing at runtime)

also is the Debug-Runtime only installed when VStudio is also installed

Looks like `&INCREMENTAL_SELECTED_POS.end()` is unsafe in windows.

2. `isUnfiltered` is not safe in windows:
```
    bool isUnfiltered() const { return selectedPositions == INCREMENTAL_SELECTED_POS.data(); }
```
We use pointer based arithmetic in windows to determine a vector is filtered or not, where `INCREMENTAL_SELECTED_POS ` is a static field in selectionVector.
However, the initialization of static fields behaves differently than linux/mac.
```
 (lldb) p selVector.INCREMENTAL_SELECTED_POS.data()
(const unsigned long long *) $49 = 0x00007ffff97b6290 {libfts.kuzu_extension!std::array<unsigned __int64,2048> const kuzu::common::SelectionVector::INCREMENTAL_SELECTED_POS} {0}
(lldb) p selVector.selectedPositions
(unsigned long long *const) $50 = 0x00007ff74d420080 {e2e_test.exe!std::array<unsigned __int64,2048> const kuzu::common::SelectionVector::INCREMENTAL_SELECTED_POS} {0}
```
I suggest we use an enum to indicate whether it is filtered or not.

title: Optimization: Parallelize finalize state of aggregation
body:
### Description

Currently, the `finalizeInternal` function of `HashAggregate` operator is performed in a single threaded manner. 
For aggregations performed on large tables, the finalize becomes a significant bottleneck.

I'm running benchmarks on the MS MARCO dataset for FTS where we do aggregation for creating the index: https://trec-rag.github.io/annoucements/2024-corpus-finalization/

On a small segment partition (#00), the following query:

> MATCH (b:ms_marco_test) WITH tokenize(b.segment) AS tk, OFFSET(ID(b)) AS id UNWIND tk AS t 
RETURN STEM(t, 'porter'), id, count(*);

takes **134322.01ms** to run and just the finalize part takes **84198 ms**.

title: Feature: Test and support GIL-free version of Python 3.13

labels.name: type: feature
labels.description: New features or missing components of existing features

body:
### API

Python

### Description

Python 3.13 includes a [free-threaded mode](https://docs.python.org/3/whatsnew/3.13.html#free-threaded-cpython) which does not enable GIL by default. This should make Python more performant when running multi-threaded code. The free-threaded mode uses a different executable called `python3.13t`. We have been building pre-compiled bins for `python3.13t` on Linux (see https://pypi.org/project/kuzu/0.6.2.dev29/#files) but did not really test whether it works correctly. We should test it and fix any potential error, then extend the support to all platforms as it may benefit users who use multi-threading in Python.

Right now, our end-to-end testing framework runs queries through `prepare` and `execute` interfaces, instead of directly through `query`, to accommodate the needs of enumerating plans and take in encoded joins during testing.

However, this can hide unexpected problems when running queries through the `query` interface. An example is #4502.

title: Feature: Named parameters in Kuzu standalone call function and GDS CALL

labels.name: type: feature
labels.description: New features or missing components of existing features

body:
### API

C++

### Description

# Motivation: 
Some standalone call functions and algorithm functions need a way to allow users configure parameters for computation.
For example:
1. Duckdb allows users to configure the stemmer when building a fts index.
```
PRAGMA create_fts_index('documents', 'document_identifier', 'text_content', stemmer = 'english')
```
Users can choose which stemmer to use when reduce terms to their base case. If the `stemmer` parameter is not given, a default one will be used('porter').

2. Neo4j also allows user to configure parameters in their algorithm functions:
For example, users can configure the dampingFactor in pageRank algorithm by:
```
CALL gds.pageRank.stream('myGraph', {
  dampingFactor: 0.05
})
YIELD nodeId, score
RETURN nodeId, score
```

# Grammar:
Our macro functions already support named parameters:
```
create macro addWithDefault(a,b:=3) as a + b;
```
Users can call the macro function like:
```
return addWithDefault(2); => 2+3 gives 5
return addWithDefault(2, 5);  => 2+5 gives 7
```

I suggest we do something similar to the named parameters in macro functions:

## Standalone Call Functions(fts):
```
CALL CREATE_FTS_INDEX('doc', 'docIdx', ['content', 'author', 'name'], stemmer:='english', lower:=1)
```
Where stemmer and lower are named parameters. 

## GDS:
In GDS calls, we can do something similar (dp stands for the damping factor):
```
PROJECT GRAPH PK (person, knows) 
CALL page_rank(PK, dp := 0.5) 
RETURN _node.fName, rank;
```

## Rules:
The general rules of named parameteres are:
1. If the user doesn't configure a named parameters in the query, default value will be used:
```
CALL CREATE_FTS_INDEX('doc', 'docIdx', ['content', 'author', 'name'], lower:=1)
```
In this case, the default stemmer: `porter` will be used.

2. Named parameters can be given in any order in a query:
```
CALL CREATE_FTS_INDEX('doc', 'docIdx', ['content', 'author', 'name'], lower:=1, stemmer:='english') 

is the same as:
 
CALL CREATE_FTS_INDEX('doc', 'docIdx', ['content', 'author', 'name'], stemmer:='english', lower:=1)
```

3. If multiple named parameters with the same name are given, we should error:
```
CALL CREATE_FTS_INDEX('doc', 'docIdx', ['content', 'author', 'name'], stemmer:='english', stemmer:='arabic')
```

# Testing:
1. Wrong name/type of named parameters. (e.g. CREATE_FTS_INDEX expects stemmer parameter to be `STRING`, but `INT` is given).
2. Duplicate named parameters.
3. Different orders of named parameters yields the same result.

title: Feature: Support multiple statements in a single query in testing framework

labels.name: type: feature
labels.description: New features or missing components of existing features

body:
### API

Other

### Description

Our current testing framework is not able to handle multiple statements in a single query. It currently assumes that a query can only generate one statement.
For example:
```
-STATEMENT RETURN 5; RETURN 3;
-OK
```
Will seg fault.

In FTS, a single `CREATE_FTS_INDEX`call is transformed as multiple statements, so we have to support such query in the testing framework:
```
-STATEMENT CALL CREATE_FTS_INDEX('doc', 'contentIdx', ['content'])
---- ok
```
In PR: https://github.com/kuzudb/kuzu/pull/4416/files#diff-501800c4dbbeeea192cc21ad68e92c0face861a1ff5631895c0f80786ac27aa7, We do a temporary workaround to fix the seg fault.
```
TestQueryResult& testAnswer =
        statement->result[std::min(resultIdx, statement->result.size() - 1)];
```
However, the testing framework should be fixed in a principal way.

title: Optimization: Have single threaded GDS implementation not spawn a new thread
body:
### Description

Both WASM and the current FTS implementation require GDS edgeCompute() functions to run in single threaded manner. Normally no matter how many threads are used, normal execution of GDS functions spawns a new thread.  We have a solution for this in WASM where the "master" thread, which is the thread running the GDSAlgorithm runs the task. We should refactor it so that we can call the runFrontier functions to use the same mechanism and have the option to run single threaded without spawning new threads.

We should also see if we can completely get rid of the spawning thread even if we run in a multi threaded way. This requires the master thread to take the role of a worker thread and then the role of the waiting thread once it exists.

title: Optimization: Global factorized table with concurrent write
body:
### Description

The current factorized table doesn't support concurrent write. Parallelization is done by first creating a local factorized table per thread and then merge into the global factorized table with single thread. This approach works fine until we introduce GDS framework where we have to create a local factorized table per input node per thread and we end up creating millions of very small local factorized table.

A possible solution is to always maintain a global factorized table but with a partition strategy so that different thread can still write to it without lock.

title: Bug: Zone map doesn't work on integer fields smaller than `INT64`
body:
### Kùzu version

master

### What operating system are you using?

Ubuntu 22.04.5 LTS

### What happened?

In the transformer we treat integer literals as either INT64 or INT128.
If we have a table `create node table someTable(..., value INT32, ...)`, the expression `someTable.value < {some literal}` will have the LHS be of type `CAST_INT64(value)` which is of type `ExpressionType::FUNCTION`. The operator `<` can be replaced with any comparison operator.

This becomes a problem in `ColumnPredicateSet::getPredicateSet` because when we try to convert the predicate to a `ColumnConstantPredicate` in `ColumnPredicateUtil::tryConvert()` this will fail as we don't consider predicates with an LHS of type `FUNCTION` to be convertible to `ColumnConstantPredicate`.
As a result, zone mapping will never succeed as there is no `ColumnConstantPredicate` to perform zone mapping on. This will happen for any type that requires a cast to `INT64` to compare against a literal.

title: Bug: Assertion failure in PathPropertyProbe when running Fintech Benchmark
body:
### Kùzu version

master

### What operating system are you using?

Ubuntu 22.04.5 LTS

### What happened?

Occasionally in the Fintech benchmark when running queries `ComplexRead1` or `ComplexRead3`, in `PathPropertyProbe::probe` the hash table probe will fail for some path rel ID value.
```
for (auto i = 0u; i < sizeToProbe; ++i) {
        localState->probedTuples[i] = hashTable->getTupleForHash(localState->hashes[i]); // this will be nullptr
}
```
This will result in the assertion failure (which will probably manifest as a segfault if we have runtime checks disabled)
```
Error: Assertion failed in file "/home/kuzu/kuzu/src/processor/operator/recursive_extend/path_property_probe.cpp" on line 96: localState->matchedTuples[i] != nullptr
```
Another potentially important observation is if you checkpoint and run the query again the assertion failure will not occur.

More specifically, in `HashJoinBuild::finalize` when we build the hash slots the number of tuples in the fTable will be different between the two runs.

### Are there known steps to reproduce?

1. Build kuzu with runtime checks enabled
2. Open the [attached DB](https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/16od-aRrCJLfaMkk5aktKAjyERVNvgLZe?usp=share_link)
3. Run the following query:
```

  p = (account:Account {id: 4615360861165330226})-[edge1:AccountTransferAccount*1..3 (r, n | WHERE timestamp("2021-07-23T06:10:16.747Z") < r.timestamp AND r.timestamp < timestamp("2022-11-29T02:52:22.640Z"))]->(other:Account),
  (other)<-[edge2:MediumSignInAccount]-(medium:Medium {isBlocked: true})
WITH
  edge2.timestamp AS signInTime,
  properties(rels(p), 'timestamp') AS ts,
  length(p) AS pathLength,
  other, medium
WHERE
  timestamp("2021-07-23T06:10:16.747Z") < signInTime AND signInTime < timestamp("2022-11-29T02:52:22.640Z")
  AND ts = list_sort(ts, 'ASC')
WITH

RETURN otherId, CAST(accountDistance, "INT32"), mediumId, mediumType
ORDER BY accountDistance, otherId, mediumId;

title: Buffer manager allocation failures causing corruption
body:
E.g. the test `CopyTest.OutOfMemoryRecovery` (renamed to CopyTest.DISABLED_OutOfMemoryRecovery` in #4188) runs out of memory when committing (at the time of #4188) and then corrupts the database since the node group is constructed in two parts.
Generally I think we need to be more careful about potential allocation failures and try to ensure that newly allocated objects are isolated until we're done creating them to minimize the side-effects of failure.

The issue in that test in particular is that we add a new node group object to the node group collection, but don't allocate the `persistentChunkGroup` field until later. If that doesn't end up being allocated due to an exception, we will handle the exception, and then when closing the database serialize the node groups, including the one that was incomplete (which currently serializes fine the first time, but has issues after that).
It's worth noting that this particular situation is not actually unrecoverable at the moment, the other test in that file still succeeds by dropping the table.

One option for further testing of this problem in general would be to repeatedly try something, e.g. a reasonable sized-copy, and set up the buffer manager to randomly fail (or fail after `n` allocations if we want to be more exhaustive) as if it is out of memory and make sure we can recover.

title: Feature: Add "global" option to `regexp_replace`

labels.name: type: feature
labels.description: New features or missing components of existing features

body:
### API

Other

### Description

We have a function called [`regexp_replace`](https://docs.kuzudb.com/cypher/expressions/text-functions) that replaces only the first match of a string based on a regex.

However, we should also provide an option to replace all occurrences of a match, via a function `regexp_replace_all`. Example below.

I have this JSON file `persons.json`:
```json
[
  {
    "name": "Xavier Williams",
    "date_of_birth": "1989-06-28",
    "residence": {
      "address": "901 Oak Lane",
      "city": "San Francisco",
      "state": "CA",
      "zip_code": "94122"
    }
  }
]
```
I want to generate a unique string primary key that's a concatenation of all the address fields, that I can then use for relationship creation downstream. During this process, I want to remove **all** whitespaces.

I'm doing this right now:
```cypher
LOAD FROM 'persons.json'
WITH DISTINCT residence AS r
RETURN
    concat(
        regexp_replace(lower(r.address), ' ', ''),
        regexp_replace(lower(r.city), ' ', ''),
        regexp_replace(lower(r.state), ' ', ''),
        r.zip_code
    ) AS id,
    r.address,
    r.city,
    r.state,
    r.zip_code
```
Because only the first occurrence is matched, I get this result for the `id` field:
```
901oak lanesanfranciscoca94122
```
There's an extra space in the middle that wasn't removed.

If we had a `regexp_replace_all` function, this would be resolved.

title: Rework multi label scan as union all of single label scans
body:
### Description

Currently ScanNodeTable internally handles the case of scan from a single label or multiple labels. ScanRelTable and ScanMultiRelTable handles scanning from a single label and multiple labels respectively.

The logic of `ScanMultiRelTable` is to organize scanners based on boundNode's label, and for the same batch of input bound node IDs, perform scan over all needed rel tables.

Handling the logic of scanning from multiple labels actually complicate the set of scan operators unnecessarily, as union all can be used to simplify them without additionally performance overheads.
Also, potentially union all of single label scans can make the optimization easier to apply index lookup on bound node table scan when scanning from multi rel tables, which is not applied now.

title: Feature: Rel tables with only forward directed storage

labels.name: type: feature
labels.description: New features or missing components of existing features

body:
### Description

Currently, when we create rel tables, we always store rel tuples in a duplicated way that each tuple is stored in both forward and backward directed storage. This is to allow the flexibility of planner to pick plans that scan from either forward or backward directions. The downsides are: 1) storage space overheads; 2) copy/insert/update/delete overheads.

There are cases where only scan from forward or backward is needed, thus we don't need to keep the storage duplicated for both directions:
1) advanced users are aware that the rel tables can always be scanned in one direction; 
2) [full text search index](https://github.com/kuzudb/kuzu/issues/4269) always scan the rel tables from one direction.

### Syntax changes

```
// We introduce `WITH` to specify storage options.
CREATE REL TABLE Follows (FROM User TO User, since DATE) WITH (storage_direction = 'fwd');

or 

// We embed the storage option in schema definition.
CREATE REL TABLE Follows (FROM User TO User, since DATE, storage_direction = 'fwd');
```

### Storage and Operator changes
1. `Partitioner` should be aware of storage direction info so avoid duplicating partitions in both directions when `storage_direction = 'fwd'` is specified.
2. `bwdIndex` in `LocalRelTable` should be optional.
3. `bwdRelTableData` in `RelTable` should also be optional.

### Planner changes
1. When plan COPY REL statement, we need to decide if there will be two RelBatchInsert pipelines or just one.
2. Planner should be aware that the storage direction is limited to only fwd-directed Extend.

### TODOs
- [x] Apply grammar changes and catalog entry change.
- [x] Support rel batch insert for fwd directed storage.
- [x] Support insert/update/delete for fwd directed storage.
- [x] Support planner to correctly plan for scans (i.e. Extend) over fwd directed storage.
- [x] Support forward directed storage for rel table groups
- GDS algorithms
  - [ ] Check which algorithms can be modified to work with single-direction rel storage
  - [ ] For algorithms that require both directions we should throw if it tries to run on single-direction rel storage
- Correctly handle features that currently require both rel directions to work properly:
  - [ ] Rel multiplicity constraints
  - [ ] Detach delete
  - [ ] Multi-label patterns (if matched tables have different storage directions we should be able to handle that in the planner)


Note: for the current version of full text search to work, we only need to get the first two TODO items done.

### API

Other

### Description

I have this scenario where I have a CSV/Parquet file with just two columns:
```
product   price
Laptop 1100.0
Mouse 150.0
Headphones 250.0
```
In my DDL, I want to add a nullable column `historical_price` as follows:
```cypher
CREATE NODE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS Product(name STRING, price DOUBLE, historical_sales INT32, PRIMARY KEY (name));
```
I want to initialize the node table with all values in the `historical_sales` columns as nulls, and add them via `MERGE` at a later time when they become available.

## Issue
Because my input file has just 2 columns, and my DDL specifies 3 columns, I cannot use `COPY Product FROM 'product.parquet'` directly.

I instead have to do this:
```cypher
COPY Product(name, price) FROM 'data/product.parquet'
```

## Feature request

In the `COPY` pipeline, because we already know the number of columns in the input prior to importing the data, can we implicitly infer the column names so that we can use the much simpler DDL command below? It would reduce the mental burden on the user, as it's expected that the columns that are absent in the input file would have to be filled with nulls.

```cypher
COPY Product FROM 'data/product.parquet'
```

@ray6080 I think this seems like a reasonable feature, but if you think it's infeasible, feel free to close.

title: GDS and Recursive Joins TODOs
body:
This issue is intended to keep track of the suite of optimizations, refactoring, enhancements, experimentations, and documentations we plan to implement/write in both the new fast recursive join implementations and the upcoming Kuzu GDS functions.

## Recursive Joins TODOs
- [x]  Refactor: Implement getParameterTypeIDs() in each rjFunction separately in rec_joins.h. (Xiyang)
- [x] Enhancement: Currently paths return only the intermediate node IDs. Also return edgeIDs. 2 main things need to be done on the backend: (i) ParentIterAndNextPtr* need to change; (ii) My suggestion is to change SingleSPPathsEdgeCompute to also use ParentIterAndNextPtr. The SinglePaths data structure can be thrown away. See my comment in SinglePaths::setParentEdge. (Xiyang)
- [x] Enhancement: Integrate predicates to recursive joins, e.g., `(a)-[r:* |  WHERE r.since < 2022 AND n.age > 45]->(b)`. (Xiyang)
- [x] Enhancement: Make recursive joins work on undirected recursive relationship patterns (e.g., `(a)-[r:*]-(b)`) as well as when scanning the graph in backwards direction. Currently we only work for scanning the graph in the forward direction. When implementing the undirected patterns, we may need to change the ParentIterAndNextPtr to keep track of the directions of the edges. (Xiyang)
- [x] Optimization: Add early stopping to shortest paths computation when there are few destinations and have reached all.
- [x] Optimization: Fix the isMasked(offset, offset) to have a fast path. We currently use masks in Frontier implementations but we need to check a single location. So we need a fast function here. This should be very quick. (Xiyang).
- [x] Optimization: Currently when writing outputs in SingleSPOutputWriterPaths, we call the `singlePaths->getParent(curIntNode)` function, which uses `nodeID_t` and internall does a lookup on the tableID here: `parentEdges.at(nodeID.tableID).get()->buffer.data());`. For queries that contain nodes from only a single node table, we can avoid this by "fixing" the node table in SinglePaths. When writing parents (so during the actual recursive join comptuation and not when outputting the paths), we have a similar optimization where we call the `SinglePaths::fixNodeTable` to avoid any table lookups in the `parentEdges` field. We can have a similar optimization when writing paths if there is a single node table anyways. This may or may not matter since the map will be very small but it can still make a difference. (Xiyang)
- [x] Optimizations: Push down acyclic, trail, and walk constraints to the enumeration so that we don't blindly enumerate and write all paths to FactorizedTable first. Also see if anything smart can be done for variable-length joins during the path computation if we are finding  acyclic or trail paths (e.g., can we avoid visiting the same node twice).  
- [x] Enhancement: Implement weighted shortest paths.
- [ ] Enhancement: Currently the `Mask` data structures that are used in the semijoin masks as well as to pass in the possible source and destination node IDs to recursive join algorithms is using OS memory. We should make it use the MemoryManager. (Xiyang)
- [x] Change the LENGTH field to be UINT16_t instead of UINT64_t. This might be minor but leads to unnecessary writes to value vectors as well as FactorizedTable's. (Xiyang)
- [x] Optimization: Reimplement header caching-based fast scans in on_disk_graph. (Ben)
- [x] Optimization: Graph::scan functions should return iterators instead of copying the data from the buffer manager to a value vector. This may requires keeping pages in the buffer manager pinned for longer time but it should be fine as we do very quick work on each edge in edgeCompute() functions. (Ben). 
- [ ] Optimization: RJOutputWriters currently write one path at a time to the FactorizedTable. This corresponds to tuple-at-a-time processing. I am guessing this is an important bottleneck. Instead, we should buffer the writes to the Factorized Table. (Ben)
- [ ] OnDiskGraph random scan optimization: Ben also had another optimization he had added earlier to avoid scanning the entire CSR header in randomAccess mode. It apparently should only improve performance if you scanned relatively few offsets from a node group, given the header caching optimization.
- [ ] Optimization: We use virtual functions all over the EdgeCompute and VertexCompute and RJOutputWriter and Frontiers etc. implementations. We should consider templating these and benchmarking the benefits of these on large graphs. (Ben)
- [x] 	Optimization: Make VertexCompute run on entire morsels and EdgeCompute run on entire neighbors (to minimize function calls between GDSUtils and these virtual function calls). (Semih)
- [ ] Optimization: Bidirectional and direction-optimizing joins. Bidirectional joins is the optimization for cases when there is a single source and a single destination and implements the heuristic to take a step from the smaller frontier at each step. This can be used both for shortest as well as variable length joins (and will likely have an annoying backtracking algorithm). (Semih)
- [ ] Optimization: We currently materialize the outputs of each recursive join. Ideally, GDSCall (and RJAlgorithm) should either be part of a larger pipeline including the next pipeline P_{next} or take that pipeline as field and instead of calling `GDSUtils::runVertexComputeIteration()` by passing an `RJOutputWriterVC`, it should schedule the P_{next} in the task scheduler and P_{next} should be configured to scan the outputs of the RecJoin operator (for this we will need new scan operators that implement the backtracking logic that is currently implemented in the `RJOutputWriterVC` VertexCompute functions. (Xiyang)
- [ ] Experiment/Optimization: We should make the ALL_PATHS_BLOCK_SIZE configurable and evaluate its performance on recursive joins on large graphs.
- [ ] Optimization: Make the scan of rels be sequential and batched when possible. Rel table scan can take the advantage of bound nodes being sequential or adjacent to cache scanned rels from storage. The idea is to make full use of the output ValueVectors to cache at most 2048 rels when scanning from disk, and output rels for each bound node by changing SelectionVector over the output ValueVectors. Note that the caching is avoided when the input bound node is a single one, which is currently how the access is done in OnDiskGraph, as there is usually no benefit from caching for a single node. The change should be when possible, change the input nodeIDVector to be filled with a sequence of nodeIDs and populate the SelectionVector according to the caller (e.g., whether the nodeID is active or not). (Ben)
- [ ] Optimization: we should keep few elements in `ParentList` depends on the configuration of recursive join. E.g. direction is not needed if edges are all in the same direction.
- [x] Optimization: resolve left comments in #4374 
- [x] Fix on disk graph unable to read local storage (Guodong)
- [x] Fix disabled test in #4404
- [ ] Check if maintaining hash set for semantic check will improve [performance](https://github.com/kuzudb/kuzu/pull/4461#discussion_r1828741101)
- [x] Experiment with sparse frontier size and check if parallelize sparse frontier make sense or not.

## GDS TODOs
- [x] Refactor: Reimplement PageRank and Weakly Connected Components to adopt the Ligra API. (Semih/Xiyang)
- [ ] Enhancement: Make GDS algorithms extensions, so the community can develop their own GDS algorithms and share. Some of the core GDS algorithms, such as PageRank and connected components, can be at the core, but others can also be extensions. Ideally, we should develop all GDS algorithms as extensions but have the option to put some of them into our core binaries. (Ziyi and discuss with Chang)
- [ ] Documentation: Write documentation about how the community can implement their own GDS algorithms.
- [ ] Enhancement: Implement Strongly Connected Components, Betweenness Centrality, 1 popular node embedding algorithm, 1 popular community detection algorithm (Semih, Xiyang, Interns)
- [ ] Documentation: Write documentation and tutorials about both how the GDS algorithms work as well as separate documentation for each GDS algorithm we implement. We should try to come up with a template for these algorithms and suggest the community to use our documentation template.
- [ ] Enhancement: Make progress bar work for pipelines working on GDS Algorithms. (Mattias)

title: Kùzu to NetworkX fails when results of an optional match are passed onward
body:
### Kùzu version

_No response_

### What operating system are you using?

_No response_

### What happened?

Based on the additional issue reported in #3640.

When trying to isolate a subgraph via `MATCH` and an `OPTIONAL MATCH` clauses, we ran into an issue where if the `OPTIONAL MATCH` returns a null result, the conversion of the query result to NetworkX fails. Supporting this use case makes sense, as sometimes the query results can contain null values which should be ignored by the `get_as_networkx()` converter.

### Are there known steps to reproduce?

Run the following code:

```py
import shutil
import kuzu
import networkx

shutil.rmtree("test_db", ignore_errors=True)
db = kuzu.Database()
conn = kuzu.Connection(db)

conn.execute("CREATE NODE TABLE Person (name STRING, age INT64, PRIMARY KEY (name))")
conn.execute("CREATE NODE TABLE Product (name STRING, price DOUBLE, PRIMARY KEY (name))")
conn.execute("CREATE REL TABLE Purchased (FROM Person TO Product, quantity INT64)")

conn.execute("CREATE (p:Person {name: 'Alice', age: 30})")
conn.execute("CREATE (p:Person {name: 'Bob', age: 25})")

conn.execute("CREATE (p:Product {name: 'Laptop', price: 1000.0})")
conn.execute("CREATE (p:Product {name: 'Phone', price: 500.0})")

conn.execute("MATCH (p:Person {name: 'Alice'}), (prod:Product {name: 'Laptop'}) MERGE (p)-[:PURCHASED]->(prod)")
conn.execute("MATCH (p:Person {name: 'Alice'}), (prod:Product {name: 'Phone'}) MERGE (p)-[:PURCHASED]->(prod)")
conn.execute("MATCH (p:Person {name: 'Bob'}), (prod:Product {name: 'Phone'}) MERGE (p)-[:PURCHASED]->(prod)")

# Run the following query
result = conn.execute("""
    MATCH (a)-[p1:Purchased]->(pr1:Product {name: 'Phone'})
    OPTIONAL MATCH (a)-[p2:Purchased]->(pr2:Product {name: 'Tablet'})
    RETURN *
""")

G = result.get_as_networkx()
print(G.nodes)
print(G.edges)
```

Because the query's `OPTIONAL MATCH` clause asks for a non-existent relationship, we will receive null values in the query result, which throws the following error:

```
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/Users/prrao/code/kuzu/test.py", line 31, in <module>
    G = result.get_as_networkx()
        ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  File "/Users/prrao/code/kuzu/tools/python_api/build/kuzu/query_result.py", line 283, in get_as_networkx
    _id = row[i]["_id"]
          ~~~~~~^^^^^^^
TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not subscriptable
```

title: Optimization: Join order optimization across match/load from clauses
body:
### Description

For query like the following
```
load from 'relation.csv' (header=true) match (a:node), (b:node) where a.id=source_id and b.id=target_id merge (a)-[e:rel]->(b)
```
The optimizer is picking a plan with cross product between `a` and `b`, then join with `relation.csv`, which is not the optimal plan, and it can easily lead to out of memory exception when `a` and `b` are large. Ideally the optimizer should pick hash joins between `a`, `b` and `relation.csv`.
