title: Feature: Full text search

labels.name: type: feature
labels.description: New features or missing components of existing features

body:
### API

C++

### Description

# Installation and Loading
Like other extensions, FTS must be installed and loaded by:
```
INSTALL FTS;
LOAD FTS;
```

# Create FTS:
```
create_fts_index(indexName, table_name, *properties,  stemmer = 'porter',
                 stopwords = 'english', ignore = '(\\.|[^a-z])+',
                 strip_accents = 1);
```
Name | Type | Description
-- | -- | --
indexName | STRING | name of the index
table_name | STRING | name of the node table to create fts index.
properties… | STRING | column names of the text properties to be indexed (vararg), e.g., 'text_field_1', 'text_field_2', …, 'text_field_N', or '\*' for all columns in input_table of type STRING
stemmer | STRING | The type of stemmer to be used. One of 'arabic', 'basque', 'catalan', 'danish', 'dutch', 'english', 'finnish', 'french', 'german', 'greek', 'hindi', 'hungarian', 'indonesian', 'irish', 'italian', 'lithuanian', 'nepali', 'norwegian', 'porter', 'portuguese', 'romanian', 'russian', 'serbian', 'spanish', 'swedish', 'tamil', 'turkish', or 'none' if no stemming is to be used. Defaults to 'porter' (most commly used one)
stopwords | STRING | The name of the table which only has one STRING column of stop words. The default value: "english" which refers to a list of 571 predefined stop words
ignore | STRING | Regular expression of patterns to be ignored. Defaults to '(\\.\|[^a-z])+', ignoring all escaped and non-alphabetic lowercase characters
strip_accents | BOOL | Whether to remove accents (e.g., convert á to a). Defaults to true

### Workflow Example:
Let's start with a dummy `books` node table:
```
create node table books (id int64, name string, content string, author string, primary key(id));
create (b:books {id: 5, name: 'good story',  content: 'hero beats monster', author: 'jon'});
create (b:books {id: 7, name: 'monster vs superman', content: 'superman beats monster', author: 'alice'});
create (b:books {id: 9, name: 'monster vs monster', content: 'monster beats monster', author: 'dan'});
```
Then we build the fts on the `books` and `isSimilar` table 
```
CALL create_fts_index(
      'books', 'content', 'name'
  );
```

*Note (Semih): Maybe consider ["Books", ["prop1", "prop2"]] type syntax to accommodate a future usage. Or keep it simple now but have a solution for the case when we support multiple nodes.*

The CALL statement builds the index by creating virtual tables and macros:
1.  Internal macros:
    a.`Stem`
    Usage:
    `Stem` macro splits the string into a list of words according to the stemmer.
      ```
      stem(input_string, stemmer)
      ```
    b. `Tokenize`:
    Usage:
    `Tokenize` macro converts a string into tokens.
    
2. Virtual tables:

    ### a. docs (node table)
    
    | Name         | Type            | Description                     |
    |--------------|-----------------|---------------------------------|
    | doc_id  |  SERIAL | node offset of each doc         |
    | len          | INT64            | number of terms in the doc      |
    
Note: If we support fts on multiple node labels, we may need to change SERIAL to nodeID. But in an alternative design (which may be simpler), we can just store a separate `docs` node table for each of the node labels.
 
    ### b. dic (node table)
    
    | Name    | Type   | Description                                 |
    |---------|--------|---------------------------------------------|
    | term    | STRING | identifier of the term                  |
    | df      | INT64  | number of distinct documents where the term appears |
    
    ### c. terms (relationship table)
    
    | Name                  | Type    | Description                        |
    |-----------------------|---------|------------------------------------|
    | FROM:docs:doc  | PK_TYPE | PK in docs                         |
    | TO:dic:term         | STRING | PK in dic                          |
    | prop_id               | UINT64   | the property id where the term occurs | => Not needed for the initial version
    | tf                         | UINT64   | term frequency in the doc |
    
    ### d. fts_properties (node table) => *Note: Why is this a table? I think this should be part of the Catalog entry of the index when needed (and probably not in the initial version).*

# Query:
Now we have the FTS with the help of virtual tables.

We provide a user with a utility call function: `query_fts_index(node, indexName, queryString, k, b, conjunctive)` to retrive:
```
MATCH (a:Book)
WHERE a.pubData > 2012
CALL query_fts_index(a, "book-index", "monster hero randomstring")
RETURN _doc, score
```

Name | Type | Description
-- | -- | --
node | node variable (to support filters on nodes) | nodes to search
indexName | string | index name
query_string | STRING | The string to search the index for
k | DOUBLE | Parameter k1 in the Okapi BM25 retrieval model. Defaults to 1.2
b | DOUBLE | Parameter b in the Okapi BM25 retrieval model. Defaults to 0.75
conjunctive | BOOLEAN | Whether to make the query conjunctive i.e., all terms in the query string must be present in order for a document to be retrieved

# FTS Destroy:
We don't plan to suppport updates on the fts. If the user has insertions/deletions on the table, they have to drop the fts by
`CALL drop_fts_index(input_table_name)` and recreate the fts on the new table.

# Edge case testing:
1. Special characters in the match string and doc
2. Empty string or null string
3. Other languages
4. Lower and upper case fts
5. User creates the fts on table A, but uses the fts on table B. (We should error in such case).
6. User provides a column with duplicate values in create_fts_index call.



# Design in other systems:
Example dataset:
```
┌───────┬─────────────────────┬────────────────────────┬─────────┐
│  id   │        name         │        content         │ author  │
│ int64 │       varchar       │        varchar         │ varchar │
├───────┼─────────────────────┼────────────────────────┼─────────┤
│     5 │ good story          │ hero beats monster     │ jon     │
│     7 │ monster vs superman │ superman beats monster │ alice   │
│     9 │ monster vs monster  │ monster beats monster  │ dan     │
└───────┴─────────────────────┴────────────────────────┴─────────┘
```
Steps to create the sample dataset:
```
create table books (id int64, name string, content string, author string, primary key(id));
insert into books values(5,  'good story', 'hero beats monster','jon');
insert into books values (7, 'monster vs superman', 'superman beats monster', 'alice');
insert into books values (9, 'monster vs monster', 'monster beats monster', 'dan');
```

# DuckDB:
## Create FTS:
We create a FTS on the books table with the column id as the row identifier (since duckdb tables may not have primary keys). The fields to build fts on are: `name` and `content`.
```
PRAGMA CREATE_FTS_INDEX('books', 'id', 'name', 'content');
Note:
1. Books: is the name of the table to create FTS on.
3. id: is the row identifier in duckdb so they can identify each docuemnt in the FTS tables.
7. name/ content: are the column names to create fts on.
```

## Query FTS:
Duckdb provides a macro `match_bm25` to calculate the score of each record.
If the pattern is found: a similarity score is returned. Higher means better.
If the pattern is not found:  NULL is returned.
Sample usage:
1. Search the `name` and `content` columns for keyword 'superman':
```
D select name, score from 
(select *,fts_main_books.match_bm25(id, 'superman') as score from books) 
where score is not null 
order by score DESC ;
┌─────────────────────┬────────────────────┐
│        name         │       score        │
│       varchar       │       double       │
├─────────────────────┼────────────────────┤
│ monster vs superman │ 0.5857070068743867 │
└─────────────────────┴────────────────────┘
```
Let's step into the inner query which calculates the bm25 score for each row.
```
D select *,fts_main_books.match_bm25(id, 'superman') from books;
┌───────┬─────────────────────┬────────────────────────┬─────────┬───────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  id   │        name         │        content         │ author  │ fts_main_books.match_bm25(id, 'superman') │
│ int64 │       varchar       │        varchar         │ varchar │                  double                   │
├───────┼─────────────────────┼────────────────────────┼─────────┼───────────────────────────────────────────┤
│     5 │ good story          │ hero beats monster     │ jon     │                                           │
│     7 │ monster vs superman │ superman beats monster │ alice   │                        0.5857070068743867 │
│     9 │ monster vs monster  │ monster beats monster  │ dan     │                                           │
└───────┴─────────────────────┴────────────────────────┴─────────┴───────────────────────────────────────────┘
```
The `id` field is used as a row identifier(join condition) when querying the internal docs table.
```
Internal virtual docs table(created by fts) for document:
┌───────┬───────┬───────┐
│ docid │ name  │  len  │
│ int64 │ int64 │ int64 │
├───────┼───────┼───────┤
│     0 │     5 │     5 │
│     1 │     7 │     5 │
│     2 │     9 │     5 │
└───────┴───────┴───────┘
```
For each record, duckdb uses the `id` field to retrive the `docid` in the docs table, which will later be used in other queries.
That's why the match_bm25 function should take in the `id` field.

2. Only search the `name` column for keyword `monster`:
```
D select name, score from 
(select *,fts_main_books.match_bm25(id, 'monster', fields:= 'name') as score from books) 
where score is not null 
order by score DESC ;
┌─────────────────────┬─────────────────────┐
│        name         │        score        │
│       varchar       │       double        │
├─────────────────────┼─────────────────────┤
│ monster vs monster  │ 0.07973892709431926 │
│ monster vs superman │ 0.05799194697768673 │
└─────────────────────┴─────────────────────┘
```

5. If invalid row_identifier is given, Duckdb may return undefined result:
For example:
The user prepares a new table person by:
```
D create table person (id int64, name string);
D insert into person values (20, 'abc');
D insert into person values (5, 'abc');
```
The the user computes bm25 by:
```
D select *,fts_main_books.match_bm25(id, 'monster') from person;
┌───────┬─────────┬──────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  id   │  name   │ fts_main_books.match_bm25(id, 'monster') │
│ int64 │ varchar │                  double                  │
├───────┼─────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────┤
│    20 │ abc     │                                          │
│     5 │ abc     │                      0.05799194697768673 │
└───────┴─────────┴──────────────────────────────────────────┘
```
The result is undefined in such case.

## Update FTS
Update is not supported in Duckdb. Users have to drop the original FTS and create a new FTS.

# Postgres:
Postgres supports full text search with/withnot GIN.
## 1. Without GIN:
```
pgscan=# select name, (to_tsvector('english',Content) @@ to_tsquery('english', 'monster')) from books;
        name         | ?column? 
---------------------+----------
 good story          | t
 monster vs superman | t
 monster vs monster  | t
(3 rows)
```
For each content in books table:
1. Tokenize it to a tsvector.
2. Compare with the tokenized query: "monster".
If the pattern is found: returns true, otherwise returns false.

## 2. With GIN:
To expedite the full text search, duckdb allows users to create a GIN on the pattern to search for:
```
pgscan=# CREATE INDEX books_idx_1 ON books USING GIN (to_tsvector('english', content));
```
Search for the books which has the keyword 'monster' appear as its content.
```
pgscan=# select author from books where to_tsvector('english', content) @@ to_tsquery('monster');
 author 
--------
 jon
 alice
 dan
```

## 3. Update on GIN:
Similar to other indexes,GIN is updated when there is an update/insertion/deletion on the books table.

# Neo4j
## Create FTS:
Provides two grammars:
These two queries create a full text search index on nodes: movie and book on title, description and review properties:
```
For NODE:
CALL db.index.fulltext.createNodeIndex("bookDescription",["Movie", "Book"],["title", "description", "review"])
For REL:
CALL db.index.fulltext.createRelIndex("similarityIndex",["isSimilar", "isSame"],["comment"])
```
or:
```
For NODE:
CREATE FULLTEXT INDEX titlesAndDescriptions FOR (n:Movie|Book) ON EACH [n.title, n.description, n.review]
OPTIONS {
  indexConfig: {
    `fulltext.analyzer`: 'english',
  }
}

For REL:
CREATE FULLTEXT INDEX similarityIndex FOR ()-[r:isSimilar|isSame]-() ON EACH [r.comment]
OPTIONS {
  indexConfig: {
    `fulltext.analyzer`: 'english',
  }
}
```
## Query FTS:
```
Query node:
CALL db.index.fulltext.queryNodes("bookDescription", "monster") YIELD node, score
RETURN node.title, node.review, score

Query rel:
CALL db.index.fulltext.queryRelationships("similarityIndex", "good") YIELD relationship, score
RETURN relationship.comment, score
```

# MemGraph
Still an experimental feature, can only create search index on nodes by:
```
CREATE TEXT INDEX textIndex ON :Document,;
```
Only single label is supported, will index on all searchable fields of document.

Query grammar:
```
CALL text_search.search_all("textIndex", "monster")
YIELD node, score
RETURN node, score;
ORDER BY SCORE
```


Future Enhancements and Optimizations:
- Support case-sensitive search
- Add support for searching across a single properties if the index has been created on multiple properties (this is the `fields := NULL` option in DuckDB's match_bm25 function). 


# Things to dicuss:
1. Grammar 
2. Implementation:
     a. virtual table field (properties not visible to the user but can be used internally).
     b. Query node with offset efficiently. (E.g. MATCH (n:person) WHERE offset(id(n)) = 5, we should avoid full table scan in such case).
     c. Avoid storing edges in both directions with fixed join order.
     d. Implement using GDS design.

title: Bug: Query Performance Discrepancy: KuzuDB CLI vs. Rust Code

mac os somona (also tasted in winodws 11 23h2 with same result)

We encountered a performance issue when testing a large query. Initially, the query took around `3.5 seconds` to execute in our Rust code, which raised concerns about performance.

To investigate, we ran the same query in the` KuzuDB CLI`, where it surprisingly took only `252 ms` on average. Suspecting a problem in our code, we simplified the test by writing a basic program that only runs the query and measures the time. In this case, the query took `3.46 seconds`.

labels.description: Issues related to better usability experience, including bad error messages

Currently, the limit on the number of cached warnings (configurable using `CALL warning_limit={value}`) is applied per-connection. We should discuss if it is more user-intuitive for this limit to apply per-query instead, and whether there is a need for a global limit on the number of cached warnings.

For reference, [duckDB's `rejects_limit` setting](https://duckdb.org/docs/data/csv/reading_faulty_csv_files.html#parameters) for `read_csv()` applies for each input file (which is even more granular than per-query).

title: Add function call to clean up cached warnings

labels.name: type: feature
labels.description: New features or missing components of existing features

body:
When copying from files there is an option `IGNORE_ERRORS` that caches any errors encountered as warnings and continues execution skipping whatever row caused the error. Warnings can then be retrieved using the function `show_warnings()`.

Warnings are cached globally across a connection, we should offer users the ability to clean up the global warning cache if they are no longer interested in warnings from previous queries. This will help especially in the case where the global warning limit is hit (and any new warnings will not be cached).

Users will be able to do this by executing the query `CALL clear_warnings();`

### API

Python

### Description

Currently if we use Kùzu's LlamaIndex `KuzuPropertyGraphStore`, we can only create an EntityNode which has the following allowed fields: 
```
id STRING,
name STRING,
label STRING,
embedding DOUBLE[],
creation_date DATE,
last_modified_date DATE,
file_name STRING,
file_path STRING,
file_size INT64,
file_type STRING,
triplet_source_id STRING,
PRIMARY KEY(id)
```
This is too restrictive in the case where we are trying to manually insert nodes of different types having different fields. In case we add some node which has a differently named field, say `contents`, currently the LlamaIndex adaptor would allow the node to be added, but when we try to read back the same node, the new field `contents` would not show up.

By a quick inspecton of the code, I see two ways this could be done, (a) add a `map` parameter called `properties` inside EntityNodes which enable us to add any property (as long as the value is a string or a known type), or (b) allow the user to specify a custom schema for each node type.

title: Namespace organisation
body:
Continuing an issue from here: https://github.com/kuzudb/kuzu/pull/4166#pullrequestreview-2276856794. In short, I think it would be helpful to standardize how we refer to namespaces, and maybe also look at doing some re-organization of the namespaces. It's obviously not a huge deal, except that, like code formatting, it's a pain if we keep having to re-write things to clean things up, pollutes the git history and makes things harder to understand generally.

One thing I think we could do is to move `kuzu::common` into the `kuzu` namespace. This will remove the need for the frequent use of `using namespace kuzu::common`.
On the other hand, I sort of like the practice of using the root namespace for the primary public-facing APIs, which would be more like what's currently in `kuzu::main`, and since there's so much in `kuzu::common`, keeping that separate from the stuff in `kuzu::main` and so that `kuzu::main`->`kuzu` can be the obvious entry point into the API docs might be a good option. 
E.g. [in the rust API](https://github.com/kuzudb/kuzu/blob/master/tools/rust_api/src/lib.rs) everything is publicly exported into the root kuzu namespace`, but rust also has public/private designations for classes, variables etc.

I also suggest the following guidelines for referencing namespaces:
1. If a name is used once or twice, just include the namespace inline when referring to the name.
2. If a name is used many times, use `using <namespace>::<Name>`.
3. Avoid `using namespace ...` ([clang-tidy check](https://clang.llvm.org/extra/clang-tidy/checks/google/build-using-namespace.html), though it's probably too much work to go through them all and expand them out, so maybe leave the clang-tidy check for now).

This is something which is harder to enforce with QA tools (except number 3), so maybe we should start a coding style guide (maybe it's time to remove [the old one on the wiki](https://github.com/kuzudb/kuzu/wiki/GraphflowDB-Coding-Style)?) and add it to the developer section in the docs.

Those guidelines provide a soft barrier making it harder to write highly coupled code; if it seems like you're dealing with `using` and referring to namespaces too much, maybe the code is not structured very well and should be re-written. 
I think that we should avoid tightly coupled code across namespaces (with the idea that related and more tightly coupled code would be in the same namespace). In practice, I imagine there will be many exceptions to this.

title: Feature: Support an Async/Await in Rust Client with Connection Pool for Kuzu DB

labels.name: type: feature
labels.description: New features or missing components of existing features

body:
### API

Rust

### Description

We propose enhancing the Rust client for Kuzu DB by implementing async/await support and adding a connection pool. These improvements would significantly enhance the developer experience (DX) and align Kuzu DB with modern Rust frameworks and practices.

## Proposed Changes
1. Implement async versions of existing synchronous methods in the Rust client.
2. Add a connection pool to manage and reuse database connections efficiently.
3. Update the API to support both synchronous and asynchronous usage.

## Rationale
### Async/Await Support
Implementing async/await support for the Rust client would bring several benefits:
- Improved developer experience by aligning with modern Rust asynchronous patterns
- Better integration with popular async Rust frameworks like Axum, Actix, and others
- Enhanced flexibility in handling concurrent database operations

### Connection Pool
Adding a connection pool would:
- Simplify connection management in concurrent scenarios
- Provide a more idiomatic way of handling connections in async Rust applications
- Offer better control over resource usage in high-concurrency environments

## Example Usage (Proposed)

```rust
use kuzu_async::{Database, SystemConfig, ConnectionPool};

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
    let db = Database::new(path, SystemConfig::default()).await?;
    let pool = ConnectionPool::new(&db, 10).await?; // Create a pool with 10 connections

    let conn = pool.get().await?;
    conn.query("CREATE NODE TABLE Person(name STRING, age INT64, PRIMARY KEY(name));").await?;
    conn.query("CREATE (:Person {name: 'Alice', age: 25});").await?;
    conn.query("CREATE (:Person {name: 'Bob', age: 30});").await?;

    let mut result = conn.query("MATCH (a:Person) RETURN a.name AS NAME, a.age AS AGE;").await?;
    println!("{}", result.display());

    Ok(())
}
```

## Impact
This enhancement would make Kuzu DB more attractive for Rust developers working with modern async frameworks and patterns. It would improve the overall developer experience by providing a more idiomatic way of working with Kuzu DB in async Rust applications.

## Additional Considerations
- Backward compatibility with the existing synchronous API
- Comprehensive documentation and examples for the new async features
- Integration examples with popular Rust web frameworks (e.g., Axum, Actix)

We believe these improvements would greatly benefit the Kuzu DB ecosystem and its users by aligning with modern Rust development practices.

title: Bug: unable to add edges while using Kuzu's LlamaIndex PropertyGraphIndex integration
body:
### Kùzu version

v0.6.0

### What operating system are you using?

MacOS 14.4.1 (23E224)

### What happened?

I was creating a graph using LlamaIndex's `PropertyGraphIndex` integration with Kuzu. I was trying to add nodes and edges to the graph (not using `PropertyGraphIndex.from_documents`, but by manually creating nodes/relations and upserting them to the graph). I was able to add nodes to the graph, but none of the edges were showing up in the graph. Upon inspecting the code inside `KuzuPropertyGraphStore.upsert_relations`:

```py
def upsert_relations(self, relations: List[Relation]) -> None:
        for rel in relations:
            if self.has_structured_schema:
                src, _, dst = utils.lookup_relation(rel.label, self.relationship_schema)
            else:
                src, dst = "Entity", "Entity"

            rel_tbl_name = f"LINKS_{src}_{dst}"
            self.connection.execute(
                f"""
                MATCH (a:{src} {{id: $source_id}}),
                        (b:{dst} {{id: $target_id}}),
                        (c:Chunk {{id: $triplet_source_id}})
                MERGE (a)-[r:{rel_tbl_name} {{label: $label}}]->(b)
                    SET r.triplet_source_id = $triplet_source_id
                MERGE (c)-[:LINKS_Chunk_{src} {{label: "MENTIONS"}}]->(a)
                MERGE (c)-[:LINKS_Chunk_{dst} {{label: "MENTIONS"}}]->(b)
                """,
                parameters={
                    "source_id": rel.source_id,
                    "target_id": rel.target_id,
                    "triplet_source_id": rel.properties.get("triplet_source_id"),
                    "label": rel.label,
                },
            )
```

 I found that the code to add edges relies on the fact that there should be `Chunk` nodes inserted into the graph, and if they do not exist (which is the situation for me) then the edge does not get added. 
 
 Ideally, in case Chunk nodes are not found but we do supply nodes between which we would like an edge to be created, it should not be conditional on a `Chunk` node also being present.

### Are there known steps to reproduce?

A minimal example which should be enough to reproduce the issue:
```py
import kuzu
from llama_index.llms.openai import OpenAI
from llama_index.core.graph_stores import EntityNode, Relation

db = kuzu.Database("/tmp/demo_db")
graph_store = KuzuPropertyGraphStore(db=db)
```

title: Optimization: FactorizedTable Writes or Recursive Join/GDS Writers
body:
### Description

I'm working on the new recursive joins and I am seeing the following numbers on my machine, which indicate that we should be able to optimize when writing data to FactorizedTable.
I am running several versions of this query:
```
PROJECT GRAPH PK (ljNode, ljRel) MATCH (a:ljNode) WHERE a.ID = 0 CALL all_sp_paths(PK, a, 30, true) RETURN  count(*) as c; 
```
The `{all/single}_sp_{paths/lengths/destinations}` functions materialize all of their output to an intermediate FactorizedTable. I'm measuring how much memory allocation these FactorizedTable do through the MemoryManager (by keeping some extra fields in FactorizedTable in my branch). I see the following numbers:

This query: `PROJECT GRAPH PK (ljNode, ljRel) MATCH (a:ljNode) WHERE a.ID = 0 CALL all_sp_lengths(PK, a, 30, true) RETURN  count(*) as c;` writes 5.5GB and the query takes 5.1s. If I remove the writing part with a hack to only write a few tuples (so think of this as writing 0 bytes), then the query takes ~0.8s.

This query: `PROJECT GRAPH PK (ljNode, ljRel) MATCH (a:ljNode) WHERE a.ID = 0 CALL all_sp_paths(PK, a, 30, true) RETURN  count(*) as c;` writes 7.8GB data and takes 13.3s. If I do the same hack of writing 0 tuples, the query takes 0.8s. 

For reference, his query: `PROJECT GRAPH PK (ljNode, ljRel) MATCH (a:ljNode) WHERE a.ID = 0 CALL single_sp_lengths(PK, a, 30, true) RETURN  count(*) as c;` takes 1.1s and writes 170MB of data. If I do the hack, it takes 0.7s.

Finally, for reference, this query: `PROJECT GRAPH PK (ljNode, ljRel) MATCH (a:ljNode) WHERE a.ID = 0 CALL single_sp_paths(PK, a, 30, true) RETURN  count(*) as c;` takes 1.1s and writes 240MB of data. If I do the hack, it takes 0.8s.

I think we should look into what we can do to improve the write performance of FactorizedTable. I don't have a very good idea now unfortunately. We might consider changing some APIs that allow operators to write to FactorizedTable in a faster way, which usually should mean writing in bulk but not sure how to enable that. In my case, I'm writing one tuple at a time. We might instead have to write in bulk to FactorizedTable.

title: Make FactorizedTable threadsafe (especially the merge function)
body:
Currently FactorizedTable is not a threadsafe class. In particular it has a merge function to merge multiple FactorizedTables that delegates the responsibility of thread safety, i.e., acquiring the locks, to the caller. This makes the code harder to read as one needs to figure out the call stack to find whether or not a lock has been acquired. It also leads to duplicated lock acquisition code in cases when the only reason the caller uses a mutex and lock is to ensure FactorizedTable::merge's safety (which is currently what happens on ResultCollectorSharedState::mergeLocalTable and the GDS RJOutputWriterVC code in my branch).

Instead FactorizedTable should be threadsafe itself by keeping an internal lock. Even if an outside lock is acquired this is fine and in some cases, as in RJOutputWriterVC, this can help us remove the duplicated locking code from the caller. So we should refactor this.

title: Map GDS call is passing a FactorizedTable instead of a schema
body:
I was in the following situation. I'm parallelizing the writes of the GDS outputs. In this case, each thread needs to create a local copy of an FTable. The current PlanMapper::mapGDSCall passes an actual FTable instead of TableSchema down to the operators (putting this in the GDSCallSharedState). This left me in a situation where I wanted to copy or clone the FTable but there is no such function. 

Having talked to @acquamarin apparently normally the frontend passes just the schema and each operator that wants to do parallel writes, e.g., ResultCollector, use this schema to create its local copy with a line like this (see ResultCollector::initLocalStateInternal for an example):
```
    localTable = std::make_unique<FactorizedTable>(context->clientContext->getMemoryManager(),
        info.tableSchema.copy());
```

So maybe we should follow this style also in GDSCall. Or we can add a clone function to FTable and pass in FTable in other places too. Regardless, let's be consistent everywhere for code readability.

title: Exporting to NetworkX for a multi-edge graph contains duplicates
body:
This is from @kamalikaray's comment in #3640.

## Issue

When exporting a Kuzu graph that has multi-edges to NetworkX, it seems that there are duplicate edges being returned as NetworkX objects. It seems that we're not de-duplicating the edges appropriately prior to returning them as a NetworkX graph when there are multi-edges.

The actual graph in Kuzu contains the following data:

```
┌────────────┬───────┬───────────┬──────────────┬──────────┬────────────┐
│ a.username ┆ a.age ┆ c.name    ┆ c.population ┆ l.role   ┆ con.county │
│ ---        ┆ ---   ┆ ---       ┆ ---          ┆ ---      ┆ ---        │
│ str        ┆ i64   ┆ str       ┆ i64          ┆ str      ┆ str        │
╞════════════╪═══════╪═══════════╪══════════════╪══════════╪════════════╡
│ Adam       ┆ 30    ┆ Waterloo  ┆ 150000       ┆ Resident ┆ county1    │
│ Adam       ┆ 30    ┆ Waterloo  ┆ 150000       ┆ Worker   ┆ county1    │
│ Karissa    ┆ 40    ┆ Waterloo  ┆ 150000       ┆ Resident ┆ county1    │
│ Zhang      ┆ 50    ┆ Kitchener ┆ 200000       ┆ Resident ┆ county2    │
│ Noura      ┆ 25    ┆ Guelph    ┆ 75000        ┆ Worker   ┆ county2    │
└────────────┴───────┴───────────┴──────────────┴──────────┴────────────┘
```
However, the NetworkX results contain duplicate edges that have the same offset and table IDs and property information. For example, the `(City_Waterloo, County_county1)` edge appears three times in the results and contain identical information, including properties.

```
Edge (User_Adam, City_Waterloo) has properties {'_src': {'offset': 0, 'table': 0}, '_dst': {'offset': 0, 'table': 1}, '_label': 'LivesIn', 'role': 'Resident'}
Edge (User_Adam, City_Waterloo) has properties {'_src': {'offset': 0, 'table': 0}, '_dst': {'offset': 0, 'table': 1}, '_label': 'LivesIn', 'role': 'Worker'}
Edge (City_Waterloo, County_county1) has properties {'_src': {'offset': 0, 'table': 1}, '_dst': {'offset': 0, 'table': 2}, '_label': 'PartOf'}
Edge (City_Waterloo, County_county1) has properties {'_src': {'offset': 0, 'table': 1}, '_dst': {'offset': 0, 'table': 2}, '_label': 'PartOf'}
Edge (City_Waterloo, County_county1) has properties {'_src': {'offset': 0, 'table': 1}, '_dst': {'offset': 0, 'table': 2}, '_label': 'PartOf'}
Edge (User_Karissa, City_Waterloo) has properties {'_src': {'offset': 1, 'table': 0}, '_dst': {'offset': 0, 'table': 1}, '_label': 'LivesIn', 'role': 'Resident'}
Edge (User_Zhang, City_Kitchener) has properties {'_src': {'offset': 2, 'table': 0}, '_dst': {'offset': 1, 'table': 1}, '_label': 'LivesIn', 'role': 'Resident'}
Edge (City_Kitchener, County_county2) has properties {'_src': {'offset': 1, 'table': 1}, '_dst': {'offset': 1, 'table': 2}, '_label': 'PartOf'}
Edge (User_Noura, City_Guelph) has properties {'_src': {'offset': 3, 'table': 0}, '_dst': {'offset': 2, 'table': 1}, '_label': 'LivesIn', 'role': 'Worker'}
Edge (City_Guelph, County_county2) has properties {'_src': {'offset': 2, 'table': 1}, '_dst': {'offset': 1, 'table': 2}, '_label': 'PartOf'}
```

Perhaps we can utilize these IDs in combination with the property information to inform the `get_as_networkx()` method that the edges have the same source and destination and have identical properties? The de-duplication logic as we have it seems insufficient.

## Code to reproduce

Below is a minimal reproducible example:

```py
import kuzu
import shutil

# Initialize database
shutil.rmtree("./demo_db", ignore_errors=True)
db = kuzu.Database("./demo_db")
conn = kuzu.Connection(db)

# Create schema
conn.execute("CREATE NODE TABLE User(username STRING, age INT64, PRIMARY KEY (username))")
conn.execute("CREATE NODE TABLE City(name STRING, population INT64, PRIMARY KEY (name))")
conn.execute("CREATE NODE TABLE County(county STRING, PRIMARY KEY (county))")
conn.execute("CREATE REL TABLE LivesIn(FROM User TO City, role STRING)")
conn.execute("CREATE REL TABLE PartOf(FROM City TO County)")

# Insert data
conn.execute('COPY User FROM "./user.csv" (HEADER=TRUE)')
conn.execute('COPY City FROM "./city.csv" (HEADER=TRUE)')
conn.execute('COPY County FROM "./county.csv" (HEADER=TRUE)')
conn.execute('COPY LivesIn FROM "./lives-in.csv" (HEADER=TRUE)')
conn.execute('COPY PartOf FROM "./part-of.csv" (HEADER=TRUE)')

# Execute Cypher query
query1 = """
    MATCH (a:User)-[l:LivesIn]->(c:City)-[p:PartOf]->(con:County)
    RETURN a.*, c.*, l.*, p.*, con.*
"""

result1 = conn.execute(query1)
print(result1.get_as_pl())

query2 = """
    MATCH (a:User)-[l:LivesIn]->(c:City)-[p:PartOf]->(con:County)
    RETURN a, c, l, p, con
"""

res2 = conn.execute(query2)
G = res2.get_as_networkx(directed=True)
for u, v, attr in G.edges(data=True):
    print(f"Edge ({u}, {v}) has properties {attr}")
```
The data files are linked below:
[data.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/16895518/data.zip)

title: Optimization: Improve result collector performance
Backslashes are poorly supported in paths on Windows

labels.name: type: usability
labels.description: Issues related to better usability experience, including bad error messages

labels.name: area: frontend
labels.description: Frontend, i.e., binder, parser, query planning-related issues

body:
Forward slashes work, but windows also uses backslashes as a path separator, but kuzu will give a cryptic parser exception if you attempt to use them.

I think it does work if properly escaped, however in some APIs that adds an annoying extra level of string processing (e.g. having to pass `\\\\` to get a single backslash in python).
And the error message is not very helpful. Either you get vaild escape sequences (resulting in it not finding the file) or something like the following:
```
Error: Parser exception: Invalid input <copy foo from ">: expected rule oC_Statement (line: 1, offset: 14)
"copy foo from "C:\Program Files\foo.csv""
```

So maybe we need some combination of support for backslashes in paths on windows directly, and improved error messages related to the incorrect use of escape characters.

title: CI: Add a workflow to automatically create an issue on the docs repo from a PR in this repo
body:
This is a workflow enhancement suggestion to help us write and maintain better docs.

Whenever someone issues a PR to add a new feature that requires documentation, they can mark it with the label "needs-documentation". Then the CI bot would kick in and create a new issue on our [docs repo](https://github.com/kuzudb/kuzu-docs), where it links back to the PR in this repo that adds the feature. This will help on two counts:

- We can link the docs issue directly back to the feature PR that implemented it (or the issue that was flagged) on our main repo
- We can reduce the chances of forgetting to document new features

See [this workflow](https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb/blob/main/.github/workflows/NeedsDocumentation.yml) on the DuckD repo as an example. I think having a workflow like this would work great for our purposes, too!

title: Pyarrow Performance Problem

labels.name: type: perf bug
labels.description: Issues related to a regression in the performance

body:
### Kùzu version

projection-py branch

### What operating system are you using?

_No response_

### What happened?

When scanning from large python dataframes, it seems like Arrow sources are noticeably slower than Numpy sources. For example, consider the following results, where we have a 100 million row table with two integer columns.
```
loadNumpy: 0.09682886581867933s
loadNumpyProj: 0.03378376178443432s

loadArrow: 0.4811821011826396s
loadArrowProj: 0.4280042313039303s
```
The query used for normal results is
```
LOAD FROM df RETURN max(col0), max(col1)
```
Results suffixed by `proj` used the following query
```
LOAD FROM df RETURN max(col0)
```
If we consider the absolute performance difference between not projecting and projecting, both sources improve by about 0.063s and 0.053s respectively, which is most likely the performance improvement gained from not scanning the second column, plus not attempting to determine the max value of the column. However, it looks like arrow scanning comes with a significant overhead. The most likely cause of this overhead is the binding process, though I can't be sure.

### Are there known steps to reproduce?

The following script was used to generate results. It also contains commented out code for benchmarking json, but the performance results there are not expected to be significant.
```py
import kuzu
import os
import random
import pandas as pd
import polars as pl
import numpy as np
import time

conn = kuzu.Connection(kuzu.Database())
conn.execute("LOAD EXTENSION 'extension/json/build/libjson.kuzu_extension';")
# conn.execute("CALL THREADS=1")

random.seed(100)
datalen = 100_000_000
maxnum = 1_000_000_000
mp = {'col0': np.random.randint(maxnum, size=(datalen)), 'col1': np.random.randint(maxnum, size=(datalen))}
polarsDF = pl.DataFrame(mp)
pandasDF = pd.DataFrame(mp)
# open('test.json', 'w').write('[\n' + ',\n'.join(['{"col0": ' + str(mp['col0'][i]) + ', "col1": ' + str(mp['col1'][i]) + '}' for i in range(datalen)]) + '\n]\n')

def benchmark(func, params):
        begin = time.perf_counter()
        func(*params)
        end = time.perf_counter()
        return end - begin

def loadNumpy(conn, df):
        conn.execute('LOAD FROM df RETURN max(col0), max(col1)').get_as_pl()

def loadNumpyProj(conn, df):
        result = conn.execute('LOAD FROM df RETURN max(col0)').get_as_pl()

def loadArrow(conn, df):
        conn.execute('LOAD FROM df RETURN max(col0), max(col1)').get_as_pl()

def loadArrowProj(conn, df):
        result = conn.execute('LOAD FROM df RETURN max(col0)').get_as_pl()

def loadJSON(conn):
        conn.execute('LOAD FROM "test.json" RETURN max(col0), max(col1)').get_as_pl()

def loadJSONProj(conn):
        conn.execute('LOAD FROM "test.json" RETURN max(col0)').get_as_pl()

print(f'loadNumpy: {benchmark(loadNumpy, [conn, pandasDF])}')
print(f'loadNumpyProj: {benchmark(loadNumpyProj, [conn, pandasDF])}')
print(f'loadArrow: {benchmark(loadArrow, [conn, polarsDF])}')
print(f'loadArrowProj: {benchmark(loadArrowProj, [conn, polarsDF])}')
# print(f'loadJSON: {benchmark(loadJSON, [conn])}')
# print(f'loadJSONProj: {benchmark(loadJSONProj, [conn])}')

# os.system('rm test.json')
```

```cypher
MATCH (message2)-[:HAS_TAG]->(tag)
WHERE forum1.id <> forum2.id
```

```cypher
  WITH person, message, topForum2

  RETURN person, count(DISTINCT message) AS messageCount
UNION ALL
  
  
  WITH topForums
  UNWIND topForums AS topForum1
  MATCH (person:Person)<-[:HAS_MEMBER]-(topForum1:Forum)
  RETURN person, 0 AS messageCount
}
RETURN
  person.id AS personId,
  person.firstName AS personFirstName,
  person.lastName AS personLastName,
  person.creationDate AS personCreationDate,
  sum(messageCount) AS messageCount
ORDER BY
```

title: Properly handle finalize calls in Physical Operators
body:
https://github.com/kuzudb/kuzu/pull/4067/files#r1725805914

https://github.com/kuzudb/kuzu/pull/4067 adds calls to `finalize()` to all physical operators (not just sink operators). However, the current implementation that recursively calls `finalize()` on each operator's child can cause `finalize()` to be called multiple times for the same operator (due to calls across pipelines). We currently have a hack to fix this (see the linked comment), but we should properly handle this.

title: BUG: Using `CTRL C` to interrupt a query exits the shell
body:
When running a query and printing query results in the CLI, if `CTRL C` is pressed it exits the shell instead of terminating the query and starting a new line to edit. 

This is due to the way we handle `SIGINT` for the `embedded_shell.cpp` code. 

https://github.com/kuzudb/kuzu/blob/87de7f9128ff9946b95e62bad69bd8d8053a176c/tools/shell/embedded_shell.cpp#L304 https://github.com/kuzudb/kuzu/blob/87de7f9128ff9946b95e62bad69bd8d8053a176c/tools/shell/embedded_shell.cpp#L429-L438

It seems like SIGINT is not being handled by this function or it still terminates afterwards. 

One possibility is switching to using [sigaction](https://www.ibm.com/docs/en/zos/2.4.0?topic=functions-sigaction-examine-change-signal-action) instead of `signal` for more flexibility but a different solution would be needed for Windows. 

Our `CTRL C` handling works in the `linenoise.cpp` file where we change the terminal modes to process the raw input. A similar solution may need to be applied to adjust the terminal mode to correctly send `SIGINT` to our signal handler.
https://github.com/kuzudb/kuzu/blob/87de7f9128ff9946b95e62bad69bd8d8053a176c/tools/shell/linenoise.cpp#L448-L519

title: Feature: Consider adding `BOOL` alias for `BOOLEAN` to help cross-language consistency

labels.name: type: feature
labels.description: New features or missing components of existing features

body:
### API

Other

### Description

Currently, for Python and Rust, which both use `bool` to denote the boolean type natively, we also specify these types in the Kùzu language bindings API.

- Python:  `kuzu.Type.BOOL`
- Rust: `Value::Bool(value)`

When defining a Python UDF, the user has to keep in mind the fact that Kùzu's internal type is named `BOOLEAN`, but the language (Python in this case) calls it `BOOL`. During DDL, we have to maintain this difference by specifying `BOOLEAN` for Kùzu types and `BOOL` for Python types.

Having an alias `BOOL` on Kùzu's side can help keep things consistent when working with Python/Rust. The user can just use `BOOL` everywhere and not have to mix and match.

Rather than changing the language API's naming to match with Kùzu's (which would be a breaking change and affect all tests), it makes more sense to add the alias, which is a minor change, improves usability and consistency, and doesn't break any tests.

title: Bug: Segmentation fault: `WITH` / `OPTIONAL MATCH` / `WHERE EXISTS`
Bug: [Recursive, undirected relationship] Error: Runtime exception: Different path semantics for COUNT(*) optimization is not implemented. Try WALK semantic.
body:
### Kùzu version

nightly

### What operating system are you using?

Fedora 40

### What happened?

Example:
```cypher
CREATE NODE TABLE V (id INT64, PRIMARY KEY(id));
CREATE REL TABLE links_to (FROM V TO V);
CREATE (v1:V {id: 1})-[:links_to]->(v2:V {id: 2})-[:links_to]->(v3:V {id: 3}), 
(v4:V {id: 4})-[:links_to]->(v2),(v4)-[:links_to]->(v5:V {id: 5}), (v6:V {id: 6})-[:links_to]->(v1),
(v8:V {id: 8})-[:links_to]->(v9: V{id: 9}), 
(v10:V {id:10});
```
![graph](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/3b8ea6cb-c23e-43f4-95eb-ba6dc9cf55fd)

Given node `1` as input, I'd like to query the weakly connected components (directly and indirectly connected nodes neglecting the relationship direction).

Expected: `[2,3,4,5,6]`

One possible query leads to following error:
```cypher
kuzu> MATCH (:V {id: 1})-[:links_to*]-(v2:V) RETURN DISTINCT v2;
Error: Buffer manager exception: Failed to claim a frame.
```

The reason is (thanks @andyfengHKU for clarification), that by default `WALK` semantic is used for traversal, which allows arbitrary repeated nodes/edges. Hence this computation ends up costly performance-wise and produces a lot of results.

A temporary workaround - which does not solve mentioned performance issues and is more verbose - is to specify max hops:
```cypher
kuzu> MATCH (:V {id: 1})-[:links_to*..10]-(v2:V) RETURN DISTINCT v2;
┌──────────────────────────────┐
│ v2                           │
│ NODE                         │
├──────────────────────────────┤
│ {_ID: 0:1, _LABEL: V, id: 2} │
│ {_ID: 0:5, _LABEL: V, id: 6} │
│ {_ID: 0:2, _LABEL: V, id: 3} │
│ {_ID: 0:3, _LABEL: V, id: 4} │
│ {_ID: 0:0, _LABEL: V, id: 1} │
│ {_ID: 0:4, _LABEL: V, id: 5} │
└──────────────────────────────┘
(6 tuples)
(1 column)
```
Note there is also small deviation in semantics, as node `1` is included as well.

A better alternative is to use `TRAIL` semantic, which eliminates repeated edges:
```cypher
CALL recursive_pattern_semantic = 'Trail';
kuzu> MATCH (:V {id: 1})-[:links_to*]-(v2:V) RETURN DISTINCT v2;
```
But currently this will trigger following error:
> Error: Runtime exception: Different path semantics for COUNT(*) optimization is not implemented. Try WALK semantic.

Last I think, it would be best if user would not need to `CALL recursive_pattern_semantic = 'Trail';` manually for recursive relationships at all. Re-visiting edges in a recursive fashion via `WALK` - or hopping possibly infinite times between two connected nodes in case of an undirected relation query - probably does not make sense (ever?). Maybe take `TRAIL` as default for recursive relationships - or even globally? 

What might be worth to consider in this regard: Neo4j uses `TRAIL` semantic as default for one `MATCH` pattern. The openCypher standard states:
> While pattern matching, Cypher makes sure to not include matches where the same graph relationship is found multiple times in a single pattern.

### Are there known steps to reproduce?

_No response_

```
Error: Parser exception: mismatched input '<EOF>' expecting {ALTER, ATTACH, BEGIN, CALL, CHECKPOINT, COMMENT, COMMIT, COPY, CREATE, DELETE, DETACH, DROP, EXPORT, IMPORT, INSTALL, LOAD, MATCH, MERGE, OPTIONAL, PROJECT, RETURN, ROLLBACK, SET, UNWIND, USE, WITH} (line: 1, offset: 44)
"// This is a comment match (n) return n.name"
```
Multi-line comments work.

```
kuzu> /* This
..> is a comment */
..> match (n:Person) return n.*;
┌────────┐
│ n.name │
│ STRING │
├────────┤
│ Alice  │
│ Bob    │
│ Carol  │
│ Dan    │
└────────┘
(4 tuples)
(1 column)
Time: 0.09ms (compiling), 0.25ms (executing)
```

## No issues in other clients

Kùzu Explorer has no issues and parses the single line comment correctly, presumably because it uses the Node.js client under the hood. The Python client also parses both kinds of comments correctly.

## Desired behaviour

The user should be able to specify single line comments in the CLI that span an entire line, just like they do in the other interfaces to Kùzu.

A simple rule could be "if line starts with `//` parse that entire line as a comment".

### DuckDB CLI supports this

To demonstrate expected behaviour, DuckDB's CLI supports single line comments.

```
❯ duckdb ./ex_db.duckdb
v1.0.0 1f98600c2c
Enter ".help" for usage hints.
D -- This is a comment
D CREATE TABLE person (name STRING PRIMARY KEY);
```

Also, DuckDB takes care of syntax highlighting the comments in the CLI (note how it's grey in colour):
![image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/134dac27-25ed-4df6-b83f-901cf02d002f)

title: Add option for testing framework to not run queries through separate prepare and execute stages when possible
body:
### API

Other

### Description

Currently, for simplicity, our testing framework always run queries through separate `prepare` and `execute` stages, which allows us to support encoded joins and enumerate all plans.
However, the two stages execution has slight difference from `ClientContext::query()` interface in that whether `prepare` should start its own transaction and auto commit it before `prepare` finishes. Ideally we should cover queries directly through `ClientContext::query()` too.

title: Bug: READ_ONLY connection fails to read from database after ALTER TABLE is run
body:
### Kùzu version

0.5.0

### What operating system are you using?

macOS

### What happened?

The scenario under which this bug occurs is as follows:

- Copy from a Pandas DataFrame to a node table
- Alter node table to add a new column
- `LOAD FROM` a Pandas DataFrame and `MERGE` the new column to the existing Kùzu node table
- Open `READ_ONLY` CLI that tries to access the DB

The following error occurs when a `READ_ONLY` CLI is opened:

```
❯ kuzu ./test_db -r        
Error during recovery: Runtime exception: Failed to replay wal record from WAL file. Error: IO exception: Cannot write to file. path: ./test_db/data.kz fileDescriptor: 6 offsetToWrite: 45056 numBytesToWrite: 8 numBytesWritten: -1. Error: Bad file descriptor
```
The same error occurs with Kùzu Explorer as well.

When I change that to a `READ_WRITE` connection, either with the CLI or Kùzu Explorer, there's no error, and the process opens.

### Are there known steps to reproduce?

Consider this CSV file named `product.csv`:
```
"watch",200.0
"shoes",300.0
"wallet",150.0
```
Run this script:
```py
import kuzu
import shutil
import pandas as pd

shutil.rmtree("test_db", ignore_errors=True)
db = kuzu.Database("test_db")
conn = kuzu.Connection(db)

# create a table
conn.execute("CREATE NODE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS Product (item STRING, price INT64, PRIMARY KEY (item))")

df = pd.read_csv("product.csv", header=None, names=["item", "price"])

conn.execute("COPY Product FROM df")

# Alter a table
conn.execute("ALTER TABLE Product ADD has_discount BOOLEAN DEFAULT false")

df = pd.read_csv("product.csv", header=None, names=["item", "price"])
df["has_discount"] = pd.Series([True, False, True])

conn.execute(
    """
    LOAD FROM df
    WITH item, has_discount
    MERGE (p:Product {item: item})
    ON MATCH SET p.has_discount = has_discount
    """
)

res = conn.execute("MATCH (p:Product) RETURN p.*")
print(res.get_as_df())
```
The aim is to first copy from an initial DataFrame into a node table. Then, alter the node table to add a column. Finally, perform some other computations, and scan/merge from another DataFrame to the new node table column.

The script above runs to completion (no issues). The error is only *after* everything is done, when we try to open a `READ_ONLY` connection to the modified database.

body:

```
kuzu> explain match (a:Person)-[e1]->(b:Person)-[e2]->(c:Person) HINT (a JOIN (e1 JOIN b)) JOIN ((b JOIN e2) JOIN c) return *;
```

title: Join hint with implicit variable names
body:
I have Person and Likes tables. I tried the following query (which I know won't work but I am testing what the system does):
```
explain match (a:Person)-[:Likes]->(b:Person)-[:Likes]->(c:Person), (a)-[:Likes]->(c) HINT a JOIN b JOIN c return *;
Error: Binder exception: Cannot find  in join hint.
```

We should give a better error message. Something like: "HINT clause requires every node and relationship table variable to be named. You have a relationship pattern with label Likes that does not have a named variable, e.g., -[:Likes]-> should be something like -[e:Likes]->." If the pattern does not have a label, you can change that part as: "...you have an unlabeled relationship pattern, ..., e.g., -[]->". 

If the problem is due to an implicit node variable, then the error message can be something like: "HINT clause requires every node and relationship table variable to be named. You have a node pattern with label Person that does not have a named variable, e.g., (:Person) should be something like (a:Person)." Similarly if the pattern does not have a label, you can change the error message accordingly.

In general it's very useful to give clear examples in error message that point users to the mistake. If you think there are many edge cases and don't want to give an error, you can just give a generic example. For example for the first one you can say: "..., e.g., -[:Foo]-> should be something like -[e:Foo]->." and similarly for the second one: "..., e.g., (:Person) should be something like (a:Person)".

body:
### Kùzu version

master

### What operating system are you using?

macOS

### What happened?

When copying from a Pandas DataFrame to a Kùzu node table, the `DOUBLE` or `FLOAT` arrays that represent vector embeddings aren't the same for the entire DataFrame. When a `MATCH` query is run to return the embeddings from the Kùzu table and these are compared with the original DataFrame, in a dataset of 985 rows, 42 rows have the same values, but 943 do not, and their cosine similarity values are < 1, meaning that they are represented by different vectors inside Kùzu.

Code to reproduce is below:

### Are there known steps to reproduce?

I'm running this code from the latest master as follows:

```py
import shutil
import sys
sys.path.append("/Users/prrao/code/kuzu/tools/python_api/build")

import kuzu
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from faker import Faker

def cosine_similarity(a, b):
    return np.dot(a, b) / (np.linalg.norm(a) * np.linalg.norm(b))

database_path = "test_db"

shutil.rmtree(database_path, ignore_errors=True)

db = kuzu.Database(database_path)
conn = kuzu.Connection(db)

try:
    conn.execute("CREATE NODE TABLE User(id INT64, name STRING, embedding DOUBLE[1536], PRIMARY KEY (name))")
except Exception as e:
    print(e)

faker = Faker()
Faker.seed(1)

data = []
for i in range(1000):
    data.append({
        "id": i,
        "name": faker.name(),
        "embedding": np.random.rand(1536).tolist()
    })

df = pd.DataFrame(data).drop_duplicates(subset=["name"])
print("Source DataFrame:", df.shape)

conn.execute("COPY User FROM df")

db_df = conn.execute("MATCH (u:User) RETURN u.*").get_as_df()
print("Database DataFrame:", db_df.shape)

df_merged = pd.merge(df, db_df, left_on="id", right_on="u.id", how="inner")
print("Merged DataFrame:", df_merged.shape)
print(df_merged[["id", "u.id", "embedding", "u.embedding"]].tail(10))

# Check similarity between source and database embeddings
df_merged["sim_score"] = df_merged.apply(lambda row: cosine_similarity(row["embedding"], row["u.embedding"]), axis=1)
print(df_merged[["id", "sim_score"]])
print((df_merged["sim_score"] > 0.99).value_counts())
```

Python

### Description

We currently allow attaching to a remote Kuzu db if its wal file is empty. However with the new MVCC mechanism, wal files will generally be non-empty. This means we cannot attach to (most) Kuzu dbs. There are two things to do here:
1. Remedy: A good remedy is to checkpoint before closing dbs and remove the wal file contents. We can assume that users would close external dbs before attaching to them. So, this should ensure that the external dbs we attach to  have empty wal files.
2. Solution:  Attach db functionality does not assume that the wal file is empty. This is apparently also doable.

If the remedy is easy to do, I suggest we just do that and keep this issue open until we have enough time to implement the actual solution. If they're about the same amount of work, we can go for the solution and not implement the remedy.

title: Fix or a better error message (not) attaching to external kuzu databases with non-empty wal files.

labels.name: type: usability
labels.description: Issues related to better usability experience, including bad error messages

body:
Now that we moved to MVCC, we do not checkpoint immediately after every transaction. Therefore, it is possible that users will connect and do writes to databases that will leave non-empty wal files. 

However we cannot attach to kuzu databases that have non-empty wal files. I get the following error:
`Error: Runtime exception: Cannot attach a remote kuzu database with non-empty wal file.`.

First, I feel this may be a result of the assumptions we made the pre-MVCC transaction manager. We should be able to connect to remote databases that have non-empty wal files. However, if there is a real concern here then, we should at least give a better error message that suggests a solution. In this case the solution is to ask the user to checkpoint the external database. So if we cannot fix the issue, let's update the error message to: `Error: Runtime exception: Cannot attach an external Kùzu database with non-empty wal file. Try manually checkpointing the external database (i.e., run "CHECKPOINT;").`.

title: Bug: Kuzu could violate the relation uniqueness requirements of Cypher standard

labels.name: type: feature
labels.description: New features or missing components of existing features

body:
### Kùzu version

v0.4.2

### What operating system are you using?

Ubuntu 22.04

### What happened?

Kuzu seems to violate the uniqueness requirements when matching relations, as specified in the openCypher standard, chapter "Pattern-Uniqueness"(https://s3.amazonaws.com/artifacts.opencypher.org/openCypher9.pdf):
![image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/4e1594e5-4141-419c-8a3b-fb4d0cae5baf)


For example, suppose we build a database using the following queries:
```cypher
CREATE NODE TABLE L0 (id INT64, PRIMARY KEY (id));
CREATE REL TABLE T0 (FROM L0 TO L0, id INT64);
CREATE (n0:L0{id : 2});
CREATE (n0:L0{id : 5});
MATCH (n0 {id : 5}), (n1 {id : 2}) MERGE(n0)-[r :T0 {id : 24}]->(n1);
MATCH (n0)-[r0]-(n1)-[r1]-(n2) WHERE true RETURN n0.id, r0.id, n1.id, r1.id, n2.id
```
And then run the Cypher query:
```cypher
MATCH (n0)-[r0]-(n1)-[r1]-(n2) WHERE true RETURN n0.id, r0.id, n1.id, r1.id, n2.id
```
There should be no result, as such a pattern does not exist if we do not count repetitive relations (assigning relation 24 to both r0 and r1), and other Cypher-based databases indeed follow this rule, for example Memgraph and neo4j:

![image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/7df01a3d-0a29-4b4e-84ed-e18598e2d5b8)

However, Kuzu violates this property and gives the result:
![image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/d8962a56-4df6-43a8-b7b1-714ce988db25)
Such inconsistency with the standard could cause trouble when programming with Kuzu. Fix would be very appreciated. Thank you!

### Description

We could use similar table outlines in our CLI output to look better and to be more readable. Currently, it's harder to discern each individual row's data in Kùzu than it is in DuckDB (see below for example).

This is how a `LOAD FROM` currently outputs a table in the Kùzu CLI.
```
kuzu> LOAD FROM 'test_data.csv' (header=true) RETURN *;
---------------------------------------------------------------------------
| id | amount   | counts | birthdate  | is_valid | comment                |
---------------------------------------------------------------------------
| 1  | 3.635742 | 89     | 1990-01-01 | true     | This is a test.        |
---------------------------------------------------------------------------
| 2  | 9.381905 | 57     | 2001-03-27 | false    | This is another test.  |
---------------------------------------------------------------------------
(2 tuples)
(6 columns)
```

Here's how it looks in the DuckDB CLI (cleaner and easier to read):

```
D SELECT * FROM test_data.csv;
┌───────┬──────────┬────────┬────────────┬──────────┬────────────────────────┐
│  id   │  amount  │ counts │ birthdate  │ is_valid │        comment         │
│ int64 │  double  │ int64  │    date    │ boolean  │        varchar         │
├───────┼──────────┼────────┼────────────┼──────────┼────────────────────────┤
│     1 │ 3.635742 │     89 │ 1990-01-01 │ true     │ This is a test.        │
│     2 │ 9.381905 │     57 │ 2001-03-27 │ false    │ This is another test.  │
└───────┴──────────┴────────┴────────────┴──────────┴────────────────────────┘
```

Here's how our query profile boxes look - it's already looking nicer than the CLI output does, and is arguably more readable. We already appear to be using continuous lines as table outlines, rather than chaining many hyphens.
```
┌────────────────────────────────┐
│┌──────────────────────────────┐│
││        Physical Plan         ││
│└──────────────────────────────┘│
└────────────────────────────────┘
┌────────────────────────────────┐                                                                                                         
│        RESULT_COLLECTOR        │                                                                                                         
│   --------------------------   │                                                                                                         
│         Expressions:           │                                                                                                         
│   --------------------------   │                                                                                                         
│       NumOutputTuples: 0       │                                                                                                         
│   --------------------------   │                                                                                                         
│    ExecutionTime: 0.000000     │
```

Bug: Heap use after free on substring function with negative starting index
body:
### Kùzu version

v0.4.2

### What operating system are you using?

Ubuntu 22.04

### What happened?

Hi! I discovered a vulnerability where the substring function with a negative starting index could cause the heap-use-after-free vulnerability. This could have security implications.
For example, consider the following query:
```cypher
return substring('abbbb', -9999, 2);
``` 
The return result becomes abnormal with different negative starting index:
![image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/c4c9f65f-5992-433a-9f7a-f642d4a45d76)
After instrumenting with address sanitizer, it's easier to discover the root cause, as the read operation in `kuzu::common::ku_string_t::setLongString(char const*, unsigned long) kuzu/kuzu/src/include/common/types/ku_string.h:49` is previously freed by `PredictionModeClass::hasSLLConflictTerminatingPrediction(antlr4::atn::PredictionMode, antlr4::atn::ATNConfigSet*)kuzu/kuzu/third_party/antlr4_runtime/src/atn/PredictionMode.cpp:61`. To facilitate analysis, I have attached detailed log in the pastebin: https://pastebin.mozilla.org/dT7QgRjE

Thank you!

title: CLI: Remove case-sensitivity for CLI flags

When specifying full words as flags in the CLI, such as `--readOnly`, it expects exact case.
```
❯ kuzu ./test_db --readOnly
Opened the database at path: ./test_db in read-only mode.
Enter ":help" for usage hints.
kuzu> 
```
If I enter `--readonly` as the flag it errors out.

```

Flag could not be matched: readonly
```

This isn't [how DuckDB does it](https://duckdb.org/docs/api/cli/arguments).

title: CLI: Provide better error message when trying to open `READ_ONLY` connection when lock file is in use

labels.name: type: usability
labels.description: Issues related to better usability experience, including bad error messages

body:
Currently, we provide an error message that's not very helpful when a user tries to open a `READ_ONLY` connection to a database whose lock file is held by another process (e.g., a running Jupyter notebook or Python script).

This is our current CLI error message:
```
❯ kuzu ./db -r
Opened the database at path: ./db in read-only mode.
Enter ":help" for usage hints.
IO exception: Could not set lock on file : ./db/.lock
```
It just says "could not set lock on file", but that's not very helpful. Also, it says "opened the database" despite not doing so and producing an error, which is again, not helpful.

Instead, we could say something along the lines of the following:

```
❯ kuzu ./db -r
Error: unable to open database "./db": IO exception: Could not set lock on file : ./db/.lock
See the docs: https://docs.kuzudb.com/connections/concurrency for more information.
```
At least this would point the user to the actual cause and the docs page that helps them understand more.

Here's how DuckDB does it  -- it specifies the exact process ID that's conflicting and which user on the machine is the owner of that process, not sure if we can do that as well, but that would be great:

```
❯ duckdb ./test.duckdb --readonly
Error: unable to open database "./test.duckdb": IO Error: Could not set lock on file "./test.duckdb": Conflicting lock is held in /Users/prrao/.pyenv/versions/3.12.4/bin/python3.12 (PID 97844) by user prrao. See also https://duckdb.org/docs/connect/concurrency
```

title: UX: Allow read-only CLI when another process is holding the lockfile

labels.name: type: feature
labels.description: New features or missing components of existing features

labels.name: type: usability
labels.description: Issues related to better usability experience, including bad error messages

body:
### API

Other

### Description

## Use case
I have a common use case for Python data scientists as follows:
- User opens a Jupyter notebook and starts a `READ_WRITE` connection to Kùzu, and builds a graph
- User then wants to do one of the following: a) open Kùzu Explorer in `READ_ONLY` mode to query the graph visually, and/or b) open the CLI in `READ_ONLY` mode to query the graph interactively
- If there's something wrong with the data or if the data needs to be updated, the user runs more code inside the Jupyter notebook
- All this while, the lock file is held by the notebook (the same `READ_WRITE` connection and underlying process)
- To query the updated data, the user then closes and reopens the CLI or Kùzu Explorer, all the while taking care to specify `READ_ONLY` connection for these processes

## Issue
I'm going through this workflow and run into a problem with the CLI.
```bash
$ kuzu ./db -r
Opened the database at path: ./db in read-only mode.
Enter ":help" for usage hints.
IO exception: Could not set lock on file : ./db/.lock
```
Even though it says it's trying to open the DB in read-only mode, it fails to open the DB because the lock is held by the `READ_WRITE` process inside the Jupyter notebook. This seems far too strict - we're basically assuming the ultimate worst case (that the second process is also `READ_WRITE`, even though the user specified the `-r` flag when opening the CLI).

So from a user perspective, specifying the `-r` flag seems to do nothing when opening the CLI, or at least, doesn't do what it was aiming to do.

I think this is far too common a use case to resort to such a strict treatment where a CLI can't be opened if the lock file is held by a Jupyter notebook. To work around this, can we just assume that *any* process that is opened after an existing process holds the lock file should be read-only, and this is the user's responsibility to ensure that they don't open a second read-write connection? To make it more obvious, we could place a warning as follows:

```bash
$ kuzu ./db -r
Opened the database at path: ./db in read-only mode.
WARNING: The lock file ./db/.lock is being held by another process. This means that you are not guaranteed consistency of your data. To ensure proper consistency of your data, close the process that is holding the lock file and try again.
```
This would make it clear that any data corruption or lack of consistency is because the user ignored the warning and went ahead.

> [!NOTE]
> See the explanation below on why this is not a good idea, and is actually quite unsafe.

title: segfault error with `BEGIN TRANSACTION ... COMMIT`

```python
import kuzu
import tempfile
from uuid import uuid4


with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as dbpath:
    conn = kuzu.Connection(kuzu.Database(dbpath))
    conn.execute(
        """
        CREATE NODE TABLE V (id UUID, PRIMARY KEY (id));
        CREATE REL TABLE after ( FROM V TO V , ONE_ONE);
        """
    )

    id1 = uuid4()
    id2 = uuid4()

    conn.execute("BEGIN TRANSACTION")

    conn.execute(
        """
        CREATE (:V {id: $id1}), (b:V {id: $id2});
        """,
        {"id1": id1, "id2": id2},
    )

    result = conn.execute(

        return ba;
        """,
    )
    while result.has_next():

    conn.execute("COMMIT")
```
Remove the explicit `BEGIN TRANSACTION ... COMMIT` and it works again. This seems to be related to https://github.com/kuzudb/kuzu/issues/3845 , which has transaction issues as well (MVCC?).

body:
### API

Python

### Description

Tested on 0.4.3.dev57

Say I have this input CSV (files attached as zip archive):
```
id,amount,counts,birthdate,is_valid,comment
a68a8af4-4a53-4420-9cb8-4a3e1fa0f324,3.635742,89,1990-01-01,true,"This is a test. "
55cfb01c-8cfc-4e3f-8408-05f362d7cf31,9.381905,57,2001-03-27,false,"This is another ""test"". "
9cddb5ae-e1d8-4382-b364-19b67e9a45a5,1.668131,29,2004-02-29,true,"This is (yet) another \"test\". "
```
I'd like to use the following schema for the node table that's created from the CSV:
```cypher
CREATE NODE TABLE Item(
    id STRING,
    amount DOUBLE,
    counts INT32,
    birthdate STRING,
    is_valid BOOLEAN,
    comment STRING,
    PRIMARY KEY(id)
)
```
If I want the `counts` column to be INT32 instead of the default INT64, I have to manually cast it using `LOAD FROM` on the DataFrame as follows:

```
COPY Item FROM (
    LOAD FROM df
    RETURN
      id,
      amount,
      CAST(counts AS INT32),
      date
      is_valid,
      comment
)
```
There are two inconveniences here:
1. Just for casting the one column in the entire DataFrame, we have to explicitly write out every column name (which is verbose if we have 10+ columns, which is really common in real world data). If we don't do the manual casting, the `COPY` will fail.
2. The min/max integer information for a column in a DataFrame is already known beforehand, so Kùzu (in theory) can estimate the right integer type for this range, rather than the user having to manually cast the type by calculating their data ranges.

The provided code in the zip file shows how DuckDB does this - it seems to auto-detect the ranges of integers, downcasting the `INT64` type from Pandas/Polars DataFrame. Here's an example of DuckDB's output before (once the Polars df is read) and after (Outputting the results of a query and sending it to a Polars df).

Before:
```
┌─────────────────────────────────┬──────────┬────────┬────────────┬──────────┬────────────────────────────────┐
│ id                              ┆ amount   ┆ counts ┆ birthdate  ┆ is_valid ┆ comment                        │
│ ---                             ┆ ---      ┆ ---    ┆ ---        ┆ ---      ┆ ---                            │
│ str                             ┆ f64      ┆ i64    ┆ str        ┆ bool     ┆ str                            │
╞═════════════════════════════════╪══════════╪════════╪════════════╪══════════╪════════════════════════════════╡
│ a68a8af4-4a53-4420-9cb8-4a3e1f… ┆ 3.635742 ┆ 89     ┆ 1990-01-01 ┆ true     ┆ This is a test.                │
│ 55cfb01c-8cfc-4e3f-8408-05f362… ┆ 9.381905 ┆ 57     ┆ 2001-03-27 ┆ false    ┆ This is another "test".        │
│ 9cddb5ae-e1d8-4382-b364-19b67e… ┆ 1.668131 ┆ 29     ┆ 2004-02-29 ┆ true     ┆ This is (yet) another \test\.  │
└─────────────────────────────────┴──────────┴────────┴────────────┴──────────┴────────────────────────────────┘
```
After (note how the `counts` column is now an `INT32`, which presumably came from DuckDB):
```
┌─────────────────────────────────┬──────────┬────────┬────────────┬──────────┬────────────────────────────────┐
│ id                              ┆ amount   ┆ counts ┆ birthdate  ┆ is_valid ┆ comment                        │
```

title: Feature: Automatically alias column names in Kùzu result when using `a.*`

labels.name: type: feature
