title: Reading parquet in Python has some rough edges, making it hard to diagnose problems
body:
I've upgraded to the latest version `0.0.9` and there are a few rough edges with reading parquet from Python.

## Problem scenario
If I have a parquet file with two columns, `id` and `name`, of type `INT64` and `STRING` respectively.

During development, sometimes we may specify the wrong data type during table creation, for example in this case:

```py
def create_node_table(conn: Connection) -> None:
    conn.execute(
        """
        CREATE NODE TABLE
            Data(
                id STRING,
                name STRING
            )
        """
    )
```

In this case, the data type of the id should be `INT64`, but was specified as `STRING`, it just segfaults, making it very hard for the Python developer to know what they did wrong (it's not a Kùzu bug, and could have very easily been fixed if the user just had a better error message).

```sh
[1]    5208 segmentation fault  python test.py
```

In the reverse situation, the error is even more complex. Say I have a parquet file with the same two columns, `id` and `name`, but this time, the `id` column is also of type `STRING` like the `name` column is.

```py
def create_node_table(conn: Connection) -> None:
    conn.execute(
        """
        CREATE NODE TABLE
            Data(
                id INT64,
                name STRING
            )
        """
    )
```

This time, if the user specified the `id` column in the node table creation as of the type `INT64` (by mistake, when they should have specified `STRING`), it doesn't segfault but instead gives this weird error.

```sh
  File "/code/.venv/lib/python3.11/site-packages/kuzu/connection.py", line 88, in execute
    self._connection.execute(
RuntimeError: ColumnChunk::templateCopyStringArrowArray
```

What should be a 2-second fix to the data type now becomes a tedious exercise for the Python developer to go back and inspect the data and learn (after some deliberation) that the data type specified in Python was wrong.

##  Developer experience focus

These sorts of issues are more generic, and I suppose adding these edge cases to the test suite could help avoid such issues, but it's impossible for the Kùzu team to know all the kinds of ways users may break the system.

In this case, malformed data types (or the user simply making a mistake) is a common enough scenario that the test suite can be expanded, but the longer term problem of C++ error propagation to Python is still something to ponder about. What should be a *very* simple fix, can take minutes of unnecessary developer effort to build even the simplest graphs. This is quite a big source of user frustration in Python, and it's pretty natural to expect a large portion of future Kùzu users to come from Python, so this is a serious enough issue to discuss -- I think it really makes sense to deep-dive into how to present better error messages to Python users, cc @andyfengHKU @semihsalihoglu-uw

title: Buffer Manager Eviction Rework
body:
## Overview
Currently we adopt a queue-based eviction policy. A concurrent queue is used to keep track of all marked pages as eviction candidates. This poses overheads to `unpin`, as each call of this function needs to switch unlocked pages to marked, and add it to the eviction queue. 

The alternative solution described in [Virtual-Memory Assisted Buffer Management](https://dl.acm.org/doi/abs/10.1145/3588687)[^1] is to store all cached page identifiers in a fixed-size open addressing hash table. The size of the hash table is equal to the number of pages in DRAM (bounded by buffer manager memory limit). Instead of accessing eviction queue in each `unpin`, hash table is not accessed during cache hits and unpin, but only during page faults and eviction.
Moreover, the hash table makes it easier to loop over, and clean up page states from BM as we sometimes need to ` removeFilePagesFromFrames`.

This issue proposes to replace the concurrent queue with a fixed-size hash table.

## Page State and Eviction
The design of our buffer manager follows *vmCache*. See Section 3 in paper [Virtual-Memory Assisted Buffer Management](https://dl.acm.org/doi/abs/10.1145/3588687) for detailed description.

### Page State
Each page is associated with a 64-bit state entry. The entry encodes both state and version counter. 56 bits are used for the version counter. and the left 8 bits are used for state, including LOCKED, UNLOCKED, MARKED, EVICTED. Any page must be in one of these four states. The version counter is used for optimistic read. See our [code comment](https://github.com/kuzudb/kuzu/blob/4aa1d07812665b5b1067e065d40359ad7f037118/src/include/storage/buffer_manager/buffer_manager.h#L71-L162) here for more details .

### Eviction Algorithm
This issue proposes to implement hash table-based CLOCK algorithm.
The key idea is to find an old page to evict, not necessarily the oldest. We loop through cached pages in the hash table until we find one that hasn't been referenced since the last time we check it.

Eviction happens at batches of 64 pages at a time, and is performed in five steps:
1. loop over the hash table, and get a batch of marked candidates from hash table.
2. write dirty pages (optionally, this can be done with async io).
3. try to lock clean page candidates.
4. remove locked pages from page table using `madvise`.
5. remove locked pages from eviction hash table, unlock them.

Note: Currently, we already ensure dirty pages are locked. No need to lock and upgrade dirty pages as described in `vmcache`.

See code [here](https://github.com/viktorleis/vmcache/blob/28dcacfaf94dcb34a0cecd8514e87fdbadd22dc1/vmcache.cpp#L743) for implementation details in `vmcache`.

### Changes to BM
1. Remove `addToEvictionQueue` from `unpin` .
2. Rework `claimAFrame` to be on top of the hash table based batch eviction.

### Suggested Testings
As BM is critical to the system, and complicated enough to be not easily tested. We suggest following ways (but not limited to these) to test it when open an PR to fix this issue. Using `logger` is a good way to ensure the correctness of the algorithm. Also, set eviction batch size to 1 can simplify log tracing.

**Existing tests**
After changes, existing tests should still be able to pass (`make test`).


**Small BM size**
Try to set BM to a very small size to ensure BM can correctly bookkeep memory usage. For example, running query `MATCH (c:Comment) RETURN min(c.length)` requires two pinned 256KB pages, and one an extra 4KB page should be enough to evaluate the query on LDBC1 comment table with a single thread.

**Repeated query with large BM size**
Given enough BM buffer, running the same query twice: the first run will trigger cache of all necessary pages, and the second run will trigger no reads from files, and no evictions; or running the same query concurrently: each page should only be read once from file, and no evictions are triggered.

**Repeated query with limited BM size**
Given limited BM buffer, for example, around half of needed disk pages, running the same query twice. The first run will trigger read of all pages from file, and also evictions of around half of pages read from file. The second run will also trigger eviction of pages read from the first run, and re-read pages from files. If carefully designed, it's possible to see each  page is read twice from file, and evicted at least once.

**Detailed CLOCK behaviour tracing**
Given a small BM buffer, for example, 1MB, run a simple scan query (for example, `MATCH (c:Comment) RETURN min(c.length)`) in single thread, and log changes to states of pages (e.g., `pin` a page to LOCKED and add it into hash table, `unpin` a page to UNLOCKED, marking unlocked pages to MARK, lock marked pages to evict them, remove evicted pages and unlock them, etc.) and clock hand position in the cache hash table. The tracing should be able to be verified with careful simulation of CLOCK behaviour.

**Large scale queries on LDBC100**
Run our benchmark queries on LDBC100 dataset to validate it works on some level of large scale dataset with multiple threads.

[^1]: Leis, Viktor, et al. "Virtual-Memory Assisted Buffer Management." SIGMOD'23.

body:
In #2118 we switched from exporting all symbols on Windows to explicit export of symbols to avoid hitting the limit in a single windows dll. This change would have a number of benefits on other platforms too (smaller dynamic libraries, faster library loading, no accidental use of private APIs), and needs to be more rigorously tested.

TODO:
- [x] Make default visibility of functions hidden ([by making these statements unconditional](https://github.com/kuzudb/kuzu/blob/ede12a79acc262b8082dad8e927a9802d48a8c5a/CMakeLists.txt#L11-L14))
- [ ] Remove re-exported static dependency symbols from the dynamic libraries on Linux (probably macOS too since I think it's related to ELF). Maybe there are better solutions, but what I could find before was using [linker version scripts](https://www.gnu.org/software/gnulib/manual/html_node/LD-Version-Scripts.html) to filter the public symbols. They support a wildcard syntax which can probably be used to avoid explicitly listing all the symbols. I don't know how it interacts with C++ name mangling, but maybe we could just allow a variation of `kuzu*` to filter everything not in the kuzu namespace (or C functions prefixed with `kuzu_`).
- [x] Get the API tests to link against the dynamic libraries with the restricted symbols so that we can properly test the exported APIs (the main issue is that the testing helper classes use private APIs, so we either need to remove those, or maybe set up an internal static library for those helpers that they can link with alongside the dynamic library).
- [x] Produce the single file header as part of the cmake build (maybe we could set up a cmake install command at the same time).
  - [x] Get the API tests to use the single file header.
  - [ ] Test linking the rust API against the dynamic library and single file header.

title: Integer Bitpacking extensions
body:
From the extra TODOs in #2004, ordered roughly from simplest to most complicated.

- [x] Var List offsets can be bitpacked
- [x] InternalIDs can be bitpacked
- [x] INT16 and INT8 bitpacking
- [x] Small reads/writes to bitpacked data could be optimized to work on individual data instead of relying on packing/unpacking a 32-value chunk to a temporary array.
- [x] Extra values could be packed into the end of each page when the page does not divide evenly into 32-value chunks.
- [ ] SIMD bitpacking

## Notes
### InternalIDs
Stored as offset_t (uint64_t), but would need an extra layer to handle widening the results into the internal_id_t struct. This could cause significant slowdowns when decompressing since we wouldn't be able to use the fast mass decompression functions directly. Since the current random access implementation is not very efficient (unpacks 32 values to get one) it would probably be more performant to unpack to a temporary buffer and then copy the values into the value vector

### Filling the extra space at the end of each page
This would be trivial to implement when direct reads and writes of bitpacked data is implemented.

### SIMD
Mostly complicated due to handling compiler support.

## Benchmarks

It would also be helpful to set up some small benchmarks (maybe using [google benchmark](https://github.com/google/benchmark), essentially what I did when comparing implementations at the start) so that we can do some fast comparisons of the compression/decompression speed without having to deal with the overhead of the rest of the system (not that such integrated benchmarks aren't also useful).

body:
When testing the integer bitpacking, I added a test which inserts many nodes at once (`NodeInsertionDeletionTests.InsertManyNodesTest`). This is rather slow (inserting `NODE_GROUP_SIZE` values took 75 seconds), so I tried to speed it up by doing it all as one transaction rather than one automatic transaction for each insert, but that resulted in a hang, or at least it was taking much longer than 75 seconds, even for smaller sizes like the 4096 values I ended up using (which still takes a few seconds).

Note that this was reproducible on the master branch prior to my bitpacking changes in #2004.

In addition, inserting values in small chunks would cause a `Buffer manager exception: Failed to claim a frame` error.
This would occur even with just one  value (I also tested on chunks of 2, 5 and 10) inserted between calling `Connection::beginWriteTransaction` and `Connection::commit` (after many inserts at least, the other test in `NodeInsertionDeletionTests` proves that it at least works the first few times).

Tests that reproduce both of these issues can be found in [this commit](https://github.com/kuzudb/kuzu/commit/75b57305ddd0e1c1eee320cde0a9fa1ef28f0563).

title: Remove LogicalFillTableID
body:
This operator is a temporary solution for RDF predicate IRI evaluation.

Predicate internal ID is stored in both RDF rel (triple) table and RDF node (resource) table. Internal ID type consists of (table ID, offset) pairs. When we store it as a rel property we have the following problem: When storing internal IDs, our copy codeline does not store the tableID part of the internal ID since so far in our usage, the table IDs are always the same and repeated. For example when storing destination node IDs (which are internal IDs), since the destination node tables are always the same, we don't need to store the table ID parts of the dst node IDs. Then when scanning internal IDs, the scanner we have reads the table ID from the schema information of the table the internal IDs are stored in. The problem is this: when storing the integer versions of the predicate IRIs, we store them as internal IDs but the table IDs are the Resources Node Table. But the internal ID scanner fills the table ID as the Triples Rel Table ID. So for now we have this additional operator LogicalFillTableID that corrects this mistake and replaces the Triples Rel Table ID with Resources Node Table ID.

If constant compression works and we can automatically avoid writing repeated tableIDs, the right approach is to always store the entire internal ID, i.e., both the tableIDs and offsets and let the compressed scanner handle reading the correct values. If that solution does not work for some reason, we need to revisit this but we should not store repeated values unnecessarily.

body:
From https://github.com/kuzudb/kuzu/pull/2004#pullrequestreview-1619580708.

For #2004 it would be helpful to have a runtime database option (e.g. `ENABLE_COMPRESSION`) for enabling/disabling compression.

I'm not entirely sure how we would want to implement such a thing, as it presumably should be a persistent setting, not just a setting for accessing the database like bufferPoolsize and maxNumThreads in the SystemConfig struct. That being said, since #2004 stores compression information per-chunk, it certainly would be possible to change the setting after the database has been created, it would just mean that the new setting would only affect new ColumnChunks (unless there is some re-processing done to update the existing data to match the new value of the setting).

title: Unity builds
body:
Unity builds (where we amalgamate source files before compiling) can offer compilation and runtime speedups. CMake has [builtin support](https://cmake.org/cmake/help/latest/prop_tgt/UNITY_BUILD.html) for it.

Tasks:
- [ ] Ensure every header has `#pragma once` (this is not currently the case).
- [ ] Enable unity builds and test them in CI.
- [ ] Compare unity builds against normal ones and decide which to use for releases.

As for combining all the source files into one, this is generally not recommended, according to the [CMake Documentation](https://cmake.org/cmake/help/latest/prop_tgt/UNITY_BUILD_BATCH_SIZE.html), though it is possible. It is something we could consider trying out, though the memory usage promises to be extremely high. In general, we could play around with batch sizes and see what runtime gains there are to be had.

title: Pass parameters to `connection.execute` as dict instead of list of tuples
body:
## Observation

The current approach of passing parameters to a Cypher query in Kùzu via Python is a bit tedious, as the user has to type out a list of tuples that makes the code a bit ugly, and on many counts, is not "pythonic".

The Neo4j Python client [allows](https://neo4j.com/docs/api/python-driver/current/api.html#neo4j.Driver.execute_query) the specification of parameters as `dict[str, Any]`, which is much easier to use and type for Python users. In recent versions of Python, we also have `TypedDict`, which we can use to more carefully check types on parameters prior to passing them to the query.

## Proposed solution

Instead of specifying that the user pass `list[tuple[str, Any]]`, the [docstring ](https://github.com/kuzudb/kuzu/blob/9526e5eb2c00551d38e93ca9439c653554bcebb4/tools/python_api/src_py/connection.py#L76)could instead say to pass `dict[str, Any]`, in a similar way to Neo4j's Python client.

To avoid breaking anything for the C++ bindings, the dict could easily be converted to `list[tuple[str, Any]]` within the code (invisible to the user) as follows:

```sh
>>> params = {"age": 42}
>>> list(params.items())
[('age', 42)]
```

This effortless transformation could be added at the [start](https://github.com/kuzudb/kuzu/blob/9526e5eb2c00551d38e93ca9439c653554bcebb4/tools/python_api/src_py/connection.py#L85) of the `execute` statement `src_py/connection.py`, and the docstring could be updated to inform the user to passs params as `dict[str, Any]` accordingly.

I don't think this would break any existing tests, not require any changes to C++ query preparation code, and also maintain a more similar API to Neo4j's client. Hope this makes sense!

title: Integer Bitpacking Plan
body:
*Work in progress*

# Library

DuckDB is using `bitpacking.{h,cpp}` from https://github.com/lemire/FastPFor. It's not using the SIMD code from that library, and there isn't really any documentation of their design choices for this (looks like they've also implemented more complex options themselves [here](https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb/blob/1f17e1cec65e4207b6e38ca701c9d16573a98316/src/storage/compression/bitpacking.cpp)).

It doesn't have much documentation, but the algorithms are described in https://arxiv.org/abs/1209.2137. I'm fairly sure that most of these are not suited to random access (mentioned in #1474 as a requirement).

Their bitpacking helpers don't provide any functions for random access, but we should be able to compute the offsets using the data width. and implement the edge access ourselves to avoid overwriting adjacent data (i.e. use the fast functions to decompress the middle and our own probably less optimized functions for the edges (at the least we can't leverage SIMD)).

They also implement a SIMDBinaryPacking algorithm, which as far as I can tell is like bitpacking, but gets increased compression from subtracting the minimum value from each value, and would still be easily capable of random access; you'd just need to also read the minimum value with the bit width.

## Alternatives
[TurboPFor](https://github.com/powturbo/TurboPFor-Integer-Compression) seems like a newer library, but note that it's GPL licensed ("a commercial license is available", which may be an option if we want to use it without being restricted with respect to binary distribution). [It does appear to provide functions for random access](https://github.com/powturbo/TurboPFor-Integer-Compression/blob/da4fa61f6dedee61a3c0c624fc8656d84b820392/include/ic.h#L200-L208), and has [zigzag encoded versions](https://github.com/powturbo/TurboPFor-Integer-Compression/blob/da4fa61f6dedee61a3c0c624fc8656d84b820392/include/ic.h#L310-L314) for handling signed data..

https://github.com/lemire/FastPFor#other-recommended-libraries lists some alternatives

https://github.com/ademakov/Oroch: Simpler library, probably not as performant, but does automatically handle signed types with zigzag encoding.

# Implementation

Proposed steps:

0. Benchmark and compare available options, looking at signed and unsigned data.
1. Write up generic interface for compression/bitpacking and re-write the boolean packing implementation to use it
2. Make the generic interface also support uncompressed data and make integers use the uncompressed version
3. Implement integer packing algorithms using the interface
4. Benchmark, comparing performance before and after (including uncompressed to see if the interface itself is causing performance regressions). 

We probably want to combine the existing boolean implementation with the integer bitpacking. It should generally be identical, and the single bit width operators. One advantage would be zero-sized data when all values are false (it would be possible to do the same when all values are true with the binary packing algorithms (minimum and maximum value of 1 giving a bit width of 0)).

All the functions deal with unsigned data, so we will need to handle converting the output to 

## Data Layout for Bitpacking 

Store at the beginning of the chunk, or in separate stats (doesn't seem necessary if they are only needed when accessing the data):
1. The type of compression (as an enum; single byte) (assuming we want to support multiple types of compression at runtime; otherwise if hardcoded to a specific type per data type this could be omitted).
2. The maximum size in bits (absolute): six bits (0-63, if 64 is needed store as uncompressed instead (or in a seventh bit if we're not allowing uncompressed data))
3. Whether or not there are signed values: 1 bit (data needs to be 1 bit wider and will need additional processing for negative values).

title: Optimization on local storage
body:
This is a list to keep track of optimization todos related to local storage:
- [ ] In-place sliding for var list column chunk. For var list, now we scan the whole column chunk from storage, and allocate a new one to copy from scanned column chunk and local vectors. This is quite inefficient as it bloats memory usage, and may trigger unnecessary read. Ideally, we should only read the whole chunk when we figure out the data column chunks needs to be resized (thus moved to another place), and sliding should happen in-place.
- [x] When insert, we first append a new column chunk when inserting new nodes out of the max bound of existing node groups, and then perform updates. This should be rewritten as in place inserting a new column chunk through local storage.

title: Allow defining a rel table with multiple src/dst node tables
body:
Real world applications can contain relationships with a large number of SRC/DST node table combinations.
Right now, we strictly force a rel table to be defined only with one src and one dst node table, which is best optimized. However, in terms of better user experience, we should gradually relax this restriction to support defining a rel table with multiple src/dst node tables.

Sometimes it's not easy to have a fully cleaned dataset, which could be annoying when it comes to data loading, as users need to repeatedly try through `COPY` and modify their dataset as we throw errors.
To provide a more smooth `COPY` experience, it would be good to add an option to `COPY` statement which allows skipping malformed rows either silently or through logging.
This should cover copying of both node and rel tables.

title: Transaction refactor
body:
## Why we need this refactor
Since we support UDF, user created macros should have different visibilities to read/write transactions. E.g. user created macros should only be visible to the statements within that write transaction until it commits. To achieve this, binder needs to use the transaction pointer when matching macros from the catalog.

## Plan:
1. Move transaction pointer from executionContext to clientContext so binder can access this transaction pointer as well. Client context should also be saved in the executionContext, so processors (operators) can access the transaction pointer.
2. We should prepare statements in a transaction. When the user calls to `prepare()`, we should check whether there is an active transaction. If not, we should start an auto-commit transaction.
3. Refactors the catalog APIs:
We should stop exposing the `getReadOnlyVersion()`, `getWriteVersion()` to the caller. Instead, each get API in the catalog should take in a transaction pointer.

title: Pass transaction pointer to binder
body: Binder currently has no access to the transaction pointer, however, binder needs the transaction pointer to know whether it's wrapped in a read/write trx to bind the macro functions.

title: Rust API Ergonomics

Initially brought up on slack.

This is already exposed in the Python API via [PyQueryResult.getAsArrow](https://github.com/kuzudb/kuzu/blob/d6efe97a61eba936b568006509026186d820acf8/tools/python_api/src_cpp/py_query_result.cpp#L211-L223), and could be extended to at least the C++ and Rust APIs.

The kuzu Python API uses the [table](https://arrow.apache.org/docs/cpp/tables.html#tables) data format, which is limited to the C++ arrow API and the APIs built on top of it like the python API.

However it looks like [RecordBatch](https://arrow.apache.org/docs/cpp/tables.html#record-batches) can be sent/shared between implementations, so we could probably use the existing arrow C++ code that the python API uses and then send the data to other APIs.

title: Testing framework new line representation
body:
### Discussion

The `EXPLAIN` statement returns one line in the query result containing "\n" characters to display multiple lines. Currently, the testing framework reads the result from the `.test` file and considers it as multiple lines.

For example, the following test will fail even though the result looks the same as expected. The reason is that the testing framework will read 15 lines and store them in a `std::vector<std::string>`, having 15 elements. However, the actual result, which the framework will compare, is a `std::vector<std::string>` with one only string element: `┌─────────────────────────────┐\n│┌───────────────────────────┐│\n....`

```
-STATEMENT EXPLAIN create node table npytable (id INT64,i32 INT32, PRIMARY KEY(id));
---- 15
┌─────────────────────────────┐
│┌───────────────────────────┐│
││       Physical Plan       ││
│└───────────────────────────┘│
└─────────────────────────────┘
┌─────────────────────────────┐
│      CREATE_NODE_TABLE      │
│   -----------------------   │
│          npytable           │
│   -----------------------   │
│     NumOutputTuples: 0      │
│   -----------------------   │
│   ExecutionTime: 0.000000   │
└─────────────────────────────┘
```

### Possible solutions

1. This [tentative PR](https://github.com/kuzudb/kuzu/pull/1750) replaces `\n` and `push_back` to the expected result. However, it fails on the MSVC test and might not be a good practice to change the result.

2. Support writing `\n` so you can write something like this:
```
-STATEMENT EXPLAIN create node table npytable (id INT64,i32 INT32, PRIMARY KEY(id));
---- 1
┌─────────────────────────────┐\n│┌───────────────────────────┐│\n││       Physical Plan       ││\n...

```

3. Introduce a new command `-FLATTEN_RESULT` or similar to flatten the result in one single line.
```
-FLATTEN_RESULT
-STATEMENT EXPLAIN create node table npytable (id INT64,i32 INT32, PRIMARY KEY(id));
---- 15
┌─────────────────────────────┐
│┌───────────────────────────┐│
││       Physical Plan       ││
...
```

4. Instead of `-STATEMENT` create a special command `-EXPLAIN` that recognizes this situation in particular
```
-EXPLAIN create node table npytable (id INT64,i32 INT32, PRIMARY KEY(id));
---- 15
┌─────────────────────────────┐
│┌───────────────────────────┐│
││       Physical Plan       ││
...
```

5. Start the result line with a sequence of characters that will consider the whole result as one (`"""` or `___` or similar)
```
-STATEMENT EXPLAIN create node table npytable (id INT64,i32 INT32, PRIMARY KEY(id));
---- 15
"""┌─────────────────────────────┐
│┌───────────────────────────┐│
││       Physical Plan       ││
...
"""
```

Regardless of the solution, I believe option (2) should be implemented since it might be helpful in other different use cases, such as testing one tuple with multiple lines in the future.

title: Exception Handling in Java API
body:
In the implementation of the Java API, when the native (C++) code throws an exception and if that exception is not handled in the native code, the program quits with no way for the user to handle the exception on the Java end.

One potential fix would be catch every possible exception in the native code and throw a Java exception to the JVM. But this would require adding a try catch block in every native function and implementing a full set of custom Java exceptions.

title: CSV cleaner extension using LLM
body:
### Motivation

I was trying to import [WikiKG90Mv2](https://ogb.stanford.edu/docs/lsc/wikikg90mv2/) from OGB to Kùzu, but the CSV contains some small errors in different lines, for example, escaping `,`, extra `,` at the end of line, extra `"` etc. 

```
6031876,Q12857511,Template:\,Wikimedia templat
3119806,Q105422542,"Alley, Jerome",article in A Compendium of Irish Biography,
3738009,Q106122025,"Kristian Hvidt: \""Forsker, furie, frontkæmper. En bog om Lis Jacobsen\""",
```

These small errors might not be a problem for some parsers, and we can also make ours more flexible to handle known situations automatically. However, it only partially solves the problem. Real-world data is extremely noisy and full of errors and incompletions. From the user's perspective, cleaning CSV is a time-consuming task, and it is difficult to automate. 

My idea is to propose a feature as an extension to automatically clean CSV data using LLM while importing. LLMs are proven to be very efficient in spotting and fixing these errors by contextualizing the current CSV data and inferring a correction.
This optional extension should be able to learn the structure from a tiny portion of the CSV and automatically fix broken lines during data ingestion.

We should leverage the free GitHub runners to run tests on more platforms such as macOS, Fedora, SUSE, Alpine, Arch, and Windows server regularly and also move the format checkers to GitHub runners since these jobs are not large. We should restructure the CI pipeline to keep our current self-hosted runners as fast-track, while adding a slow-tracks of test jobs using the GitHub runners.

title: Support COPY TO statement
body:
### Proposal

This feature will enable users to export query results to either CSV or PARQUET files using our current `COPY` command. In the same way, we already perform `COPY FROM`, the idea is to use the same statement using `COPY TO`, similar to [DuckDB Copy](https://duckdb.org/docs/sql/statements/copy.html).

### Examples

Add HEADER and DELIMITER properties
`COPY Person TO "person.csv" (HEADER=true, DELIM='|');`

Write a specific query result to `result.parquet`
`COPY (MATCH (a:person) RETURN a.name) TO "result.parquet"`

**TODO**

The idea is to break down the deliverable of the complete feature in the following order:

1. Implement `COPY ([query]) TO "file.csv"`
2. Support `.parquet` file type
3. Optimize via parallel processing

title: DataType struct packing issue
body:
C++ compilers don't guarantee that the size of a struct equals to the sum of the struct fields.
E.g. `blob_t` is a struct with single field of `ku_string_t`.
The compiler doesn't guarantee that sizeof(blob_t) == sizeof(ku_string_t) due to different struct padding techniques.
Given the physical type of `blob_t` is `ku_string_t` and we allocate valueVector buffer for blob based on the size of ku_string_t, this may cause bugs in some compiling env.

title: Proposal of Kùzu GUI / Visualization
body:
This issue proposes a frontend user application for Kùzu that aims to provide end user: interactive querying, graph visualization, and schema design functionalities.

## Main Features
### Schema Design
The schema design feature should provide user with a graph visualization of the current schema and allow user to add/remove new  node and rel tables, as well as modifying the existing tables (add / drop properties). The UI design of this feature should be the standard node-link diagram that's provided by many existing systems. Where the nodes corresponds to the node tables and the edges correspond to the rel tables. How to visualize [RDFGraphs](https://github.com/kuzudb/kuzu/issues/1570) when they are integrated is to be decided. When the user clicks on a node/edge, the properties of the table should be displayed in a side panel with the options to modify it. There should also be a button to add a new node table. Connecting the node tables results in a new rel table to be created.

### Interactive Query and Visualization
This feature is for users to run a Cypher query interactively on the UI and get the query results back in both tabular and graph format. This is a standard feature on every graph DBMS application that I'm aware of (e.g., Neo4J, Nebula, Memgraph). I propose to support the following features:
- Query syntax highlight.
- Switching between table view and graph visualization.
- Pagination/infinite scroll in the table view.
- The graph visualization's appearance should be customizable. The user can specify the colors of each type of nodes and edges, the attribute to be displayed on each node/edge, and the size of the nodes from the side panel.
- Zoom and pan of the visualization. 
- Interaction: when clicking on a node, its properties should be shown on the side panel and it should be highlighted.
- Hide/unhide nodes.
- Scale up to a few thousand nodes.

### Graph Explore
This allows a user to pick up a starting point and interactively navigate the graph. By double clicking on a node, the nodes which has a connection to the node via a relationship should show up in the visualization. This is similar to [Neptune graph explorer](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/neptune/latest/userguide/visualization-graph-explorer.html). 

### Loading Data
We should provide users with a collection of bundled dataset for quickly exploring Kùzu. The bundled dataset can be loaded to a database with one click.

## Tech Stack
We will use the web stack to build this application. The frontend will be a Vue.js-based single-page application. The backend will be in Node.js. For graph visualization, we are considering the following libraries:
- [sigma.js](https://www.sigmajs.org/)
- [visjs](https://visjs.github.io/vis-network/examples/)
- [G6](https://github.com/antvis/g6)
- [3d-force-graph](https://github.com/vasturiano/3d-force-graph)

If none of the libraries meets all the design requirements, we can also use D3.js to render SVG manually. 

## Deployment
We have several options here:

### Docker
This is what we should start with because a Docker deployment would be suitable for the users whose databases are located on a remote server (instead of their local machines). Since Kùzu is an embeddable database, there is not an option to connect to a remote Kùzu server. But with the Docker image, the user can simply start a Kùzu web server on the remote machine via:
```
docker run -it -p 8080:8080 -v /path/to/database:/db kuzudb/kuzu-gui
```
Then, the application can be accessed in the browser. 

The downside of this approach is that for users who are solely working locally, they would have to install Docker on their machines.

### Electron App
For users who are solely working locally, with the [Electron wrapper](https://www.electronjs.org/), the app could be downloaded to local machine and started immediately without any additional setup. The user simply needs to download the app for their operating system and launch it, then open the local database file.

### Sandbox
We should also install a sandbox deployment Kùzu's homepage to allow users to try Kùzu without downloading/installing anything.

Since all three deployment share the same frontend codebase, they should provide a similar user experience and it should be relatively easy to port a web application into different platforms. 

## Accessing the Same Database Through Multiple Processes
As stated in [our documentation](https://kuzudb.com/docs/client-apis), Kùzu currently does not provide any safety guarantees if multiple processes access the same database:
>  Each database you create is identified by its directory. If you are going to concurrently interact with the same database through more than one Database instances, you should ensure that you only issue read queries to the system. Your writes from one Database instance will not be visible to your other program and you can easily corrupt your database. Kùzu currently does not ensure that you are connecting to the same database directory through a single Database instance. 

If the GUI application writes to the database while the user is running a script in Python or using the CLI writing to the same database, users might corrupt their databases. In fact it is not even safe for there to be 1 write process and one or more read-only processes. That's because we currently do not have a mechanisms for different processes to coordinate with each other. For example, currently if there are multiple threads in the same process that are using the same `Database` object, we have a way of coordinating them, e.g., if one of them is committing a write transaction, we can ensure that all read transactions first complete and leave the system and no new transaction starts. When multiple processes access the same database directory using different `Database` instances, the process that is writing could not block other processes starting transactions during checkpointing. Therefore if we will allow multiple processes to access the same database directory, we need a mechanism to ensure that either: (i) there is only one process accessing the database and it can read and write freely; or (ii) there are multiple read-only processes accessing the same database (so none can write to the database). To enforce these, we first need to introduce the notion of creating a read-only `Database` instance and then keeping track of the processes accessing a directory.

title: std::bad_alloc when returning maxNodeOffset as UINT64_MAX
body:
### Introduction

When running a match query on an empty node/rel tables, a `std::bad_alloc` is caused.
As pointed out by @andyfengHKU: 

```
> it's because the following line
static inline uint64_t getMaxNodeOffsetFromNumTuples(uint64_t numTuples) {
        return numTuples == 0 ? UINT64_MAX : numTuples - 1;
}
> when the table id empty
> we return maxNodeOffset as UINT64_MAX
> but our semi mask was interrept 64_MAX as a valid maxNodeOffset
> so it tries to generate a bitmask with size of 64_MAX which explore the memory
> that's why there is no error msg being throw out
```

### To reproduce:

Run the following in a new database:
```
create node table person (ID INT64, PRIMARY KEY (ID));
create rel table knows (FROM person TO person, int64Prop INT64, MANY_MANY);
match (p0:person)-[r:knows]->(p1:person) WHERE p0.ID = 0 return p1.ID;
```

title: Integrate NPY copy into the existing COPY pipeline
body:
We support npy as a file format to be copied into node tables, specifically into fixed size array columns.
Currently, npy copy goes through `NodeCopyExecutor`, which is separate from our query processor. While copying of csv and parquet files goes through the query processor (in the issue title, I call it "COPY pipeline").
For simplicity of code, we should move npy copy to go through the query processor too.
Specifically, we need to remove `NodeCopyExecutor`, and move the logic of copying npy files to `CopyNode` and `ReadFile` operators.

Two main issues need to be addressed for this change:
1. Change `NpyReader` to read a DataChunk at a time, so it can fit into `ReadFile` opeartor. The use of `mmap` can be removed since we read sequentially, which should be fine from the perspective of IO performance.
2. [NPY copy](https://kuzudb.com/docs/data-import/npy-import.html) follows the syntax of `COPY BY COLUMN`, thus one file corresponds to one column, which is quite different from CSV and Parquet files. CSV and Parquet files cover all columns in a single file. So `CopyNode` should be aware of that npy is copying a DataChunk into one column at a time, instead of all columns.

title: Broken LDBC SNB Interactive Complex Queries
body:
I'm adding some interactive complex queries to the testing files in PR #1664 . Reference implementations can be found in https://github.com/ldbc/ldbc_snb_interactive_impls/blob/main/cypher/queries/interactive-complex-10.cypher, although the individual queries need to be "translated" to Kuzu's Cypher. Here's a list of the queries that currently aren't working and what needs to be changed in order to make them work: 
- [ ]  IC1: This query has a bug with the CASE WHEN, see issue https://github.com/kuzudb/kuzu/issues/1710
- [ ] IC5: Requires correlated optional match.
- [x] IC7: Can't be implemented until issue #1665 is fixed for collect(), as well as issue #1666 
- [x] IC9: Can't be implemented until issue #1665 is fixed for unwind()
- [ ] IC10: The issue with this query is the `size([p IN posts WHERE ...])` line. This can be worked around easily if either (i) correlated optional match is implemented, or if (ii) issue #1665 is fixed for unwind(), or if (iii) `COUNT { subquery }` syntax is implemented. There might be another workaround, but I couldn't find it after working for an hour or so on it. 
- [ ] IC13(b). IC13 is implemented, but according to SNB v2.0, there should be 2 test cases - one where a path is guaranteed (IC13(a)) and one where one isn't (IC13(b)). Currently only IC13(a) is implemented, IC13(b) needs correlated optional match (or something else to return 0 when a shortest path isn't found)
- [ ] IC14: I don't know exactly what needs to be implemented for IC14 to work, but at the very least we need weighted shortest paths. 

All of these queries might have workarounds that don't involve the posted, please let me know if you find a different way of implementing any of these.

title: COLLECT() and UNWIND() return INTERNAL_ID type instead of Node
body:
Currently, running a query with Collect and Unwind return a list of types INTERNAL_ID instead of the node itself, leading to queries such as this one failing (on the ldbc-sf01 dataset): 
`MATCH (root:Person)-[]-(friend:Person) WITH collect(friend)[1] as first_friend RETURN first_friend.id;`
with error: 
`Error: Binder exception: LIST_EXTRACT(COLLECT(friend._id),1) has data type INTERNAL_ID. (NODE,REL,STRUCT) was expected.`

It seems that collect() returns a list of INTERNAL_ID's instead of a list of nodes, and the same sort of thing happens with UNWIND() as well.

Clearly this specific query has an easy workaround (I can post a better example later), but there are some queries (such as in the LDBC SNB interactive complex query set) that can't be implemented correctly with this issue.

title: Support for working with DataFrames in Polars
body:
[Polars](https://pola-rs.github.io/polars-book/user-guide/) is a great alternative to pandas to do data manipulation via DataFrames. It offers the following key benefits over pandas for users that may want it:

* Speed (there are numerous benchmarks online, but in general Polars seems way faster because of Rust)
* Has a lazy API for larger datasets
* Much cleaner and simpler API than pandas (more similar to Spark's DataFrame API)
* [No indexes](https://pola-rs.github.io/polars-book/user-guide/migration/pandas/#polars-does-not-have-a-multi-indexindex), reducing boilerplate and repetitive code like in pandas
* MUCH better support for `null` data type for missing values (pandas just defaults any missing value to `NaN`, leading to weird, inconsistent data types in certain columns)
* Concurrency and parallelism (column transforms are run concurrently, not sequentially like in Pandas)

## Use case

* For users that have a large CSV or parquet file, and need to perform some wrangling to get the data in the format they need, Polars can be massively faster and more performant
* For cases where there are `null` values in a column, Polars has a very good `null` data type that's different from the `NaN` that's assigned by default in pandas. Working with missing data is very common for a lot of users, so avoiding data type inconsistencies ( Even a single `NaN` automatically promotes an `int` column to a `float` in pandas, which is incredibly annoying)

Even though we may not transform data back and forth between the DataFrame and the table (as we may do in DuckDB) in Kùzu, allowing the user to convert the final query result to a Polars dataframe for any downstream use would align with any upstream data cleansing that may have happened, allowing users to choose their dependencies as they need  (either  pandas or Polars), and not forcing users to use pandas.

## How DuckDB does it

[DuckDB allows users the option](https://duckdb.org/docs/api/python/result_conversion.html) to convert its internal representations to either Pandas (`.df()`) or Polars (`.pl()`), depending on what they want to work with.

title: Feature Complete Towards openCypher
body:
This issue keeps track of features that are either missing or implemented with a different semantic compared to Neo4j Cypher. The general goal is to make Kùzu feature complete towards Cypher.

# Data Types
Kùzu takes Postgres data type system as a reference.

## `LIST` Data Type
Neo4j's `LIST` allows arbitrary elements type. Kùzu, on the other hand, requires `LIST` elements to have the same type.  Kùzu enforces these type constraints for compression and fast-processing purpose. To support arbitrary type, we can add `UNION` data type which can contain values of different data types. See DuckDB's [`UNION`](https://duckdb.org/docs/sql/data_types/union).

- [x] Support `UNION` data type.
- [x] Support `LIST` of `UNION`.

## `MAP` Data Type
Kùzu currently does not support `MAP`,  we should implement `MAP` as a `LIST` of `STRUCT` so that it can contain arbitrary number of key-value pairs where all keys must of the same type and all values must of the same type. To support key-value pairs with arbitrary types, we can again use `UNION`.

- [x] Support `MAP` data type.

## Spatial Data Types
Kùzu does not have native support for spatial data types.

# Data Definition
Although Neo4j is schema-less, it does support index and constraints.

**Constraints**
The following constraints are available in Neo4j but missing in Kùzu.

- [ ] Unique constraint
- [ ] Existence constraint

**Index**
Kùzu supports primary index but does not support indexing arbitrary property.

- [ ] Create Index
- [ ] Drop Index

# Query
Kùzu support `OPTIONAL MATCH`, `RETURN`, `WITH`, `UNWIND`, `WHERE`, `ORDER BY`, `SKIP`, `LIMIT`, `UNION` in the same way as Neo4j.

## Match

In graph theory, `trail` means an edge cannot be repeatedly visited and `walk` means any vertex or edge can be repeatedly visited. Both semantic could be useful depends on the use case. 

Neo4j's adopts `trail` semantic within a single `MATCH` clause. To achieve `walk` semantic Neo4j requires multiple `MATCH` clauses, e.g.
```
Trail
MATCH (a)-[e1]->(b)-[e2]->(c)
```
```
Walk
MATCH (a)-[e1]->(b)
MATCH (b)-[e2]->(c)
```
Kùzu on the other hand, use `walk` semantic by default and user can achieve `trail` semantic with predicates, e.g.
```
Walk
MATCH (a)-[e1]->(b)-[e2]->(c)
```
```
Trail
MATCH (a)-[e1]->(b)-[e2]->(c) WHERE id(e1) <> id(e2)
```
Kùzu has implemented the majority features in `MATCH` clause except

#### Return properties for recursive relationship
Kùzu currently only returns internal IDs for recursive relationship.
- [x] Return properties for recursive relationship

### Predicate on recursive relationship.
Kùzu currently does not support where predicate on recursive relationship
- [x] Support predicate on recursive relationship.

#### Bounded recursive relationship
Kùzu requires recursive relationship to be bounded, i.e. with a lower bound and a upper bound (capped at 30), to avoid long running queries.

#### Named path
Kùzu does not support named path because we think most of the functionality of named path can be substituted with named nodes and (recursive) relationships. So implementing named path is not a priority for us.

#### All shortest path
Kùzu hasn't implemented all shortest path
- [x] All shortest path

## LOAD CSV
Kùzu uses `COPY` for bulk loading. Direct scan from CSV is not yet implemented.
- [x] Support `LOAD CSV`

## Subquery
Kùzu supports non-correlated `EXISTS { subquery }` . 
- [x] Support `COUNT { subquery }`
- [ ] Support `CALL { subquery }`
- [x] Support correlated subquery with un-nesting, i.e. avoid executing subquery with index nested loop join.

## CALL procedure
Neo4j procedure seems to be a similar concept as SQLite `PRAGMA` statement which is used to modify / query non-table data.
- [x] Support `PRAGMA`

## Syntax sugar
The following syntax sugar does not affect functionality but could be good to have.

- [x] omit relationship pattern, e.g. `(a)->(b)`
- [ ] where predicate inside node/relationship pattern, e.g. `(a:Person WHERE a.age > 20)`
- [x] use `expression IN list` instead of `list_contains(list, expression)` 

The following syntax will not be implemented with priority
- `FOREACH` clause. User can always `UNWIND` clause as a substitution.

# Data Manipulation
Kùzu supports `CREATE`, `DELETE` and `SET` clause. However, our data manipulation works in s similar fashion as relational database like SQLite. So we don't support

**Create a node or relationship with multiple labels**
In our storage, each label is mapped to a physical table, so a node / relationship record must explicitly belongs to a single physical table. For creating with multiple labels, e.g. `CREATE (a:Person:Student)`, Kùzu doesn't have a way create to create a single record that exists in both `Person` and `Student` table.

**Reading after updating in a single statement**
Kùzu does not yet support reading after updating in a single statement , e.g. `MATCH (a) SET a.age = a.age + 1 RETURN a.age`. One solution is to issue multiple statements.
- [x] Support read after write in one statement

## MERGE
`MERGE` is similar to `UPSERT` on `INSERT .. ON CONFLICT` as in many relational database. We are currently missing this feature.

- [x] Support `MERGE`

## Syntax sugar
The following syntax sugar does not affect functionality but could be good to have.

- [x] Delete node / relationship with multiple labels. User can delete one label at a time.
- [x] Set node / relationship properties with multiple labels. User can set one label at a time.
- [x] `DETECH DELETE`. User can first delete all relationships then delete nodes.
- [ ] `REMOVE`. User can use `SET property = NULL`

# Functions
There is not a well-defined function set that a database should support. By default, Kùzu take Postgres and DuckDB's function set as a reference and will keep expanding on top of them. Let us know if any function is of interest to you but missing in Kùzu!
- [x] Support UDF

# Use Graph
We currently do not support multiple databases and query between different databases.

title: COPY Pipeline
body:
This issue is to document our designs to integrate `COPY` with our processor pipelines.
*This is a draft now to be further discussed and more details need to be added.*

## Overview
The pipeline should be flexible enough to cover both node/rel property graph tables, and rdf graphs.
Also, the new design should make COPY generally efficient and more robust on large-scale datasets. Here, by robustness, I mean the system doesn't crash due to limited memory resources, and the performance of copy doesn't degrade too much when memory is not enough (involving spill to disk during loading).
Changes to COPY need to be in tandem with our new storage design changes, as we're changing underlying storage layout a lot.
So this design will be broken into steps to be gradually done. Hopefully we can get most done when we've moved to the new storage layout.

## Pipeline
The source operator of the COPY pipeline is always `READER`.
The `READER` operator takes a morsel ( a chunk of a file) as input, and outputs a `DataChunk`. Internally, it parses a chunk from input files (e.g., some num of lines from a csv file, a row group from a parquet file, etc.) and converts the chunk into a `DataChunk`, which can be passed along operators.
The conversion handles the mismatch between arrow arrays and ValueVectors, and should be zero-copy when possible. For example, converting a INT64 arrow array to a ValueVector requires copying of null mask, but can redirect pointers in ValueVector to the arrow array data.
Note: we will start a project on the side to replace arrow with our own csv and parquet readers, which will be described in a separate issue.

Multiple `READER` objects (in different threads) in the same pipeline share a `ReaderSharedState`. Same as any other source operators, such as `ScanNodeID`, `ReaderSharedState` is used to coordinate tasks in the pipeline. 
The shared state should cover different file formats, such as CSV, Parquet, NPY, etc. and also different data sources, such as local fs, cloud fs, python objects, etc.
`READER` operates in two modes: *SERIAL*, and *NON-SERIAL*. Currently, only copying of node table with serial data type as the primary key requires serial mode, as it requires that node tuples are given offsets in the same order as they are stored in files. In the serial mode, the READER will guarantee that it reads sequentially, and also reads a whole node group at one time, so each `COPY_NODE` object will pull the whole node group and process it without coordinating with other threads.
While in the non-serial mode, `READER` outputs one data chunk (2048 tuples) at one time, and each `COPY_NODE` object will merge the data chunk into its own current node group without knowing tuples' positions in files.

### Node copy pipeline
Node copy will be in two pipelines:
```
     COPY_SINK
         |
    BUILD_INDEX ----
                   | sharedState: primary key column
      COPY_NODE ----
         |
       READER
```

The node copy pipeline should avoid reading the original csv files twice (thus, we can't rely on the first pass reading to figure out num of rows, which hash index requires for bulk reserving), and also separate index building, which can be reusable in the future for `CREATE INDEX ...`.
To avoid flushing the primary key column to disk and read again, we need to introduce a caching mechanism, that we always keep the primary key column in RAM before we start to construct the index (assuming the column won't be too large, if it's too large, we should still flush to disk, and scan from disk sequentially again, which should be fine, too).

### Rel copy
Rel copy process is also broken into two pipelines (suppose it's a `MANY_ONE` relationship, that's why it contains both `COPY_REL_COLUMNS` and `COPY_REL_LISTS`):
```
# pipeline 2 (parent)
      COPY_SINK
          |
    COPY_REL_LISTS
          |
    COPY_REL_COLUMNS
          |
    DATA_CHUNK_SCAN   --
                        | sharedState: shuffled data chunks and tuple pointers for each node group
# piepline 1 (child)    |
     REL_SHUFFLE      --
          |
     INDEX_LOOKUP
          |
        READER
```
Pipeline 1 reads input files in data chunks (same as node copy), and perform index lookups on both src and dst node keys to get their internal node offsets. Based on src and dst node offsets, `REL_SHUFFLE` partitions each tuple into corresponding partitions (i.e., node groups). Note that we duplicate rel data in both forward and backward directions.
`REL_SHUFFLE` is a sink operator, it accumulates all data chunks read from source in memory, and for each node group, it records logical pointers (might be something similar to tuple idxes) to tuples in accumulated data chunks. Accumulated data chunks and logical pointers will be stored inside the shared state between `REL_SHUFFLE` and `DATA_CHUNK_SCAN`.

Pipeline 2 scans tuples per node group from the shared state, and populate columns and rel lists accordingly.

### RDF copy
TODO(Guodong): For rdf graphs, we should combine node copy and rel copy pipelines to avoid reading original rdf files twice (one for node table and one for rel table). Need to discuss with @gaurav8297 .
```
# pipeline 2 (parent)
      COPY_SINK
          |
    COPY_REL_LISTS
          |
     COPY_COLUMNS
          |
    DATA_CHUNK_SCAN   --
                        | sharedState: shuffled data chunks and tuple pointers for each node group
# piepline 1 (child)    |
     REL_SHUFFLE      --
          |
    BUILD_INDEX
          |
    COPY_COLUMNS
          |
       READER
```

## TODOs
Just a list of stuff in my mind here. Not ordered here. Need to be improved later.
- [x] Move csv and parquet node copier to operators.
- [x] Move NPY copier to operators.
- [ ] Separate hash index build and column copy.
- [x] Move csv and parquet rel copier to COPY pipeline.
- [x] Node group based node copy pipeline.
- [x] Node group based rel copy pipeline.
- [x] RDF copy pipeline.

title: List function framework refactor
body:
Current list function reuses the binary operation executor which blindly sets the result to null if any of the parameter is null.

Consider this function: list_append([1,3], null). The binary operation executor will set the result to null because one of the parameters is null.
We should consider fixing this bug by creating a new function execution framework for lists.

title: Full support of SERIAL data type
body:
For now, `SERIAL` is added as an experimental feature.
Users can define the primary key property of node tables as `SERIAL` to avoid the creation of HashIndex in node tables, thus can speed up data ingestion a lot (no index construction and lookups).

Internally, `SERIAL` is interpreted as `INT64`, and its values are auto-incremented as new nodes are appended.
Essentially, `SERIAL` is an alias of a [SEQUENCE](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-createsequence.html) with data type as int64, start as 0, increment as 1.
For node tuples, we assume their `SERIAL` values are aligned with our internal node offsets.

Given a node table `person` with the schema `(ID SERIAL, age INT64, name STRING, PRIMARY KEY(ID))`.
To completely support `SERIAL`, we should consider following cases:
1. Support copy to specified table properties only. For example, users can specify `COPY person(name) FROM 'person_names.csv'` to copy from a csv file with only one column ("name") into `age` and `name` properties. This will let `ID` and `age` be their default values, `ID` will be set as SERIAL auto incremented starting from 0 (suppose the table is empty), and `age` will all be set to 0.
2. Copy to SERIAL property from csv files. We should also allow users to copy from csv files into a SERIAL property. This is to handle the case where a table only contains SERIAL properties. For example, `CREATE NODE TABLE n(ID SERIAL, PRIMARY KEY(ID))`. In this case, we have the constraint that values in the csv file must match the auto increment pattern.
3. We need to handle creations of node tuples following deletions, where we reuse deleted node offsets, thus we reuse deleted serial values too.
4. Consider add the support of `SEQUENCE` if necessary in the future.

This is still debatable. Let me know if there are any ideas around this.
