title: Error when a ReadOnly Transaction tries to run a CREATE/SET command
Disallowing multiple Database instances (e.g., from multiple processes) running on the same database directory

labels.name: type: feature
labels.description: New features or missing components of existing features

body:
Currently we do not have a mechanism to block multiple Database instances to be , i.e., multiple embedded Kuzu instances running on the same database directory. This should not be allowed as long as  we do not have a mechanism to make Database instances read-only. This is because this leads to the following problem if these processes are allowed to write.

Suppose there are 2 separate OS processes: P1 and P2 running Kuzu:
- P1 writes something to the database. For example adds a new User node. Suppose there was 5 User nodes before. Now there is 6.
- P2 will not be able to see this write because parts of the database data, e.g., catalog or node_statistics_and_deleted_ids, as always kept in memory and there is no mechanism for P2 to know that these parts have been modified, and refresh them. In this example, there is no way for P2 to know that node_statistics_and_deleted_ids have been modified. So it will think  that there are still 5 User nodes. 

Probably the most common case this would appear is if there are 2 separate OS processes running Kuzu but this is not really about number of processes. This is about number of `Database` instances. Database here refers to the object in program lines like this: `auto database = make_unique<Database>(*databaseConfig, *systemConfig);`.

We should add a note about this to the documentation's Client APIs and solve this immediately after phase 1 release.

The script for generating the CSV file `gen.py` :

```
import csv
import sys
import random
import os

sizes = [10 * 1024 ** 2, 1 * 1024 ** 3, 10 * 1024 ** 3, 50 * 1024 ** 3]
random.seed(10)

with open(sys.argv[1], 'w', newline='') as csvfile:

title: Committing largeList optimization
body:
Currently, when we want to commit elements from relUpdateStore to persistent storage, we copy the whole list from the persistent store and relUpdateStore to a struct called inMemList. For largetList, we don't need to copy the data from persistent store to inMemList. Instead, we can simply read the relUpdateStore data to list, and append the data to largeList.

Solution:
When the relPropertyListIterator wants to update a large list, there are two possibilities:
1. This large list is a small list before we insert rels to it. It becomes a largeList after we insert rels to it. The adjlistUpdateIterator has already updated the header for this list. In this case, inMemList contains data from relUpdateStore and persistentStore.
2. This large list is a large list before we insert rels to it. In this case, InMemList only contains data from relUpdateStore.
To differentiate these two cases, the relPropertyListIterator should use the read-only version of listHeader(the one before the adjListUpdateIterator updates) to figure out the two cases. 
The changes should happen in `ListsUpdateIterator::updateLargeList`
1. If the list is a small list before we insert rels, we should write to the large list from the beginning.
2. If the list is a large list before we insert rels, we should just do append.

title: Add identifier for f-table and keep track during planning.
body: For acc-based join (specifically correlated subquery), we need to first accumulate a table on left and scan it on right. This creates a problem that a f-table scan cannot access shared state at the time it is mapped. Currently we reply on post-mapping process to set shared state. This can be solved by keeping track of a unique identifier for f-table during mapping stage. See comment in PR #797 for details.

title: Change how we detect when a filter can be pushed down
body:
Filter push down is detected based on whether the dependent nodes and edges for an expression have been matched or not. This is creating problem for correlated subqueries. Consider the following query

`MATCH (a:person)-[:knows]->(b:person) OPTIONAL MATCH (b)-[:knows]->(c:person) WHERE c.age > a.age RETURN COUNT(*)`

when planning optional match part, `a` is not in scope so `c.age > a.age` is applied immediately after c is matched and leads to a bug.

title: Use reading clause in normalized query (part)
body: We used to only keep query graph in normalized query(part). As unwind clause comes in, we should keep reading clause instead of query graph (similar to bound query part).

title: Copy CSV and Storage TODOs for Phase 2
body:
### Functionality
- [x] Partition large relationship files into smaller files to be able to load them one partition at a time. We can have a threshold for this > 5GB files are broken down into k many pieces. This requires an additional step in the loader, where we inspect the file size and decide on a safe partition size (e.g., something that will split it into roughly 1GB each if the edges were distributed uniformly). This could be achieved as follows:
	- Suppose a relationship file, say knows.csv is 100GB and we know that its source node labels have 10K, 20K, and 15K many nodes. We pick the smallest one, e.g., 10K, and compute the "num-vertices-in-partition" that would lead to roughly 5GB partitions. In this case we would extrapolate that 500 vertices roughly correspond to 5GB. Then we scan through the file, and for each bucket of 500 src vertices, so vertices 0-499, 500-999, etc. we create a partition. That is every line of the knows.csv, where the source node's ID is between say 500-999, goes to the partition for 500-999. This is partitioning will help creating forward adjacency and property lists. We then repeat this process this time for destination vertices (this is for backward adjacency and edge property lists).
- [x] Ability to ingest multi-partition files vPerson0.csv, vPerson1.csv, ... We need a feature where the pattern for the file can be specified as a regex (or we treat the filename as regex.
- [x] Add header with version info into the metadata, also the logic to check storage version compatibility when we load the system up. (Phase 2)
- [x] Allow the user not to provide the columns of the table in the csv file in the order that the DBMS expects. (Phase 2)
### Usability
- [ ] Warning Error Reporting Mechanism That Doesn't Fail: Add a thread-safe warning and error reporting logic to not fail during loading if a particular line in a node or edge file had a problem. Instead, we should accumulate a list of warnings and errors and log them both when they are found and also as a report. Also save this report somewhere.
	- Example of a log error: "Skipping line 3 on eStudyAt.csv: "person,0,organisation,11344,2021", nodeID 11344 does not exist in the vOrganization.csv file.

title: Remove looping in allocateOverflowBlocks and optimize factorized table merge logic
body:
1. In `FactorizedTable::allocateOverflowBlocks`, there is a looping to find a block that has expected free size. However, when the num of overflow blocks is extremely large, this looping is a bottleneck. This is observed in our ASP join's result collector.
2. In `FactorizedTable::merge`, we allocate new blocks for flat tuples, loop over all of them, and copy them one by one. This is unnecessary for most blocks in each thread. We should be able to directly move all blocks, except for the last one, which might contain empty space. I didn't observe bottlenecks due to this yet, but it seems potentially it can cause problems.

title: Maintaining Free Pages in Lists and Possible General Solution to Maintaining Free Pages in Storage Structures
body:
Currently the page lists of chunks cannot shrink. That is suppose we have a non-empty UnstructuredPropertyLists and with some data and we remove all unstructured properties in it. Then although the headers are all 0 now, the pages that were in the page list of any non-empty chunk are not reclaimed. That is, if a chunk has used some number of list pages and then "shrinks", those pages remain "reserved" for the chunk and become useless. We need a mechanism to reclaim them and when we need more pages from .lists, when calling VersionedFileHandle::addNewPage(), we should reuse those empty pages. 

This may require some logic outside of VersionedFileHandle and directly in Lists or a new storage structure called FreePages, which can be put into other StorageStructures. Or this may even be a core piece of any StorageStructure, i.e., be implemented at the StorageStructure level. It's unclear what is more appropriate.

title: Optimize Updates to Lists
body:
Our update logic to lists is being done in an unoptimized manner at this stage. Our primary goal is not performance but correctness. There are many places where we can improve the performance of updates:

[ ] Implement updating lists in batches.
[ ] Make CSRs with 1.2x or some other ratio gaps. That will allow localizing updates. This requires changes to both the loader and the updates.
[ ] Support updating large lists without re-writing the entire list in Unstructured Properties (at the time of writing this issue updates to AdjLists and PropertyLists are not implemented, so whether this applies to them is not yet clear).
[ ] Parallelize prepareCommitOrRollbackIfNecessary where we implement the CSR-reconstruction algorithm. This could be implemented by creating a simple plan upon connection->commit() (which is what eventually calls prepareCommitOrRollbackIfNecessary) that puts each UnstructuredPropertyList that needs to be updated into the task scheduler, which grab morsels and performs the preparation of updates to the chunks in parallel.
[ ] We cannot make large lists small again. Any list that became large remains large.
[ ] Manage free pages in lists (https://github.com/graphflowdb/graphflowdb/issues/731).

title: Make Overflow Files manage its free space
body:
We currently have 3 problems with how we manage OverflowFiles that leak disk space.

- [ ] Serializing nextBytePosToWriteTo: OverflowFile keeps a nextBytePosToWriteTo to decide the free space to allocate for the next large strings and lists. We do not serialize this. Therefore each time the system starts up this is set to the beginning of the "next page" on the disk, so we leak whatever space that was available on the last overflow page.
- [x] Rolling back nextBytePosToWriteTo: Currently when a write transactions starts and starts updating or inserting strings or lists, we start allocating new positions on the OverflowFile pages and update the `nextBytePosToWriteTo` pointer in the OverflowFile. However, if the transaction rollsback, we do not rollback this change. So all of the tentative updates that were performed occupy space. This one should be easy to fix, if during rollback, the WALReplayer calls a rollbackInMemoryOverflowFile() function that rolls back the pointer. (solved in https://github.com/graphflowdb/graphflowdb/pull/729)
- [ ] When strings are updated or deleted, their space is never reclaimed. We need a mechanism to keep track of the empty spaces and reuse them. We can do this by changing how we implement OverflowFiles as follows: We keep track of multiple DiskArrays that are responsible for keeping strings/lists of exponentially increasing sizes. That is we have a DiskArray that stores strings of size up to 16. Another one upto 32, another one upto 64, etc. up to some maximum limit. For each of these DiskArray we also have a separate DiskArray that keeps track of the free locations on these lists. Hopefully free lists should be very small. Then we allocate free spaces from the DiskArray. Doing this change would also reuse DiskArray update features, which should simplify atomically updating overflow files.

There is also a very minor bug reported here about a possible leak of page 0 of the overflow files: https://github.com/graphflowdb/graphflowdb/issues/725.

title: Implement popBack in DiskArray
body:
Currently DiskArrays can only grow in size through pushBack. Implementing popBack is tricky because it requires thinking hard about how to avoid dangling pages if we support pushing_back and popping back within the same transaction. Consider the following case: 
1) We push back enough to create ArrayPage with apIdx 2 and say with arrayPageIdx 5. Suppose this creates a WAL version for page 5 of the fileHandle at WAL page 22.
2) Then within the same transaction we truncate one page. At this point, fileHandle's numPages need to be updated to 4. However, we have already logged a WAL record saying that page 5 of the file has been inserted with WAL version of the page at WAL Page 22. This may be OK, if we insert a new log record saying that page 5 is now deleted.
3) Now suppose we push back again to create a new array page. That will have page 5. Now should we re-use its previous WAL version? Probably not and we should generate a new WAL version and group but what to do is not obvious.  In general we need to guarantee/prove that replaying the WAL record many times will lead to the same database, i.e., that replaying the wal leads to idempotent operations.

title: Make InMemDiskArray use BufferManager for in-memory Array Pages
body:
Currently InMemDiskArray manages the ArrayPages directly through the OS memory. This allows faster access to these pages, but we can achieve something similar by using BM but always pinning in-memory pages. This has the following benefit: During updates, we currently create 3 versions of pages for any storage structure that uses InMemDiskArray: 1 in the InMemDiskArray, 2 in the BufferManager when calling StorageStructureUtils::createWALVersionOfPageIfNecessary(). This is so, because we have utility functions like createWALVersionOfPageIfNecessary, which were developed
for updating Columns transactionally and we wanted to reuse them. iIf we make InMemDiskArray use BufferManager, we would solve this redundancy.

InMemDiskArray also contains some logic to either read values directly from in-memory array page or BM, which might simplify if all pages were BM-backed.

In general, we should consider having a BufferPool for in-memory always pinned pages, which in-memory implementations of storage structures can use to avoid any pins.

title: DiskArray Multi Element Updates
body:
Currently DiskArray supports update and pushBack elements that take in single elements. This can be quite slow when updating many elements (e.g., when inserting a batch of updates). We need faster support for updating and inserting a batch of elements in DiskArray level.

Once this feature is implemented to DiskArray, we should change our update functions (e.g., CSR reconstruction algorithms) to use it when possible.

title: DELETE NODE BUG
Store primaryKeyIdx in createNodeTable logical/physical operators, boundCreateNodeClause
body: We currently store the primary key name in  createNodeTable logical/physical operators, boundCreateNodeClause. However, it is better to use primaryKeyIdx rather than the actual primary key string.

title: Enhance InMemDiskArrayBuilder with a to simplify population of lists in_mem_node_builder/in_mem_rel_builder

labels.name: type: feature
labels.description: New features or missing components of existing features

body:
Currently InMemNodeBuilder uses InMemUnstructuredLists unstrPropertyLists, which uses its own structures to populate the actual lists of lists, such as InMemFile. This is not true for ListMetadata and Lists, which uses InMemDiskArray. If we switch to using DiskArray and InMemDiskArrrayBuilder for the actual lists too some of the loading code can simplify. In particular, parts of code that are populating InMemFile work at a low-level abstraction, where they figure out where the actual page locations they need to update. Instead, if we worked at the abstraction of an array or vector, which can be supported by DiskArray, and had utility functions, such as copy(uint64_t beginOffset, uint8_t* from, uint64 numBytes) or push_back<T>(element), where T is the type of DiskArray etc, and the DiskArrayBuilder figured out exactly which pages to update could be much simpler.

As a concrete example, at a high level, the InMemNodeBuilder::putUnstrPropsOfALineToLists code, reads a line of csv, parses each unstructured property and copies to a particular offset in an array. But the code looks lower level and the following function calls happen
```
1. InMemNodeBuilder::putUnstrPropsOfALineToLists: unstrPropertyLists->setUnstructuredElement(...)
2. InMemUnstructuredLists::setUnstructuredElement:  InMemUnstructuredLists::setComponentOfUnstrProperty(...)
3. Inside InMemUnstructuredLists::setComponentOfUnstrProperty, we find the in-mem page or pages that need to be updated etc.
``` 
All this complexity can be hidden if we make lists to use DiskArrays enhance InMemDiskArrayBuilder to have several utility functions that automatically writes the given data to the correct in-memory locations and are saved to disk correctly as well.

title: HashJoinSharedState::nonKeyDataPosesDataTypes should be constructed inside mapper instead of init
body:
`HashJoinSharedState::nonKeyDataPosesDataTypes` is appended inside `init()`, which is incorrect, as `init()` is called concurrently in each thread, and each thread will try to append some information into `HashJoinSharedState::nonKeyDataPosesDataTypes`, leading to the incorrect result.

title: Optimization for aggregation/order by/union scan
body:
For example:
`MATCH (a:Person) return a.fName order by a.fName`
The plan for this query is: `SCAN() -> ORDER BY() -> ORDER BY MERGE() ->  ORDER BY SCAN -> PROJECTION -> RESULT COLLECTOR`
The orderByScan scans the factorizedTable to a vector of valueVectors, and passes the valueVectors to resultCollector. Then, the resultCollector saves the vectors in its local factorizedTable.
The conversion of  factorizedTable -> valueVector -> factorizedTable is unnecessary and should be optimized.

title: Aggregation compute hash optimization
body:
Currently, we are storing the combineHash result in a temporary result vector and move the temporary result vector to hashVector:
`VectorHashOperations::combineHash(hashVector.get(), tmpHashResultVector.get(), tmpHashCombineResultVector.get());`

The reason why we can't do inplace update is that the binary operation executor changes the state of the result valueVector. If we do inplace update like this: `VectorHashOperations::combineHash(hashVector.get(), tmpHashResultVector.get(), hashVector.get());`, the binary operation executor will set the hashVector state = tmpHashResultVector state, and then read the curIdx of hashVector.

title: Add end-to-end tests for hash index with mixed reads/writes
body:
After we add IndexScan and finish the transaction support of the hash index,  we are able to test the index with end-to-end queries.
To do this, we need to issue both some read and write queries, that read queries trigger hash index lookups (both read and write transactions), and write (insert/delete) queries on nodes trigger the insert/delete of hash index.
Meanwhile, a read and a write transaction are started to separately check if they read the correct content.

title: Simplifying NodeIDCompressionScheme as a Constraint

labels.name: type: feature
labels.description: New features or missing components of existing features

body:
Currently nodeID compression scheme is computed based on the maxNodeOffsetPerLabel when we construct a RelTable. This needs to change for 2 reason: 
     -(1) The compression scheme should not be computed during loading but be stored in catalog or nodesmetadata. One possibility is that we implement this as a max value constraint on the nodeOffsets and ensure in nodesmetadata. That is nodesMetadata errors if the maxNodeOffset > maxPossibleNodeOffset and does not allow that node insertion. Then we can have a separate DDL statements to change these nodeIDCompression's. As a usability feature, we can use 4 bytes or 8 bytes (and forget about 1 and 2 bytes), and use 4 bytes only if the # nodes < 2 billion (so we have a possibility to grow by 2x) and 8 bytes otherwise.
    - (2) We need a mechanism to change the nodeID compression scheme if needed. This looks very hard and potentially rewriting every single adjacency list and adjacent column that stores these node offsets. This can be a manual task done by a DDL command.

title: Add vector hash operations
body:
Currently, we don't use UnaryOperationExecutor when calculating the hashes of a valueVector. 
For maintainability, we should refactor the hash operations to use UnaryOperationExecutor.
The difficulty is that:
Suppose we want to compute the hashValues of two flatVectors: A, B (A, B are on different dataChunks with different curIdx).
We first use unaryOperationExecutor to calculate the hashValues of A and store the result in a resultValueVector(which should share the same datachunk as A).
Then we need to combine the resultValueVector with B, however the unaryOperation executor assumes that the input and result valueVector share the same datachunk. So we may get incorrect results.

title: Inconsistent flat information when scanning from factorized table

In the planner, when scanning from a table, an output vector could either flat or unflat. title: Inconsistent flat data chunk information between planner and mapper for optional match.
body:
Both planner and mapper maintains flat information by themselves. This is needed because flat information is changing as new operators being appended. So we can not maintain a global shared flat information. 

Ideally only flatten operator is allowed to change flat information. However, for optional match, because we are referencing data chunks (see comment in planOptionalMatch() in enumerator.cpp), a referenced data chunk could directly be flat without a previous flatten operator. This is a quite annoying bug, two possible solutions are

- Avoid referencing and deep copy from one data Chunk to another. Flat data chunk can be copies into unFlat ones whose size always equals to 1.
- Switch to HashJoin type of optional match. Personally I prefer this one which should be a more principled design and will also fix issue #438

body:
I see many users of GDBMSs and in particular Cypher want to do query processing ignoring nodes with high degrees. We need a way for users to specify this. Queries can look like:
MATCH (a)-[:friend]->(b)
WHERE a.degree (or degree(a)) < 10

I'm also open to moving to phase 1. My guess is that it is actually a very useful feature.

title: Make variable-length joins non-pipelining only for long path queries

labels.name: type: feature
labels.description: New features or missing components of existing features

body:
In our current design of variable-length joins that @acquamarin is implementing now, during query plan generation we blindly put in a variable-length join sink + variable-length join operators. This allows us to parallelize the frontier extensions that start from a single node. However, we should only execute this way: (1) if the variable-extend is guaranteed to start from a single prefix; and (2) the maxLen of the path is very long (e.g., contains > 4 edges and each edge is over one/many-to-many). Another smarter way could be to use the average degree of an edge label and make this decision based on that (e.g., if avg-deg^{maxLen} > 1M).

We should have a more standard completely pipelining variable-length join operator that we use if at least the 2nd condition fails. That is if the max-length of these conditions do not hold. For example one approach could be the following: 
Consider this example: MATCH (a:Person)-[:Knows..2...4]->(b:Person). So minLen = 2 and maxLen=4. Suppose we scanned (a) variable. We could add 1 regular Extend operator and then add 3 StandardVariableExtend operators. A high-level description of StandardVariableExtend is:

StandardVariableExtend (SVE): Contains 2 valueVectors: (i) to store the (b) values; and (ii) to store a temporary valuvector, which can be extended to (b). Let's call this temporary vector's variable _tmp. SVE first checks if the (b) vector has data in it. If so, it just passes it to the next operator. If not, it checks if _tmp has data in it. If so, it flattens the values in _tmp and extends it to (b) and calls the next operator. If both (b) and _tmp are empty then that means there are no more extensions to do. 

The pipelining version of varLenExtend is implemented in these two PRs:
1. VarLenAdjListExtend: #527 
2. VarLenColExtend: #537

body:
In RelsLoader, there is an optimization where we need to sort overflow pages of columns/lists, currently, a bug introduced by this pr (https://github.com/graphflowdb/graphflowdb/pull/223) changes the behaviour of sorting over adj prop columns.
To fix this, we have two options:
- Like previously done, we separate sorted and unsorted into two set of overflow pages, and release the unsorted one after sorting.
- We change the behaviour of loading to that each rel loading task will grab 512 nodes, and manage its own overflow pages, so it's guaranteed that within a task, overflows are already sequentially stored.

Also, LIST should follow STRING to have the same sorting behaviour.

**UPDATE**:
The sorting of LIST overflow pages is added in #549. And the bug introduced by #223 is also fixed.

title: Smart group by keys selection for aggregation
body:
Consider the following query pattern `... GROUP BY a.primary_key, a.prop, b.primary_key, b.prop, COUNT(*)`. Although explicitly we have 4 group by keys, `(a.primary_key, b.primary_key)` dictates `(a.prop, b.prop)` so it's sufficient to only hash on  `(a.primary_key, b.primary_key)`. In order to do this optimization, we need the following changes

- Front-end should detect dependencies between these keys
- Aggregate hash table should additionally take payloads `(a.prop, b.prop)` that are not aggregate states. These payloads will not be updated during processing.

title: Parallel distinct aggregate
body:
Currently, distinct aggregate is only executed with single thread because it's unsafe to perform thread-local aggregation without first taking distinct values. Imagine the following example of calculating COUNT(DISTINCT a.age) with 2 threads. Both threads t1 and t2 get input 20. 20 is a distinct value in their own thread so both threads have COUNT = 1. However, when we combine the state between t1 and t2, we lose track of input vectors and thus lead to the wrong aggregate value.

## Solution
A possible solution is to first calculate thread-local distinct values in parallel which is the same as the current implementation of DISTINCT. Then during task finalize, we first obtain global distinct values by merging all thread-local distinct hash tables. Then we loop through the global distinct hash table and update aggregate states for each row.

title: Use an efficient way to solve orderBy multiplicity problem
body:
Currently, we encode a tuple multiple times if it's multiplicity is not 1. This is not an efficient way to encode tuples.
We should have a flag about whether multiplicity is guaranteed to be 1 or it could change. Maybe we can always encode the multiplicity with the keys. But the frontend should check if multiplicity is guaranteed to be 1 or not and: 
1) use this information to set whether the output of order_by_scan should be unflat or flat (if multiplicities of output tuples is not guaranteed to be 1, we cannot output unflat vectors)
2) give this information to order_by_scan, so that order_by_scan knows whether or not it's scanning to flat or unflat datachunk/resultset and if it's scanning into flat datachunk/result set, it should also put the multiplicity back into the datachunk. But regardless of what we end up doing, in in order_by, each row r should get stored in localRowCollection once and the key columns of r should get encoded once.

The current solution is enough to solve this problem, so I close this issue.

title: Order by rules from user's perspective
body:
ORDER BY IN RETURN: Always works.

ORDER BY IN WITH. Only allow "Top k" type queries with LIMIT and/or SKIP. That is an ORDER BY clause can follow a WITH if and only if there is a LIMIT and/or SKIP following ORDER BY. And if there is a LIMIT and/or SKIP, the LIMIT and SKIP will consume its input/result set according to the given order. But any operator after that ignores the order. 

If a query uses ORDER BY IN WITH and is not followed with a LIMIT or SKIP, we error.

title: ordering of tuples after orderBy operator
body:
The ordering of tuples can't be guaranteed after the orderBy operator if we multi-threaded the execution of following opeators.

We defined some rules of the behaviour of operators after orderBy:
1. ORDER BY IN RETURN： the ordering of result tuples is preserved.
2. ORDER BY IN WITH:  Only allow "Top k" type queries with LIMIT and/or SKIP. That is an ORDER BY clause can follow a WITH if and only if there is a LIMIT and/or SKIP following ORDER BY. And if there is a LIMIT and/or SKIP, the LIMIT and SKIP will consume its input/result set according to the given order. But any operator after that ignores the order. 
If a query uses ORDER BY IN WITH and is not followed with a LIMIT or SKIP, we error (or we should ignore the ORDER BY clause but ignoring could be harder to do. Erroring is more explicit. 

Currently, we just make the opeartors after orderby single-threaded.

title: Add support for unflat columns in orderBy operator
body:
Currently, the orderBy front end just flats all key columns for orderBy. 

Problem:
If there is an unlfat key column in orderBy, the orderBy will flat the column and store it in rowCollection.  If we want to read a key column to an unflat valueVector, we have no idea about the number of row to put in that valueVector.

title: problem with stringBuffer life cycle in pipelines
body:
Currently, the valueVector owns the string buffer. If the valueVector goes out of scope, the stringBuffer will be destroyed. 

As a result, there is a problem for the string overflow buffer lifecycle between two pipelines.

For example:
Pipeline 1 : Scan(a.ID)->ORDER BY(a.name)   (valueVector1)
Pipeline 2: ORDER BY SCAN(a.name)  -> ResultCollector (valueVector2)

The valueVector1 stores the overflow buffer for a.name. When pipeline1 goes out of scope, the overflow buffer will be destroyed. Thus the orderByScan operator in pipeline2 will read invalid strings from the overflow buffer.

We should reconsider the lifecycle of string overflows.

title: Subquery plans with multiple pipelines

labels.name: type: feature
labels.description: New features or missing components of existing features

body:
Exists and LeftNestedLoopJoin operators contain an outer-plan and a subquery plan. Currently, subplans can only be executed entirely as part of another pipeline that has been wrapped around in a ProcessorTask. This is because the pipeline that contains Exists of LeftNestedLoopJoin needs to call sub-plan in the middle of a pipeline, and the TaskScheduler currently cannot start a new task/pipeline without finishing an existing task/pipeline. It is also not clear if we ever want to decompose sub-plans into tasks and have worker threads execute them separately. This does not like a good design. 

The practical implication for us right now is this: we cannot have a sub-query plan (SQP) that consist of more than 1 pipeline, where one of the pipelines of SQP requires the call on finalize. This is because, since SQP is are part of an outer plan OP, worker threads will call finalize on OP and not SQP. So the pipeline of SQP that requires finalize will never be called. So SQP needs to be a single pipeline that does not require finalize to be called.

One general idea to fix this, which is probably the right way is that we never parallelize sub-plans as we do (which I think is the right thing for the foreseeable future), but we add a flag to operators to indicate whether they are part of a subquery, which means they are guaranteed to be executed with only one thread. And then at the end of execute() calls or maybe some other operator function, we can check whether this is an operator that is guaranteed to be executed by a single thread, in which case we can make any necessary finalize calls. 

The other fix we need is that if SQP consists of multiple pipelines SQP1 and SQP2, say SQP1 ends with a HashJoinBuild, and SQP2 is the HashJoinProbe pipeline. Now currently we will decompose SQP into SQP1 and SQP2 and we will execute SQP1 first by calling HashJoinBuild::execute(), which completes and constructs its hash table and then we will execute SQP2 by calling ResultCollector::execute(). Now because SQP's root operator is ResultCollector, we somehow need to be able to call HashJoinBuild::execute() first. It is not clear how to do this without a significant change to our current query plan execution architecture.

For now, we need to ensure that the enumerator never uses a HashJoin or an aggregation or anything else that is not a single pipeline. So we should focus on scans, extends and filters.

body:

This design is no longer true for LeftNestedLoopJoinOperator where the subPlan does not have a sink operator but still requires a different resultSet.

```
resultSet = prev.initResultSet()
insert vectors into resultSet as necessary 
```

For binary operators, the logic would be
```
leftResultSet = left.initResultSet()
rightResultSet = right.initResultSet()

title: Scalable RETURN all unstructured properties of node
body:
Currently, when a user asks the query:
```
MATCH (a:Person)
WHERE a.firstName = "Ramon"
RETURN a
```
And we are given a graph that has 1000 different possible unstructured properties across Person nodes (which is an information kept in the catalog), we will try to construct a plan with 1000 property readers, what will try to read each possible property one after another, and put a null or a value in one ValueVector. So for a node that has only 1 unstructured property, we will try to read 1000 possible properties. In addition, we will output 999 nulls.

Instead, we should have a special ValueVector (possibly of dataType Map or currently we can call it UnstructuredPropertyMap) that and a special AlllUnstructuredPropertiesReader that reads all unstructured properties of a node and puts it into a single ValueVector.

title: Remove the ValueVector sequence

labels.name: type: feature
labels.description: New features or missing components of existing features

body:
Currently, a `ValueVector` can be a sequence so that we only store the first value and its size. We used this for `Node` type as an optimization in `ScanNodeID`.
However, this optimization is complicating code logic in the processor to loop through a ValueVector because we need to specialize code path for node sequence.
A cleaner way is to remove this optimization for now (and maybe revisit it later in the optimization phase, another way might be that we can add a special `normalize` function that populates all values in the sequence when necessary so then it can be processed without any specialization) and simplify our code in the processor.

However, this complicates the logic in RowCollection. We should de-couple ValueVector (factorization) related logic from the fixed-sized row reads/writes, so that there will be one/two extra classes to handle the transformation between rows and ValueVectors.

labels.name: type: feature
labels.description: New features or missing components of existing features

body:
Currently, the orderBy operator has a null flag which indicates whether this value is a null or not. 
If the column doesn't have null values, it is unnecessary for us to use an additional byte for the null flag. We can optimize the radix sort by having a shorter binary string encoding.
We can add a field to the catalog to record whether the current column has null or not.

labels.description: New features or missing components of existing features

Currently binder has two casting functions

- non-string -> string

Mapper has one casting functions

title: Incorrect nullmask setting for the evaluation result of IS NULL and IS NOT NULL
body:
`IS NULL` and `IS NOT NULL` check if a value is `NULL` or not, and return `TRUE`/`FALSE` for each value.
Currently, we set the unary expression result to share the same nullmask with its child one, which causes incorrect output for `IS NULL` and `IS NOT NULL`.
For example, given an input vector `[NULL, 10, 20]`, whose nullmask is `[True, False, False]`. When we apply `IS NULL`, the expected output is `TRUE, FALSE, FALSE`, while currently, due to the sharing of nullmask with the input, the actual output is `NULL,FALSE,FALSE`.

title: Add projection map to physical operators
body:
The projection map should be passed to each physical operator, and some operators which need to scan on multiple dataChunks / valueVectors might need the projection map to figure out which dataChunks/valueVectors are already discarded in the resultSet. Currently, hash join build, projection, and order by should take in such information.
This issue is related to the pr #353 .

Also, we should remove `dataChunksMask` in `ResultSet`, instead pass the projection map to ResultCollector.

title: Copy and reset string buffer
body:
Currently, the string buffer is continuously allocated during query runtime, but its memory buffer is never reclaimed before the query ended because we want to avoid copying in pipeline sinks.
This is a non-robust way to handle string buffers. Instead, we should copy and reset the string buffer during the sink. So in each getNextTuples call, the source operator will start from a fresh new string buffer.

`>> Executing time: 1.42ms`
`----------------`

`----------------`

We get incorrect result when doing a query on a string column in a relation

- Currently, CAST operations are in a different code path from other operations (arithmetic, comparison, boolean, hash). In the end, we want to unify all operations to be executed through the operation executor combined with value-level operations.
- Our cast rules should be re-designed that we have a more clear guideline on what implicit castings are allowed, and when explicit castings are required.
- `CAST_UNSTRUCTURED_TO_BOOL_VALUE` doesn't follow our principle that when an operation consists of both structured and unstructured values, structured values should be cast to unstructured ones.

labels.name: type: feature

The current binder only supports timestamp/date appearing on the left-hand side of a binary expression(+).
For example:
We currently support: DATE + INT = DATE.
However, we don't support INT + DATE = DATE (binder error) yet.

To support this, we can swap the left-hand side expression(INT) and right-hand side expression(DATE) during the normalization step(not implemented yet).

title: Using unique_ptr of logical operator in logical plan

labels.name: type: feature
labels.description: New features or missing components of existing features

body:
Currently our logical plan uses shared_ptr for logical operator because the previous level of DP table is shared across the next level.

```
E.g. Match (a)->(b)->(c) 
Scan(b) -> Extend(a)
Scan(b) -> Extend(c)
Two plans above shares the same Scan(b)
```

However, our optimizer outputs a single plan (or in the testing case, we output all plans by copying each of them and apply further optimization), we should consider using unique_ptr which has a more clear ownership info

title: Add a system-level mechanism (possibly lock) to coordinate changes that might affect multiple components
body:
We are implementing several functionalities that change some components of the system, e.g., the buffer manager's buffer pool size, or updates, which affect the storage files. These need to be: (1) coordinated and; (2) happen when the system is idle, i.e., no queries, updates, or some system configuration changes are happening. We need a mechanism to coordinate these.

One idea is to have functions waitUntilSystemIsIdleAndAcquireSystemLock() and releaseSystemLock() somewhere, possibly in System. The first function could do two things: (i) acquire a system-level lock that the query compiler, BufferManager::resize(), and future components related to updates (e.g., transaction manager) can acquire before doing such changes; and (ii) monitor the query processor to ensure all query processing tasks have been completed.

labels.name: type: feature
labels.description: New features or missing components of existing features

body:
Currently, the optimizer takes a heuristic value for PREDICATE_SELECTIVITY, based on which the optimizer is not able to figure out the best join order for some simple cases involving filtering on primary key, e.g., `match (a:Person)-[e1:knows]->(b:Person)-[e2:knows]->(c:Person)-[e3:knows]->(d:Person) where a.id=933 return count(*)`.
The optimizer rules out the plan that starts from scan of `a` on LDBC10 dataset.
One thing we can add is to calculate the cardinality information based on what we have in graph and catalog, since values of the primary key is distinct, e.g.,`a.id=933` gives us one node out of `N` nodes.

title: Project Literal Expression
body:
Currently we don't support `RETURN 1` or `WITH 1 AS one ...` because literal expression is never explicitly written into datachunks.

We should support such case by writing literal expression as a valuevector. There are 2 possible solutions when it comes to multiple literals

- Each literal gets its own datachunk which has a flat single state
- All literals exists in the same dataChunk (also flat single state) but append as different valuevector

title: Avoid quadratic behavior in join order enumeration

labels.name: type: feature
labels.description: New features or missing components of existing features

body:
Consider the following query
`MATCH (d)<-(a)->(b)->(c) WHERE d.age = c.age`
We might enumerate join order abcd which leads to the following plan
`Scan(a)->Extend(b)->Extend(c)->Scan(c.age)->Extend(d)->Scan(d.age)->Filter`
Although Extend(d) and Scan(d.age) only depends Scan(a), this plan has to repeat the work for every flat (a,b) tuple which might be even worse for longer join path.

A possible solution is to embed the following optimization in join order enumeration.
When we match "a", we extend variables that depends on "a" at the same time. So Extend(b) and Extend(d) will happens together.

title: Uncessary Flatten Append
body:
Consider query ` MATCH (a:person) WHERE a.unstrNumericProp - 10 > a.unstrNumericProp2 RETURN COUNT(*)`
We will enumerate the following plan
```
LOGICAL_FILTER[a.unstrNumericProp - 10 > a.unstrNumericProp2]
LOGICAL_FLATTEN[_0_a.unstrNumericProp]
LOGICAL_SCAN_NODE_PROPERTY[_0_a.unstrNumericProp2]
LOGICAL_SCAN_NODE_PROPERTY[_0_a.unstrNumericProp]
LOGICAL_SCAN_NODE_ID[_0_a._id]
```

title: Push Scans of Properties down
body:
We have potentially a very bad performance scenario by not pushing down scans. 
Consider the following query: 
```MATCH (a)-[:e1]->(b)-[:e2]->(c) WHERE e1.date = e2.date RETURN *``` 
and the following plan: 

```Scan(a)->Flat1(a)->Ext1(b)->Flat2(b)->Ext2(c)->PR1(e1)->PR2(e2)->Filter.```
Let there be 3 datachunks: DC1(a), DC2(b, e1, e1.date), DC3(c, e2, e2.date). Suppose DC1
is flattened at currIdx=0, so a is fixed to say a0. Now suppose DC2 has 3 values (so a0 has 3
edges.) DC2 will be flattened iteratively to currIdx=0, 1, 2 and for each i, we will
read a0's forward (and possibly large) date property list over and over again.

To avoid this, we should either have a caching logic, possibly a boolean in adj_list_extend or read_rel_property_list to
ensure that the same list is not read over and over again. Or we should make sure scans are pushed down and happen immediately after joins or nodeIDSequence scans. For now I suggest simply pushing down scans.

title: Supporting extending to multiple destination node labels (related to queries with unlabeled node/rels)
body:
This feature is related to "Unlabeled Node and Rel Queries". We do not currently support extending through single relation label to nodes with possibly multiple labels. Our storage supports such lists and even our lists.cpp can read such adjacency lists into ValueVectors. But we don't seem to have the correct logic in the query plan and extend operators to handle this case. Specifically here is a test that should pass and currently fails.
The dataset under `dataset/read-list-tests/3-bytes-per-edge' is a dataset where there are both `animal` and `person` nodes and a `knows` relation over {animal,person} x {animal, person}. In this particular dataset there are 6000 person nodes and 1 animal node. person0 connectes to person0 to person5000 (so 5001 edges). animal0 connects to person6000 (all through `knows` edges). 

When I issue the following query: `MATCH (a:person)-[:knows]->(b:person) WHERE a.id = 0 RETURN COUNT(*)`,  the plan that stats scanning from b returns 5002 instead of 5001. Note that id here is an INT64 column (that also happens to be the primary key) and  exists for both animals and person. I did not look very closely but I am guessing that the filter that a should be a person does not seem to be passed along to the filter or extend to filter out the a:0 when the scan b scans p6000.

This is the plan that's failing:
```
LOGICAL_FILTER[a.id = 0]
LOGICAL_SCAN_NODE_PROPERTY[_0_a.id]
LOGICAL_EXTEND[_1_b._id<-_0_a._id]
LOGICAL_FLATTEN[_1_b._id]
LOGICAL_SCAN_NODE_ID[_1_b._id]
```
I believe LOGICAL_SCAN_NODE_PROPERTY scans a0's id column (this is not important but incidentally, I believe this operators is configured with the ID column of p, so in fact it's reading p0's id column, but regardless reads a 0) which passes the filter.

The following end to end test can be written for the 3-bytes-per-edge test. All of these should pass but the first one was failing, which is what triggered this issue.
```
-NAME NodeP0ExtendToPerson
-QUERY MATCH (a:person)-[:knows]->(b:person) WHERE a.id = 0 RETURN COUNT(*)
---- 5001

-NAME NodeP0ExtendToAnimal
-QUERY MATCH (a:person)-[:knows]->(b:animal) WHERE a.id = 0 RETURN COUNT(*)
---- 0

-NAME NodeP1ExtendToPerson
-COMPARE_RESULT 1
-QUERY MATCH (a:person)-[:knows]->(b:person) WHERE a.id = 1 RETURN b.id
---- 1
5000

-NAME NodeP1ExtendToAnimal
-QUERY MATCH (a:person)-[:knows]->(b:person) WHERE a.id = 1 RETURN COUNT(*)
---- 1
0

-NAME NodeP5500ExtendToPerson
-COMPARE_RESULT 1
-QUERY MATCH (a:person)-[:knows]->(b:person) WHERE a.id = 5500 RETURN b.id
---- 0

-NAME NodeP5500ExtendToAnimal
-QUERY MATCH (a:person)-[:knows]->(b:person) WHERE a.id = 5500 RETURN COUNT(*)
---- 0

-NAME NodeA0ExtendToPerson
-QUERY MATCH (a:animal)-[:knows]->(b:personerson) WHERE a.id = 0 RETURN b.id
---- 6000

-NAME NodeA0ExtendToAnimal
-QUERY MATCH (a:animal)-[:knows]->(b:animal) WHERE a.id = 0 RETURN COUNT(*)
---- 0
```

This test can go under read_list_end_to_end_test.cpp.
```
class EndToEndReadLists3BytesPerEdgeTest : public DBLoadedTest {
public:
    string getInputCSVDir() override { return "dataset/read-list-tests/3-bytes-per-edge/"; }
};

TEST_F(EndToEndReadLists3BytesPerEdgeTest, 3BytesPerEdgeTest) {
    vector<TestQueryConfig> queryConfigs;
    queryConfigs =
        TestHelper::parseTestFile("test/runner/queries/adj-list-reading/3-bytes-per-edge.test");
    ASSERT_TRUE(TestHelper::runTest(queryConfigs, *defaultSystem));
}
```

title: Incorrect result flat/unflat information for leaf expressions in the ExpressioEvaluator
body:
Currently, each ExpressionEvaluator depends on its children to figure out the state of its intermediate resultVector in the `isResultFlat` function, however, the leaf property expression's state is not correctly set by accessing the result vector, due to that that this function is called during construction, while the result vector's state will only change during runtime (e.g., after the flatten operator).
The leaf expression's result vector state should be set in the ExpressionMapper, and the info can be passed from the logical expression.

A case query is ```MATCH (a:person)-[:knows]->(b:person) RETURN a.age+b.age```.
The second plan with join order b->a will fail the assertion `assert(!vector.state->isFlat());` in `FactorizedTable::appendUnFlatVectorToOverflowBlocks` due to that `b` is flatten during runtime.

title: Remove Graph and move its contents to System
Remove the rewriting variable as projecting all proerties in WITH clause
body:
Example query:
`MATCH (a:person)-[e1:knows]->(b:person) WITH b AS d MATCH (d)-[e2:knows]->(c:person) RETURN COUNT(*)`

In the example query, currently the enumerator will treat WITH clause the same as RETURN clause, and rewrites the variable as projecting all properties (`b` -> `b.id, b.fName, b.gender, b.isStudent, b.isWorker, b.age, b.eyeSight, b.birthdate, b.unstrProp1, b.unstrProp2, ...`), adding property scan operators.
However, this can lead to lots of unnecessary scans and should be avoided either by adding a post-optimization to remove useless scans, or only rewrite the variable to scan its internal system id property.
The former one can lead to lots of operator creations/removing, which seems unnecessary. We can choose the latter approach, which can also simplify other optimizations on the plan tree.

title: Fix alias rewriting in binder and unify the usage of alias, variableName and rawExpression in Expression
body:
Example query:
`MATCH (a:person)-[e1:knows]->(b:person) WITH b AS d, a.age * 2.0 AS foo MATCH (d)-[e2:knows]->(c:person) WHERE foo = c.age * 2.0 RETURN COUNT(*)`

1. In the example query, the binder will always rewrite alias (d, foo) as original expressions (b, a.age * 2.0), so alias is removed after binding, which is not the right way to do it.
2. Currently, Expression has three public members, including `variableName`, `alias` and `rawExpression` that can be used during mapping. Sometimes it is confusing to choose the correct one as the expression name. There should be a unified interface/member to serve that purpose.

title: remove getDataType() specialized functions from Column/Lists
Unnecessary Scans/Reads -> Extra I/O
body:
Consider the following query:

MATCH (a)-e1->(b)
RETURN e1.time;

Currently, we consider two possible QVOs [a, b] and therefore generate two plans:
```
P1: Scan(a) → Extend(b) → ScanEdgeProperty(e1.time) → Project([e1.time])
```
OR
```
P2: Scan(b) → Extend(a) → ScanEdgeProperty(e1.time) → Project([e1.time])
```

The extension to (b) comes from the fact that we tend to cover all of the query edges and vertices blindly regardless of what the query actually requests. The two plans should actually be:   
```
P1: Scan(a) → ScanEdgeProperty(e1.time) → Project([e1.time])
```
OR
```
P2: Scan(b) → ScanEdgeProperty(e1.time) → Project([e1.time])
```


In other cases, where we don’t actually need any properties all together, we should simply get the size from the Lists header and therefore not pin/unpin unnecessarily. The query:

MATCH (a)-e1->(b)
RETURN count(*);

Should generate:
```
P1: Scan(a) → GetListSize(e1) → GROUP BY (COUNT(*))
P1: Scan(b) → GetListSize(e1) → GROUP BY (COUNT(*))
```
We need to be more aware of the actual properties needed. ID is just another property we do a join on.

title: Simple Hash Table for Hash Join
body:
The goal of this issue is to introduce a simple non-parallel hash table for future integration with hash join. A parallel version is gonna be extended based on this implementation.

#### Storage Layout
The storage of a simple hash table is divided into two parts: tuple blocks (`htBlocks`) and directory (`htDirectory`).
Tuple blocks hold all materialized tuples, and the directory contains slots with pointers. Inside tuple blocks, each tuple reserves a pointer space pointing to a previous tuple within the same hash slot, in this way, we implement a chain-based collision handling.
For each tuple, the storage layout is: `|key|payloads|prev|`.
Inside the tuple payloads, we might have variable-length items, whose content will be stored separately in the `overflowBlocks`.

#### Materialization of build side tuples
Hash (based on the join key) can happen on both a flat vector and a list. For the join key, we only consider equality of nodeID for now (no join on property values, and no multiple join conditions).

**Query example for join on a flat vector**: `(a)->(b)->(c)->(d)->(e) WHERE a.id=1 AND e.id=1`. this is a bidirectional query, hash join happens on `c.id`. and the build side is the subquery `(a)->(b)->(c)`. which starts from `SCAN(a)`, then `EXTEND(b)` and `EXTEND(c)`. thus, c might be a list chunk.
**Query example for join on a list**: `(a)->(b)->(c), (b)->(d)->(e)`. the hash join happens on `b.id`, and the build side is the subquery `(a)->(b)->(c)` , which starts from `SCAN(a)`, then `EXTEND(b)`. thus, `b` might be a flat chunk.

During materialization, there are two cases for a list chunk:
- if it's the key, we would duplicate tuples in build chunks;
- else, each list vector is treated as a variable-sized value in the tuple.

#### Interface
Currently, the hash table only supports hash on a single NodeID field, and we assume this is the main usage scenario for hash join, too.
```c++
    HashTable(MemoryManager& memoryManager, vector<PayloadInfo>& payloadInfos);
    // add a DataChunks into the hash table
    void addDataChunks(
        DataChunk& keyDataChunk, uint64_t keyVectorIdx, DataChunks& payloadDataChunks);
    // initialize and construct the hash table: allocate the HT directory
    void buildHTDirectory();
```

**Usage example:**
```c++
...
    while (right->hasNextMorsel()) {
        // fetch all data chunks from the right side, and add to ht
        right->getNextTuples();
        hashTable->addDataChunks(*rightKeyDataChunk, 0, buildDataChunks);
    }
    hashTable->buildHTDirectory();
...
```

#### Memory Management
Large intermediate memory allocation and de-allocation should be managed by a unified memory manager, which is separate from our buffer manager for now.
The memory manager can limit the usage of memory under a specified `maxMemory` size.
If the allocation is beyond the limit, the memory manager should perform one of the following:
- throw an exception, which will be caught by the server and kill the current query gracefully. 
- evict unused memory blocks, and allow spilling to disk.

Currently, we add a simple memory manager, which is only responsible for allocating memory blocks (the releasing is done by the requester through deconstructing the block handle), if the allocation is beyond the max memory size limit, an exception will be thrown.

**DO NOT USE THIS MEMORY MANAGER FOR OTHER OPERATORS FOR NOW**
A more advanced one will be integrated later and described in a separate issue.
